name: Alaska Beacon
title: After years of problems, Alaska plans to outsource payroll for 14,000 public employees
description: By the end of 2027, as many as 14,000 Alaska state workers could be paid by someone outside the state. After years of trouble within the payroll department within the Alaska Department of Administration, the agency is planning to outsource the state’s public employee payroll to an outside company. Proposals from interested companies were due […]
text:
The Alaska State Office Building in Juneau, the state capital, is seen on Feb. 16, 2023. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)By the end of 2027, as many as 14,000 Alaska state workers could be paid by someone outside the state.
After years of trouble within the payroll department within the Alaska Department of Administration, the agency is planning to outsource the state’s public employee payroll to an outside company.
Proposals from interested companies were due Thursday, and in an internal letter, DOA Commissioner Paula Vrana said “it likely will be several weeks before a final decision is made.”
Vrana implied that if the proposals aren’t affordable or are otherwise unfavorable, the state will not proceed with outsourcing. 
“As of now, we are exploring what options are available to the state and what value may be realized by this approach,” she wrote. “The final decision will be based on the proposals we receive.”
Vrana wrote that the department will begin talking with unions “to explore the options for transfers/placements of employees displaced by outsourcing” and if DOA does choose to outsource, “we will also work with the vendor to include as many existing state payroll employees as possible in their staffing plan.”
The state’s payroll department has struggled with staffing issues for years, leading to times when employees missed paychecks or encountered other problems with their pay. 
In April, DOA published a request for information from companies that might be interested in providing “comprehensive payroll processing” for the state.
A three-page feasibility study dated Sept. 28 states that payroll work involves 78 employees in different agencies; all would be affected by outsourcing.
According to the state’s formal request for proposals, it is prepared to pay $4 million per year for a company to handle payroll. It currently spends about $10 million per year on payroll employees and functions, the feasibility study stated. 
According to the study, in fiscal year 2025, state employees filed more than 1,500 “notice of pay problem” reports, and reducing the number of problems could make employees in other departments happier.
The first outsourced paychecks would come to a handful of departments on April 1, 2027, and other departments would be transferred to the outsourced payroll company through the rest of the year.
The outsourcing company would have to use the state’s existing payroll software programs, the document states, and the work would have to be done in the United States, but the contractor could get a waiver from the state that would allow payroll work to be done in a foreign country.
“The goal is not to change the system used to process payroll but to make payroll processing more efficient and ensure the state’s existing systems and processes are supported by qualified contracted professionals who can maintain continuity, reduce errors, and uphold the state’s obligations to its employees and the public,” the document states.
DOA provided a copy of the RFP documents to the Beacon this week; they were not previously published on the state’s public notice system, and the two public employee unions whose members would be affected by the outsourcing said they also had not previously seen the documents.
The Beacon asked DOA for an interview with Vrana or someone else involved with the outsourcing decision but was turned down.
In response to a written question asking why the department is planning to outsource, a spokesperson said by email: “Ensuring that employees are paid correctly and on time is the essential duty of payroll. Challenges stemming from high turnover and persistent vacancies within the Department have resulted in pay problems for some state employees. The administration has determined that outsourcing payroll may both provide significant recurring cost-savings to the State and improve services to its employees. However, no final decision on outsourcing payroll will be made until responses to the RFP issued earlier are evaluated.”
Jeff Kasper is the business manager of the Alaska Public Employees Association, which represents payroll workers. He’s not a fan of outsourcing. 
“It usually costs more and doesn’t provide the efficiencies that you’re looking for. When you’re talking about public services, you’re essentially having the public pay more for something that’s probably not as good,” he said. 
Kasper isn’t convinced that the Department of Administration has done enough to fix the problems that have deterred Alaskans from working for the payroll department.
“If people aren’t applying for jobs and accepting jobs, it’s usually because it doesn’t pay enough or it doesn’t provide benefits or it’s bad working conditions. This one could be all three, and I don’t think any of them have been addressed,” he said.
The state’s own feasibility study acknowledged those problems.
“Payroll processing occurs on a bi-weekly basis and does not have down time. This work environment and the entry level pay range are likely reasons for low retention and high staff turnover,” the study concluded.
As of last month, the study said, 58% of all payroll positions in the state are vacant, and it can take as long as a year of training before a new worker is capable of working independently.
MaryAnn Ganacias is the interim executive director of the Alaska State Employees Association, whose members are paid by the payroll department. 
“Alaskans deserve to know what the problem is with the state and what they’re trying to solve by privatizing payroll,” she said. 
Ganacias said state money spent outside Alaska is money that doesn’t benefit Alaskans.
“We need to do better investing in our own employees here in Alaska, and not outsourcing where the money actually goes,” she said.
Kasper said he doesn’t think the timeline described in the state’s RFP follows collective bargaining agreements or is realistic.
“The union’s not just gonna sit down and let this happen,” he said. “We don’t think the state has been following the process that’s in the contract.”
Kasper said his union’s contract with the state requires a 30-day consultation period before any outsourcing takes place, and even though the state’s RFP calls for a contract in November, he doesn’t think one is likely before Gov. Mike Dunleavy leaves office in the first week of December. 
Kate Sheehan, policy adviser for the Department of Administration, said by email in response to Kasper’s comments, “The State engaged the Confidential Employees Association (CEA) on September 25th, and we have entered into the 30-day period for the union to submit any alternate plans to be considered during this process. DOA does not intend to contract out prior to the Union’s response and analysis of their input.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mike Minogue talks Medicaid cuts, primary care spending, and immigration impacts on the health care workforce
description: Minogue, who spent 19 years as CEO of Abiomed, the Danvers-based heart pump company, joined hosts John McDonough of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Paul Hattis of the Lown Institute on this month's Health or Consequences podcast.
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Paul Hattis & John McDonough
GUESTS: Mike Minogue, former chairman, president, and CEO of Abiomed and Republican candidate for governor of Massachusetts






MIKE MINOGUE, THE REPUBLICAN mega-donor and candidate for governor, said this week he supports the concept of a legislative push to raise the share of health insurance spending on primary care — but worries that the state could find itself scrambling to funnel more and more money into the health care space unless costs can be controlled. 
Minogue, who spent 19 years as CEO of Abiomed, the Danvers-based heart pump company, joined hosts John McDonough of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Paul Hattis of the Lown Institute on this month’s Health or Consequences podcast. (Gov. Maura Healey’s office did not respond to the show’s invitation to appear.) 
A primary care taskforce and the state Senate have endorsed requiring insurers to raise primary care spending from roughly 7 to 8 percent of premiums today to 15 percent over several years. Minogue questioned whether the mandate would simply shift money from one part of the health care system to another without addressing underlying costs. 
“Instead of a problem solved, you take a piece of pie from someone and give it to someone else,” he said. “I haven’t seen that work in health care. The way I like it is, let’s get rid of some of the waste and fraud.” 
Minogue, who has rolled out a “Patients First” campaign platform, pointed to pharmacy benefit managers as one target, arguing that PBMs have financial incentives to keep patients on brand-name drugs rather than cheaper generics, costing the state hundreds of millions of dollars. 
On the Trump administration’s so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s Medicaid cuts — which the Congressional Budget Office projects will cause 326,000 low-income Massachusetts residents to lose coverage and cost the state $2 billion a year in federal revenue — Minogue said he opposes anyone losing health care. His proposed response focused largely on administrative fixes: a 1-800 number and multilingual website to help Medicaid enrollees navigate new work requirements before they lose coverage. 
McDonough noted that about 7,500 documented legal immigrants were set to lose MassHealth, the state’s Medicaid coverage, on October 1. Trump administration restrictions on visas could make closing physicians and nurses staffing shortage more difficult, he said.   
Minogue did not address the MassHealth population directly, and said the state could “have incentives for people to stay here.”  
He mentioned Temporary Protected Status as a lawful way for people to be in the country. The Trump administration has been aggressively rolling back TPS status for many of the countries that support the health care workforce.  
Minogue noted that mental health needs are a significant strain on the system, touting work by the Michael & Renee Minogue Foundation on homelessness and addiction services. 
“We are not ready for the mental health crisis,” he said. “And I look at the mental health crisis as a health care issue, because what a lot of people do for care is they go to that emergency room. That emergency room is the most expensive, least compassionate, and efficient way to treat them.” 
On the Health Policy Commission, the independent state agency focused on health care affordability, Minogue declined to propose specific changes.  
“Well, I haven’t been on the inside,” he said, but “what I would say is that the results are the results. We have the most expensive [commercial] health care in America. We have the longest [emergency room] wait times on record since we’ve been tracking in the Boston ERs.” Those sorts of realities, he said, mean “we need to do something different.” 
He said he would seek a shared savings model agreement with federal health officials, where the state establishes a benchmark budget and works to manage care more efficiently. If the state spends below that agreed-upon baseline, the resulting “savings” are split between the federal government and the state. Minogue said he would push to keep 80 percent of any savings generated. 
When Hattis pressed him on hospital market consolidation, which state data has consistently linked to higher prices, Minogue said he would push large systems to expand into communities through surgery centers and clinics, reducing pressure on Boston hospitals.  
Minogue also addressed the state’s individual health insurance mandate, the mechanism that has helped keep Massachusetts’s uninsurance rate at 2 to 3 percent, the lowest in the country, for 20 years. He said he wouldn’t commit to supporting or opposing it without more study. 
“In concept I agree with it — that people should pay something for health insurance,” he said. “The problem is who pays and makes up the difference. There’s a reason we’re the most expensive health care in the country.” 
On the episode, McDonough, Hattis, and Minogue discuss primary care spending mandates (7:30), the Medicaid cliff (13:00), hospital consolidation (20:00), and the Massachusetts individual mandate (26:30).
Health or Consequences has launched as its own podcast feed, featuring the same in-depth health policy conversations you’ve come to expect from The Codcast. Follow hosts Health or Consequences on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and YouTube to get notified of new episodes.

title: DNR fines companies for littering, fish kill, excessive air and wastewater emissions
description: The Iowa Department of Natural Resources is levying thousands of dollars in fines against companies that violated various environmental regulations.  Consent orders published by DNR show a landfill in Winnebago County was fined the department’s maximum of $10,000 in multiple instances for failing to contain litter. An iron foundry in Jefferson County also re[...]
text:
(Main image by Peter Dazeley/Getty Images; DNR insignia courtesy State of Iowa)The Iowa Department of Natural Resources is levying thousands of dollars in fines against companies that violated various environmental regulations. 
Consent orders published by DNR show a landfill in Winnebago County was fined the department’s maximum of $10,000 in multiple instances for failing to contain litter. An iron foundry in Jefferson County also received the maximum administrative penalty for failing to test air emissions, as did an agricultural rendering facility for discharging wastewater to the city with pollutants above its permitted amounts. 
DNR also entered a consent agreement and fined the agricultural business Chem Gro for spilling a diluted pesticide mixture in June that resulted in a fish kill of 1,792 fish in an unnamed creek near Houghton. Chem Gro has agreed to pay a $5,000 administrative penalty and $2,157 in fish restitution.
Landfill
DNR published three consent orders with Central Disposal Systems, Inc., of Winnebago County for a violation in May 2025 and two incidents in February 2026 where the solid waste landfill was not adequately covered, causing litter outside of working areas and outside of the landfill.
According to the consent orders, DNR had a previous consent order with Central Disposal Systems in March 2025 addressing violations of daily cover requirements. Landfills are required to have six inches of daily “cover” or earthen materials that go on top of the solid waste materials. 
In May 2025, the landfill ceased operations due to high wind and DNR observed “off-site litter along the ditches and fields” near the landfill several days later. DNR informed the company it was in violation of the consent order to apply daily cover and control litter. Central Disposal agreed to a $10,000 administrative penalty. 
In February 2026, DNR received a complaint from a neighbor of the landfill that alleged litter from the landfill was entering his yard and cattle barn. DNR investigated and reported off-site litter in fields and ditches near the landfill and “an extensive amount” of litter on-site but away from the working area of the landfill. DNR fined Central Disposal $10,000 administrative fees for violations on Feb. 18 and Feb. 20. 
Air emissions
HyCast Foundry, an iron casting foundry in Fairfield signed a consent order with DNR agreeing to test the emissions on certain furnace stacks, submit the test results to DNR and to pay a $10,000 penalty. 
According to the consent order, DNR alleged HyCast gained an economic benefit by operating the plant while in violation of National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants, or NESHAP, requirements and delaying stack testing.

The consent order explains that DNR requested information from HyCast, which bought the facility in 2024 and began operations in 2025, about emissions testing on induction furnace stacks at the facility. 
According to the consent agreement, HyCast told DNR it would inform the department and complete stack testing prior to restarting the equipment, but a DNR inspection of the facility several months later revealed the stacks were in operation. 
At the beginning of the year, DNR issued a notice of violation for operating the furnaces in violation of the NESHAP permit, and required HyCast to test the stack emissions by March 2026. 
By May, HyCast revealed it had tested the stacks and that the emissions were above the emission standards, but wouldn’t share the results with DNR. Finally, in June, HyCast submitted the results which showed particulate matter results in excess of 8 pounds per ton. The limit for an existing iron and steel foundry, according to code cited in the consent order, is 0.8 pounds of particulate matter per ton of metal charged. 
The company is required to conduct stack testing by Nov. 1 and submit results to DNR, in addition to paying the fine.
Rendering facility fined for wastewater discharges 
Central Bi-Products, a pork rendering facility in Estherville owned by Farmers Union Industries, agreed to a $10,000 administration penalty from the department for violating its agreement with the city wastewater treatment plant by discharging excessive volumes or quantities of wastewater. 
According to the consent order, Central Bi-Products has been served a number of notices of violation from DNR since 2021 for the same issue. 
In August 2025, the consent order reports that construction at the facility led to a broken wastewater line. Repairs to the line resulted in a backup of wastewater in the facility’s basement, which caused some wastewater to leak into a tile drainage line running underneath the facility. 
The tile line discharged to a neighboring pond, where DNR staff observed “a white greasy film” and a “foul, rotten odor.” Central Bi-Products produces bone, blood meal and yellow grease, according to the consent order. 
DNR said that after the discharge into the pond, the company made “significant efforts to address the release.” As part of the consent order, the company is required to submit the results of an engineer’s investigation into the sources of the discharge. 
In March 2026, DNR again issued a notice of violation to the company for its discharge of wastewater to the city treatment plant and for “the prohibited discharge to a Water of the State.” 
DNR said the facility’s “ongoing non-compliance” and “failure” to implement the necessary pretreatment upgrades and to “comply with treatment agreement limits risks” has “compromised” the City of Estherville wastewater treatment facility.
“Such conduct may result in (National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System) permit violations and subsequent degradation of water quality, posing a risk to both the receiving water body and public health,” the consent order said. 
Central-Bi Products is required to either comply with its treatment agreement or negotiate higher treatment agreement limits with the city within 30 days of the order, in addition to paying the $10,000 fine.

title: Removing federal protections for wolves would be catastrophic

text:
A gray wolf prowls the winter forest (Photo courtesy of National Park Service)President Donald Trump recently issued an executive order that seeks to sacrifice wolves to placate farmers and ranchers for h
President Donald Trump recently issued an executive order that seeks to sacrifice wolves to placate farmers and ranchers for his tariff policy. This order is nothing more than smoke and mirrors, and it’s obvious that it won’t make a real difference for ranchers and farmers who are struggling.  
The executive order gives the U.S. interior secretary 90 days to decide whether to remove Endangered Species Act protections for gray wolves and Mexican wolves in the United States. The order also calls for Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to prepare a legislative recommendation for Trump to fully delist or downlist wolves and, upon determination that recovery criteria have been met, encourage states to delist wolves and revise state standards for the killing of wolves in order to help ranchers. 
In other words, though it does not immediately remove federal protections for wolves, it’s clearly intended to provide momentum for either Congress or the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to do so. 
Delisting would be catastrophic for Minnesota’s wolves, which would almost certainly face trophy hunting and recreational trapping seasons. Such killing rips wolf families apart, as studies show that killing just one wolf can lead to the dissolution of the pack and the deaths of other members. 
When Minnesota’s wolves were delisted in 2011, more than 900 were killed in just three seasons. Nearly half of the wolves were killed using steel-jawed leghold traps or strangling snares. When wolves were delisted again in 2020, Minnesota held off on a hunt until the state could update its wolf management plan. Prior to the finalization of that plan, a federal judge overturned the delisting decision, and wolves were again federally protected as “threatened” in Minnesota.  
If wolves are delisted again, however, the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources would very likely propose a hunting and trapping season. There have also been attempts in the Legislature to require the state to hold a wolf season if they are delisted. 
To be clear, Minnesota farmers experience very few conflicts with wolves. According to the state Department of Natural Resources, only 2% of livestock farms in parts of the state where wolves live experience confirmed conflicts each year. For those who do experience conflict, nonlethal tools like fencing, guardian dogs and removing attractants are the best way to prevent conflicts and reduce the vulnerability of farmed animals.  
A cattle ranch near Voyageurs National Park is a perfect example of the efficacy of non-lethal tools. There, the Voyageurs Wolf Project with the University of Minnesota has documented that a 7.5-mile fence has effectively prevented any conflicts since 2023 on a farm that is at the center of multiple wolf pack territories.  
The state provides grants and expertise to help farmers implement nonlethal tools, and USDA Wildlife Services staff have also found success in Minnesota with those deterrence methods. Although studies demonstrate that killing wolves does not solve conflicts, the fact that they are listed in Minnesota as “threatened” under the federal Endangered Species Act means that officials already can — and do — kill wolves in response to conflicts. 
According to the USDA, most livestock losses are caused by bad weather, respiratory issues and disease, or birthing problems. But you can’t kill the weather, so it is easier to blame wolves.  
It is likewise easier to pin culpability on wolves for perceived reductions in the deer and moose populations. Yet, as researchers with Voyageurs Wolf Project pointed out in 2023, “Hunting wolves won’t save Bambi.” Deer fawn survival rates in Minnesota are on par with rates elsewhere, including places without wolves. The scientific consensus is that wolves are not a main factor limiting deer populations and that killing them won’t increase deer abundance.  
The same facts pertain when it comes to Minnesota’s moose population, which has been stable for more than a decade; studies have indicated that parasites, climate change and other factors pose the biggest threats.  
Wolves keep deer and moose herds healthy by preying on weak or otherwise compromised animals who would likely die from other natural causes. Wolves also play a critical role in mitigating the spread of disease in prey species. Recent studies also show that wolves can reduce deer-vehicle collisions by altering deer movements, saving lives and dollars. 
Delisting a species is not just about numbers. Wolves face many threats to recovery, including poaching, habitat loss and state agencies bowing to pressure from trophy hunters and recreational trappers.  
Minnesota needs wolves and Minnesotans value them. Polls conducted by both chambers of the legislature at the 2023 Minnesota State Fair found that more people oppose wolf hunting than support it. A 2019 study by the state in partnership with the University of Minnesota found that 86% of Minnesotans want to maintain the wolf population at its current level or higher.  
Keeping federal protections in place is our first line of defense against trophy hunting and recreational trapping, and our members of Congress and officials at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service must hear that message from us. At the same time, we must remain vigilant here in Minnesota to ensure that if wolves do lose their federal protections, we keep them out of the crosshairs of those who view these highly intelligent, family-oriented animals solely as trophies or pelts or the objects of misplaced fears and irrational hatred who deserve to be killed.

name: VTDigger
title: The first to finish: Carter Smith’s Curtis Fund story
description:
Affordability shaped Carter Smith’s college search. A Curtis Fund scholarship made Norwich University possible, breaking a family pattern in which money had cut education short. Now studying accounting, Carter hopes to build his career in Vermont, close to family and the community he knows.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The first to finish: Carter Smith[...]
text:
Carter Smith worked as much as he could last summer and saved every extra dollar. He has a scholarship, but he still keeps a backup fund. When money has been tight your whole life, you do not stop worrying just because the numbers look better on paper. “I’ve always been very financially focused,” he says. “Maybe even to a fault.” 
That did not come from nowhere. Carter is the oldest child. His parents were young when he was born, and money was tight throughout his childhood. He learned early to watch what he spent, plan for gaps, and not assume things would hold. 
When it was time to choose a college, Carter ran the numbers. He compared community colleges, state schools, and private schools by price. Norwich University was out of reach. “Price and how much I was going to spend were huge factors,” he says. “That was just the reality.” 
Carter is not the first in his family to want a degree, but finishing one has been harder. His stepdad dropped out. His stepdad’s father did too. Money was part of the reason both times. Carter getting to Norwich on a Curtis Fund scholarship and staying there is a real shift for his family. 
Then the Curtis Fund scholarship came through. Carter could choose a school that gave him the best chance at the kind of life he wanted, not just one that fit his budget. “Having that freedom of choice was an amazing feeling,” he says. “Just being able to say: I can actually afford to do this.” 
So he picked Norwich. The accounting program gives him a path he’s excited to pursue, and he’s found people and opportunities he would not have found at another school. 
Chelsea, his VSAC counselor, helped him through the applications. Without her, Carter isn’t sure he would have made it to college at all. He knows not everyone gets that kind of support. One friend had to drop out when the money ran out. Another never even started because the numbers did not add up. The Curtis Fund’s support meant Carter did not have to make that choice. 
He’s in accounting because numbers have always made sense to him. One of his professors works with local businesses, and Carter has seen what that work looks like: helping someone keep a business going after they built it from scratch. “I’d like to help the people who are trying to start their own business and make their own life,” Carter says. 
He plans to stay in central Vermont after graduation. His family and friends are here, and he is building connections through Norwich. He likes the scale of the state and the way communities know each other. “I really enjoy the small, tight-knit community,” he says. For Carter, practical and personal reasons are closely linked. 
The Curtis Fund awards over 600 degree scholarships each year to Vermonters like Carter, and another 250 scholarships to students pursuing credentials through short-term professional training programs. Since 1910, more than 14,000 Vermonters have been able to pursue post-secondary education because of it. For the Smith family, that number just went up by one.

To read more stories about Curtis Fund scholars, visit: https://www.thecurtisfund.org/meet-the-scholars 
Learn more about how to support Vermont students like Carter: https://www.thecurtisfund.org/donate#give-now

name: Michigan Advance
title: Care and Costs: What can be done about the price of healthcare?
description: The feeling that affordability is just out of reach is everywhere. It shows up in childcare, housing, utilities, food, and, of course, healthcare. Ask five people what a specific medical procedure would cost them, whether an MRI, open heart surgery or having a baby, and you’ll get five different answers, or most likely, “Who knows!” […]
text:
Getty ImagesThe feeling that affordability is just out of reach is everywhere. It shows up in childcare, housing, utilities, food, and, of course, healthcare.
Ask five people what a specific medical procedure would cost them, whether an MRI, open heart surgery or having a baby, and you’ll get five different answers, or most likely, “Who knows!” What you owe depends on your plan type, monthly premium plus your deductible, copays, and coinsurance. Don’t forget to factor in the unique rate agreements and discounts every insurer and health system negotiate. When it comes to the cost of care, “it depends” is probably the most specific answer you’ll find.
That uncertainty is hard enough. Rising premiums make it harder. As coverage gets pricier, more people choose high-deductible or limited-benefit plans, or drop coverage altogether. This year, ACA marketplace enrollment fell for the first time in seven years. In Michigan, people covered through the individual marketplace declined by more than 130,000 between 2025 and 2026. That drop coincided with the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits, which made marketplace coverage significantly more affordable, after Congress declined to extend them.
Health insurance is a sort of “green light” for accessing care and an important form of financial protection. Without it, people tend to put off checkups, prescriptions and screenings. A recent KFF survey found that even across insurance statuses, delaying or avoiding care because of cost concerns is most prevalent among women.
Take prescription medication as just one example of how fears about cost affect health outcomes. Going without the medication that helps manage a chronic condition such as diabetes or high blood pressure makes that management harder, and, later, treatment more expensive. A few weeks back, I picked up a prescription that cost me $2 but would have cost $143 if I had not had health insurance.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Coverage protecting people from steeper costs is most evident when we look at declines in medical debt after Michigan expanded Medicaid. Nationally, about 1 in 12 adults has more than $250 in medical debt. In Michigan, the rate is approximately 1 in 11. Although medical debt affects both the insured and uninsured, data shows that those without health coverage disproportionately carry the burden. Recent efforts to forgive Michiganders’ medical debt are likely to most benefit middle-aged and younger adults who, in a 2025 survey, reported having the greatest share of medical debt.
Health insurance isn’t a fix for high healthcare prices, but it can keep one unexpected diagnosis from becoming years of debt.
Ask why healthcare in the U.S. costs so much and you’ll either get another “Who knows!” or you’ll get an earful: an older, sicker population, rising labor costs, consolidation, new drugs and technology…. There’s disagreement about which contributes most to our high costs, but what’s clear is that this burden of high costs is shared. For example, most privately insured people get their coverage through their job, where employers pay a share of the plan cost. This means premium increases affect employers and employees alike. Hospitals absorb costs too. When someone without an ability to pay seeks emergency care, providers are required to stabilize them. But that unpaid bill becomes uncompensated care, which over time erodes operating margins and strains hospital finances.
High healthcare costs do not exist in a vacuum; the financial fallout of a strained budget ripples across the entire system.
Despite the clear value of health coverage and the need to tackle underlying price drivers, federal policy changes — such as the Medicaid eligibility restrictions enacted under the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — confuse reducing coverage with reducing costs.
iStock / Getty Images Plus
Medicaid is a more than 61-year-old state-federal partnership serving more than 2.4 million Michigan residents. As of August 2026, more than 650,000 Michigan adults have coverage through Medicaid expansion. The successes of Michigan’s expansion program are numerous and include increasing access to routine healthcare, reducing use of emergency services, and reducing uncompensated care and medical debt.
Yet instead of building on these successes, federal law enacted in 2025 will reduce federal Medicaid spending, largely by adding new requirements for adults to keep Medicaid coverage. Work reporting requirements, more frequent eligibility checks, narrower eligibility for some lawfully present immigrants and other federal changes have been framed as protecting program integrity. In reality, these changes increase the likelihood that eligible people will lose coverage and increase state administrative costs by asking caseworkers to process more paperwork more often. Making Medicaid harder to access is not a strategy for lowering healthcare costs. Rather, it will leave more people uninsured while leaving the causes of high costs untouched.
There are solutions, though. At the federal level, restoring the enhanced premium tax credits that lapsed at the start of this year would be one of the most direct ways to improve marketplace affordability and stability. Closer to home, several proposals are moving through the Michigan Legislature. Price transparency, medical debt protections, investment in primary care, prescription drug price reforms and a Basic Health Program are just a handful of state strategies aiming to address the high price of care or protect people from its consequences. None depend on taking coverage away from someone who qualifies.
Managing our health is something we all face, sometimes without warning: a sick-kid visit when the high fever just won’t quit, an urgent care trip to find out whether that fall caused a break or a sprain, or finally deciding it’s time to talk with a professional about your mental health. When those moments come, the first question should not be, Can I afford to get help? Lowering costs and keeping people covered aren’t competing goals. We need both.

name: Nevada Current
title: Nevada Health Link plans will see double-digit rate increases… again
description: Health care costs are continuing to rise. Nevadans who get insurance through Nevada Health Link, the state-based Affordable Care Act marketplace, can expect to see an average rate increase of 17% for 2027 coverage. The Nevada Division of Insurance announced the approval of the rate increases last week. It marks the second year of double-digit […]
text:
(Nevada Health Link video screengrab)Health care costs are continuing to rise.
Nevadans who get insurance through Nevada Health Link, the state-based Affordable Care Act marketplace, can expect to see an average rate increase of 17% for 2027 coverage. The Nevada Division of Insurance announced the approval of the rate increases last week.
It marks the second year of double-digit rate increases for Nevadans who secure their insurance through the state-based marketplace and not an employer, Medicaid, or Medicare.
Open enrollment will begin Nov. 1 and run through Jan. 15, 2027. In preparation, Nevadans can compare plan options and determine their eligibility for subsidies at NevadaHealthLink.com.
More than 100,000 Nevadans get health insurance through the marketplace. Most receive a federal tax credit that lowers their premium.
Nevada Health Authority (NVHA) representatives last month during a meeting of the Economic Forum said approximately 82% of 2026 enrollees received credits. While still a majority of enrolled consumers, that percentage is lower than it used to be after Republicans blocked Democratic efforts to extend existing premium discounts in late 2025.
NVHA said the average monthly out-of-pocket premium cost for Health Link plans in 2026 is $234 after subsidies and $659 before subsidies.
For 2027 coverage, 12 companies will offer 165 plans, both on and off the exchange, according to the Nevada DOI. This includes the state’s public-option, called Battle Born State Plans, which 1 in 10 marketplace enrollees have opted for.
Nationally, rates for ACA plans are expected to increase by 15% or higher, according to KFF.
Off-exchange rates will see an average rate change of 10.9%.
According to Marsh, a global professional services firm, employer health care costs are expected to rise 8.2% on average in 2027, “even after accounting for planned cost-reduction measures.” That’s the highest increase since 2003, the firm noted.
Last year, Nevada Health Link plan rates jumped 26%, driven by inflation and the expiration of the federal subsidies. State data shows 10% of consumers downgraded their plans — moving from their existing plan to a lower-premium one.
For example, approximately 9,100 consumers moved from a “silver” to a “bronze” plan for 2026 coverage, compared to 1,300 the prior year.
Silver and bronze plans make up the majority of plans selected by enrollees — 56% and 40%, respectively.
Insurance cancellations due to non-payment increased by 40% as of June 2026 compared to the prior year. That translates to about 13,000 individuals leaving the marketplace, or a 6% decline in enrollment.
Health officials are anticipating more people will drop off next year, potentially upwards of 12.5%. That, combined with new federal work requirements affecting Medicaid eligibility, are expected to lead to Nevada’s uninsured rate increasing.
But they are attempting to emphasize to the public the importance of staying insured.
“I remain very sensitive to the fact that once again rates are increasing. During this time of increased inflation, every dollar counts,” said Nevada Insurance Commissioner Ned Gaines. “I urge all Nevadans who purchase their health insurance on the Exchange to fully analyze each product offering to find the best option for you and to take advantage of all subsidies available. The cost of coverage can be high but the cost of not having coverage is potentially higher should you encounter an unexpected illness or injury.”

title: Judge up for fifth term on Clark County bench
description: Eighth Judicial District Court Judge Michelle Leavitt is seeking a fifth term on the bench, as she faces a challenge from Clark County public defender Dan Gillium. Leavitt has retained the Department 12 seat for more than two decades after first being appointed by former Gov. Kenny Guinn in 2002. Before that, Leavitt  was appointed […]
text:
Michelle Leavitt, Dan Gillium. (Candidate photos)Eighth Judicial District Court Judge Michelle Leavitt is seeking a fifth term on the bench, as she faces a challenge from Clark County public defender Dan Gillium.
Leavitt has retained the Department 12 seat for more than two decades after first being appointed by former Gov. Kenny Guinn in 2002. Before that, Leavitt  was appointed by the Las Vegas City Council to fill a vacancy on the Municipal Court, where she was re-elected twice.
She graduated from the University of Las Vegas, Nevada in 1987 and received her law degree from California Western School in 1994. 
As a district court judge, Leavitt handles both criminal and civil cases. In an interview with Our Nevada Judges, Leavitt said she typically deals with the most serious criminal offenses, including homicide. 
Her error rate, or the rate of overturned decisions, for civil cases is 39.24% while her error rate for criminal cases is 12.47%, according to Our Nevada Judges. 
Leavitt earned a 74.2% retention rating from attorneys who participated in the Las Vegas Review-Journal Judging the Judges 2025 survey. The retention rate represents the percentage of attorneys who affirmed a judge should stay on the bench. 
Leavitt has handled several high profile homicide cases, the most recent being the 2022 murder of local journalist Jeff German by former elected Clark County official Robert Telles. 
Her opponent, Guillium, has worked in the Clark County Public Defender’s office since 2021. He attended Ohio State University where he received his undergraduate degree in education in 1996, and his law degree in 2004.   
He worked in the Clark County Public Defender’s office from 2005 to 2007, but left to practice as an assistant city attorney in the City of Henderson, where he mostly worked on misdemeanors. 
In that role, Guillium also helped train new Henderson Police Department recruits on search and seizure laws and probable cause requirements, Guillium said in an interview with Vegas Legal Magazine. 
He left the City of Henderson in 2014 to open his own practice, the Gilliam Law Group. His law firm was merged with multi-jurisdictional law firm Bighorn Law in 2018, where he handles criminal defense cases. 
Gilliam unsuccessfully ran for Eighth Judicial District Court Judge Department 24 in the 2020 general election after advancing in the primary. 
As of July, Gilliam reported contributions of $15,000 and had $6,200 on hand. His largest contributors were his own law firm and Jacqueline Bretell, who shares the same address as his law firm, according to financial disclosures. They each donated the max contribution of $10,000. 
For the same period, Leavitt reported she’d raised more than $91,000 and had roughly $131,000 on hand.  Her largest donors were the Hutchinson & Steffen law firm, the Eglet Adams law firm, the Sahara Center, and Senior Vice President and General Manager of Boyd Gaming John Sou. Each donated the max contribution of $10,000. 
Leavitt has been endorsed by several unions including, SEIU Local 1107, Bartenders Local 165, and Culinary Workers Union Local 226. 
She’s also been endorsed by various law enforcement groups including, the Nevada Association of Public Safety Officers, the Washoe County Sheriff Deputies Association, and the Las Vegas Peace Officers Association.  
Gilliam did not list any endorsements on his campaign website. 
Neither candidate responded to Nevada Current’s interview requests. 
In an interview with Our Nevada Judges, Leavitt said she regularly volunteers to handle overflow cases and has helped municipal courts establish misdemeanor jury trials. 
Leavitt also serves as a member of the Criminal Task Force of the Judicial Assessment Commission; the Education Commission of the Nevada Judges Association, and the Supreme Court’s Mandatory Sentencing Review Commission.
Gilliam was previously involved with the Clark County Law Foundation’s Trial By Peers program, which allowed first-time juvenile offenders charged with misdemeanors to be tried, defended, and sentenced by their peers. However, the teen court model was shifted to a restorative justice model under state law in 2021.
On his campaign website, Gilliam listed equal justice for all, accessibility to justice, and transparency and efficiency as his main priorities.
In the interview with Our Nevada Judges, Leavitt said her years on the bench and lengthy career has given her a wide range of experience in handling all aspects of the law, from civil to criminal to water law. 
Leavitt said she is committed to continued education and expanding her knowledge of case law. 
She emphasized the importance of moving cases through the court system in a timely manner while also protecting the defendant’s constitutional rights.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT veterans can get free bus passes. Here’s how to apply
description: As of this summer, CT makes public transit available at no cost to veterans. Here's what you need to know about the program.
text:
The Connecticut Department of Veterans Affairs and Department of Transportation  launched a free bus pass program for veterans on July 31. 
The program, which received funding in the recent legislative session,  makes public transit available at no cost to veterans to get to appointments, work or run everyday errands. 
To apply, veterans must fill out an online application and verify their identity. They can choose from a number of bus route options, from those serving larger urban regions, such as CT Transit, to smaller regional districts. Passes must be renewed monthly. 
Here’s what veterans should know.
How do I apply for a free bus pass?
Veterans must apply online and submit a valid form of ID to verify their veteran status. These include: the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’ Veteran Health Identification Card; a Connecticut driver’s license with the flag indicating veteran status; or a Connecticut non-driver ID with the flag veteran indicator symbol.
The bus pass application also allows veterans to pick the bus routes they need passes for, with most being good for either 30 or 31 days.
How do the passes work?
When using a pass, the veteran must show a bus operator the active pass and also one of the valid forms of ID. Officials said this will ensure fraud prevention, as the bus passes do not currently have photo ID.
Because the passes expire monthly, veterans will get a 10-digit veteran pass ID after they request a new pass to use for renewals. Officials recommend leaving ample time between the request for a new pass and the expiration of the old one, because passes are mailed to recipients to whatever address is provided. 
What if I don’t have an ID or permanent address?
Veterans who do not have a valid ID or a permanent address can apply for a health identification card through the VA, or by calling 1-877-222-8387. 
Or veterans can use the Department of Veterans’ Affairs website to download and process the forms to get a Department of Motor Vehicles ID with a veteran flag. 
Once the forms are processed and eligibility is verified, the VA will mail a confirmation letter to give to the DMV to request an updated ID. Calling the DMV ahead of time is recommended, to confirm what’s needed and how the process works.
A veteran can also get a veterans health identification card when they enroll in VA healthcare. Those in need of healthcare can apply by phone, mail or in person.
What routes are passes available for?
Veterans are encouraged to only apply for the routes that serve their needs best to prevent ticket waste. The VA purchases passes based on use, so applicants are asked to request only what they need to help keep the program costs down.
Below are the routes available through the program:

CTtransit (includes Hartford, New Haven, Stamford, Waterbury, New Britain, Bristol, Meriden, Wallingford, CTfastrak service)
Greater Bridgeport Transit Authority
Housatonic Area Regional Transit (HART)
Milford Transit District
Northeastern Connecticut Transit District
Northwestern Connecticut Transit District
Norwalk Transit District
River Valley Transit
Southeast Area Transit District (SEAT)
Windham Region Transit District (WRTD)

If I have more questions, who do I contact?
For questions about receiving or renewing bus passes, status of a request or about the identification process, the Connecticut Department of Veterans Affairs’ Office of Advocacy and Assistance can help. 
Veterans can also check out the program’s website or email DVABusPasses@ct.gov for pass replacement or renewal questions.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah’s top election chief says Trump admin’s ‘gamesmanship’ with voting keeps her up at night
description: Editor’s note: This story is part of We Vote Utah, a partnership between KUER, PBS Utah and Utah News Dispatch to cover Utah’s 2026 elections. The top election official in the red state of Utah has been loud and clear — on and off social media — about her concerns with the Trump administration when it […]
text:
Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson poses for a photo in the Gold Room at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on Thursday, Feb. 15, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Editor’s note: This story is part of We Vote Utah, a partnership between KUER, PBS Utah and Utah News Dispatch to cover Utah’s 2026 elections.
The top election official in the red state of Utah has been loud and clear — on and off social media — about her concerns with the Trump administration when it comes to voting rights. 

Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson has refused to release private voter data despite threats of criminal prosecution by the U.S. Department of Justice. Last month, she learned the DOJ was investigating her as a result of her refusal. 
She’s also pushed hard against President Donald Trump’s executive order seeking to change how the U.S. Postal Service processes mail-in ballots. That rule would have mandated states collect information from voters and send that information to the federal government while also banning the Postal Service from delivering or collecting mail-in ballots from people who haven’t been confirmed as eligible voters. 
That rule has since been tied up in the courts — but had it been allowed to take effect so close to this year’s election, Henderson has said it would be an “unmitigated disaster.” 
Henderson has also heavily criticized Sen. Mike Lee’s proposed SAVE Act as legislation that would “hurt Utah voters and preempt state laws in ways that don’t make sense” while being  “impossible to implement.”
She doesn’t mince words. Even though she shares her Republican party affiliation with Lee and the president, she’s been a fierce advocate against their efforts, which she has said would erode voting rights. 
Utah clerks don’t expect lawsuits over Trump’s mail-in voting rule to impact elections this year

In Utah, voting by mail has a long history, and has long been lauded as a safe and secure method by the state’s leaders across the political spectrum, Republicans and Democrats alike. In recent years, however, as Trump has continued rhetoric of widespread fraud without evidence, Utah lawmakers have made moves to slowly pull back on universal, automatic voting by mail by enacting more ID requirements and requiring voters to opt in to receive a by-mail ballot by 2029. 
The Republican-controlled Utah Legislature started allowing counties to conduct elections entirely by mail nearly 15 years ago. Since 2018, nearly all of Utah’s counties have run their elections primarily by mail while also providing in-person voting options. Since 2020, it’s been the state’s default voting method, with all registered voters automatically sent a ballot. As voting by mail has gotten more popular, so has voter turnout, according to research by the conservative think tank Sutherland Institute. 
As the political winds have changed, Henderson has remained a firm advocate for voting by mail, defending Utah’s system as one that’s highly secure — and accessible — while also supporting efforts to improve wherever possible. 
In a recent sit-down interview with KUER, PBS Utah and Utah News Dispatch as part of the We Vote Utah partnership, Henderson discussed what it’s like to push back against the Trump administration and Lee’s efforts to change how Americans vote.
In that interview, Henderson said the effort to implement the SAVE Act immediately — rather than providing a longer runway for such drastic changes — only has one purpose, and “that is just to disenfranchise people.” 
“And that’s crappy,” she said. “That should not happen. That’s despicable.” 
To Utah’s chief election officer’s surprise, the DOJ says it has been investigating her since 2025

She also said the Trump administration’s “gamesmanship” with voting rights for political gain is what keeps her up at night. 
“It is hard because there are so many forces — forces much greater than me, greater than the Legislature, greater than our state — that are trying to muck things up for our voters,” Henderson said. “And I take Utahns’ voting rights very, very seriously. They are sacred, and they ought to be protected, and they ought to be preserved, and they shouldn’t be mucked around with for political purposes.”
Henderson said she also doesn’t know what the “end game” is for all of these efforts “because I am not creative enough, maybe — or devious enough — to think about what in the world the motivation could be.” 
“But I don’t think it matters, even if the motivations are really good, right?” Henderson said. “The chaos and confusion that’s being created, the guardrails that are being destroyed — it’s not worth any motivation.”
Below is a transcript of the interview with reporter Sean Higgins for KUER’s State Street podcast. It was edited for length and clarity.
Interview transcript
You’ve been a vocal defender of Utah’s election system for years now. You’ve also been under a lot of pressure from the Trump administration, the DOJ, and elsewhere this year, and are now under investigation. How are you feeling all of this right now? 
Henderson: I feel fine, everything’s fine.
You know, I’m just doing my job. Honestly, there are days where it’s hard, and it’s like, ‘What? One more thing? Like, can we just have a day that doesn’t have some big catastrophe and crazing thing coming from the federal government?’ But I’m just doing my job. 
Is there a scenario where you would comply with some version of the DOJ’s request for voter rolls?
Henderson: Well, I’ll comply with anything that’s lawful, of course. I don’t think their request is lawful, and 23 courts now have agreed with me. So, if for some reason, you know, it ends up that a court orders me to do that, and we have no other alternatives, obviously, of course, I will comply with that.”
Outside of a court order, was there anything else in the order or the request that would need to change for you to say, ‘Oh maybe there is a legal case for me to give this information?’
Henderson: We offered to send them the public version of our voter rolls, and you know, we can do that, but that’s not what they want.
Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson speaks during an interview with KUER, Utah News Dispatch and PBS Utah about her experience pushing back against the Trump administration’s efforts to restrict voting by mail in her office at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo courtesy of PBS Utah)
You signed onto a brief with election officials from both red and blue states, asking the court to preserve mail-in ballot processes for this election. What does that bipartisan coalition tell you about how officials who actually run elections view this fight maybe differently from politicians who just talk about it?
Henderson: Well, the big difference is election officials don’t have the luxury of just talking about stuff. We actually have to do stuff, and this is not a partisan issue. We can’t change tack like this and implement this rule. 
We would have to reprint all the ballots. We’ve got our overseas and military ballots going out … Some states have already sent out their early ballots. We just, we just can’t do it. And the bipartisan coalition just shows that this is not just a partisan thing, where one party doesn’t like the party that’s in power. This is an actual practicality thing as well.
I want to turn to your relationship with Sen. Mike Lee now. You and Lee co-wrote a 2022 op-ed defending Utah’s election system as a federalism model that the rest of the country could look to. What do you think changed for him between then and now? 
Henderson: That’s a question you’re going to have to ask Sen. Lee. I have no idea. 
Want to elaborate at all?
Henderson: Sen. Lee is doing the job the way he wants to do it and the way he sees fit. I’m doing my job the way I see fit, and I really can’t elaborate on that.
You wrote, I believe this was back in March, that you can count on zero fingers the time that Sen. Lee consulted you before pushing the Save Act. Has that changed at all since March? Have you spoken with him specifically about what’s going on now with the DOJ, what’s in the Supreme Court, or the SAVE Act since then? 
Henderson: The only time I hear about Sen. Lee is when he tweets about me.
If mail-in voting is eliminated or heavily restricted nationally after this cycle, what would happen in Utah specifically? We’ve built this whole system since 2018 that’s hinged on vote by mail. What would actually happen to the way the state conducts elections? 
Henderson: Well, I mean, if this rule is allowed to go into effect, it’s going to have a much broader impact than just Utah not being able to do vote by mail. It really will change the dynamic between what’s in the Constitution and what is actually being practiced by a federal executive branch.
I think the implications will be far-reaching and incredibly negative. If Congress wants to pass a law to alter a vote by mail or to restrict it or somehow enforce it in certain ways, that’s up to Congress to do. They represent the people. They have the authority in the Constitution to change election laws. Otherwise, it’s up to the states, and that’s in our U.S. Constitution. So, I think there are much broader implications if this rule goes into effect than just how Utah will have to scramble and do balloting, voting differently.
Taking this out of the nitty gritty of policy and the way things are written and the way the courts interpret things, what is this really about, in your opinion? What is trying to be accomplished here? 
More than 5,000 Utah voters need to provide proof of citizenship under new state law

Henderson: It’s a good question. I don’t know what the end game is, and probably most of the reason I don’t know what the end game is is because I am not creative enough, maybe — or devious enough — to think about what in the world the motivation could be. 
But I don’t think it matters, even if the motivations are really good, right? The chaos and confusion that’s being created, the guardrails that are being destroyed — it’s not worth any motivation. Even someone who thinks they have good motivations, and I’m sure some of the people who are supportive of this think they have good motivations. But in my mind, it doesn’t matter because this is not what the Constitution says, it’s not what Congress has authorized, and it’s not what our state legislature has authorized.”
What do you think Utahns need the most this election cycle, from either from you or from the powers that be in Washington D.C.?
Henderson: When it comes to elections, Utahns need confidence. They need a chaos-free election. They need to know that the motivations, at least of their election officials, are good, and that … we’re not trying to put our thumb on any scale. What we want is for every eligible voter to be able to cast a ballot and know that that ballot will be counted accurately. That’s what Utahns need to know.
Looking at this issue a little bit more broadly, Utah passed its own citizenship verification law last year, but it doesn’t kick in fully until 2029. Either the Save Act or what’s happening right now with the Department of Justice or the USPS ahead of these midterms, does it almost ignore the exact lesson Utah tried to teach with implementing its own law?
Henderson: Yes. … One of the reasons that I started our own citizenship review of our voter list last year was because of all of these questions. Everybody was asking. People were throwing around wild numbers, saying that there was this huge, huge, widespread problem. And I’m a pragmatist, and if there’s a problem, I want to know about it. I want to know exactly what the problem is, and then work on solving it. 
‘Not a widespread problem’: Lt. gov. releases early findings from voter citizenship review 

So we did this review, and we did find some areas that could be improved. We did find little places that we can tweak and and and do better, and that was a really good thing. We also found a few noncitizens on our voter rolls, and a few of those that we found actually had voted. Very, very, very, very few. So what we found was, yep, room for improvement. We made a few tweaks and modifications, and there’s no big, huge problem. 
And that is not a narrative, unfortunately, that the federal government wanted to hear. I learned a long time ago that, like they don’t want to know that we’re doing things OK. They don’t want to know that things are going well, because it goes against a narrative that is being pounded relentlessly of mass fraud or ineligible people voting. 
And the facts just don’t support that narrative, and one would think that that would be relief to people. ‘Oh, phew. OK, we thought there was this problem, but now we see that there isn’t this problem.’ Well, that’s not what’s happening, unfortunately, with some people, and they’re just doubling down and creating problems where none exist, and that’s frustrating.
If we strip away all the personalities from this conversation, is there some version of federal election integrity legislation that you would actually support, and what would that look like? 
Henderson: Well, yeah, of course, there are some versions of federal legislation that I would support. 
Traditionally, at least in the last 50 years, the federal legislation … the motivation behind it, or the purpose of it, has been to help expand access to voting for eligible voters because states were being naughty. There were states that were actually restricting the right for eligible citizens to vote, especially in the South, and that’s why there needed to be federal legislation to expand it. I would be very supportive of legislation that helped preserve and protect people’s constitutional voting rights. 
I would also be in favor of some sort of federal ID requirement. Most states have these ID requirements. Utah certainly does, or even documented proof of citizenship. If there is enough leeway for people to actually get their documents — having something like the SAVE Act that’s implemented effective immediately, the purpose of that is just to disenfranchise people, and that’s crappy. That should not happen. That’s despicable. 
But if you really want, in good faith, to say we should have a national ID or we should have, you know, documented proof of citizenship in a federal requirement, those are valid conversations to have if people from both sides of the aisle can come together in good faith and figure out how to actually solve that problem without creating a whole bunch of new ones.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
What keeps you up at night about all of this? 
Henderson: Look, I am grateful to be in the spot I’m in. It’s an honor. I never expected to be here. I certainly don’t want to complain about any of the challenges. I’m happy to bear those challenges, but it is a burden to be the one person in the state that has the responsibility to be over elections right now. 
It is hard because there are so many forces — forces much greater than me, greater than the Legislature, greater than our state — that are trying to muck things up for our voters. And I take Utahns’ voting rights very, very seriously. They are sacred, and they ought to be protected, and they ought to be preserved, and they shouldn’t be mucked around with for political purposes.”
Politics is part of our country, but politics is sharing ideas, debating ideas, making sure that your side is articulating what you want to do. Politics should not be messing around with the rules of the game to benefit one side or another. That should never happen, and that gamesmanship keeps me up at night.
What would success look like for you at the end of all of this?
Henderson: Success at the end of all of this, to me, looks like a very boring election, right? Not only on Nov. 3, but in the days leading up, in early voting, and then, you know, we’ve got a couple of weeks after where we canvass the results. The counties canvass their results. They conduct audits. If there’s a close race, they do recounts, and then the boards of canvassers certify the results. Like all of that happening and being very boring and having absolutely no news stories about any of it, to me, that would be success.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington needs this aging state ferry to keep running and running
description: When the Washington state ferry Tillikum entered service in 1959, Albert Rosellini was in his first term as governor and Dwight Eisenhower was in his second as president.  The showy tail fins of Chevrolet and Plymouth sedans on its car deck could have made a killer whale jealous. The auto-and-driver fare to cross Puget Sound […]
text:
The 67-year-old Tillikum is the longest-serving Washington state ferry in active operation. It was expected to retire years ago, but can’t due to the shortage of working boats in the state fleet. (Photo by Tom Banse)When the Washington state ferry Tillikum entered service in 1959, Albert Rosellini was in his first term as governor and Dwight Eisenhower was in his second as president. 
The showy tail fins of Chevrolet and Plymouth sedans on its car deck could have made a killer whale jealous. The auto-and-driver fare to cross Puget Sound was $1.75.
Back then, the Tillikum was one of three Evergreen State-class ferries. Around a decade ago, the other two were decommissioned. However, that won’t happen anytime soon for the Tillikum. It must sail long past its expected retirement date because Washington State Ferries is so short on vessels, it cannot afford to let go of a single boat. Decommissioning is now projected in 2033 for this remarkably long-lived ferryboat. 
“She’s a sweetheart,” said Captain Justin McCaughan of the boat he and the crew affectionately call the “Tilly.”
“She’s a little underpowered, but she is fairly maneuverable,” continued McCaughan during an interview in the teak-trimmed pilothouse. “She’s more reliable than a lot of our newer boats because she is simpler.”
McCaughan said he trusted this “moving piece of history” to last until new boats join the fleet. The controls and instruments in the pilothouse have been repeatedly modernized. But the mates at the helm go gentle on the throttles to protect the ancient machinery down below. 
“Because we want to keep her around, we take it easy on this boat,” McCaughan said as the ferry chugged toward Friday Harbor. “So, we are not using maximum power unless we really need maximum power. We try to bring the throttles up slowly.”
The 87-car, 310-foot Tillikum was constructed in 1958 by the long-defunct Puget Sound Bridge and Drydock Company. Its drive motors were salvaged from a surplus World War II Navy ship. Replacement parts to keep it running sometimes have to be fabricated from scratch at the ferry system’s maintenance yard or are stripped from Tilly’s   mothballed sibling, the Klahowya.
Only one active vehicle ferry in America is older. The SS Badger, which was launched in 1953, sails daily during the warmer half of the year across the midsection of Lake Michigan. The 410-foot, coal-burning steamship is a floating, moving National Historic Landmark. The Tillikum burns conventional diesel for propulsion.
Wearing earplugs, oiler Earl Clark stands beside one of the two engines of the ferry Tillikum. (Photo by Tom Banse)
The view from the engine room
Below the Tillikum’s car deck, the vintage engines and diesel generators make a deafening din. Tight passageways wind past twisty pipes, conduits, valves and steel going every which way.
Inside a sound-insulated, air-conditioned engine control room, the chief engineer and two oilers monitor tiers of analog dials and gauges from the past century. Modern digital screens glow on another side of the room, mixed in with blinking instruments that could date to a mid-life overhaul in 1994.
The hull looks good and the ship’s steel, while old, “was done properly,” vouched Chief Engineer Alex Stamati.
“As long as they give us the time in drydock and maintenance money, we can keep the boat running,” said oiler Earl Clark. “The longer it lives, obviously the more expensive it is going to get.”
“She can last to 80 or 90 [years old] with proper maintenance, absolutely,” Stamati added.
So what about retirement?
The state ferry system is in a race against time to build new ferries before its aging vessels conk out. Five ferries now in operation are more than 50 years old. At 67, the Tillikum is the grande dame. 
So far, the state Legislature has only been able to scrape together enough money to order three new ferries due to their high price. The first of those hybrid-electric boats isn’t expected until 2030. The next vessels are due in 2031 and 2032.
“As we get closer to the first new ferry entering service in 2030, we’ll work with Gov. Bob Ferguson and the Legislature as they decide whether to follow past practice and retire an older vessel as each new one enters service, or invest in keeping our three oldest boats operating longer so we can begin growing the fleet sooner,” ferry system chief Steve Nevey told riders in a recent newsletter.
“We have 21 vessels today, down from 24 in 2015,” Nevey wrote. “One unexpected breakdown can cause a ripple effect across the system.”
Top brass at the ferry system prefer to add one or two relief vessels to the fleet before decommissioning aging boats, if possible. There is also public interest in restoring the long-suspended international run to Vancouver Island from Anacortes, which would require growing the fleet by another vessel.
“Put all of that together and 21 ferries aren’t enough. We need at least 24 to operate our current service,” Nevey said.
The upshot is that the Tillikum will likely be counted on well into her seventh decade. The most recent fleet planning document shared with state lawmakers shows its retirement happening in 2033.
The Tillikum has operated on nearly every Puget Sound route over the past six decades. Today, it’s the slowest member of the state fleet with a listed top cruising speed of 13 knots and is consigned to the San Juan Islands interisland circuit.
The Tillikum became the “big boat” on the Seattle-Bainbridge ferry route when it entered service n 1959. The Smith Tower, at top right, was still the tallest building in Seattle back then. (Photo courtesy of Washington State Archives)
Affection, frustration and amazement
The interisland service provided by the Tillikum evokes complex feelings among regular commuters. Some are “amazed” it is still running while others continue to be frustrated with unreliability on a vital route they consider a literal lifeline.  
The San Juans interisland service had the lowest rider satisfaction scores of all Puget Sound ferry routes in a survey conducted for the Washington State Transportation Commission earlier this year. The top reasons for dissatisfaction were late departures and arrivals. Other gripes included loading procedures and inadequate parking near the terminals.
“I don’t think it’s fair to equate the service dissatisfaction with the boat,” said frequent rider Justin Paulsen, the San Juan County Council Chair. “I think there’s a lot of love in the county for that boat.”
Across the first three quarters of this year, the Tillikum had 275 sailings completely cancelled out of 6,463 scheduled sailings. The most common cause of those cancellations was lack of sufficient crew. Mechanical problems on the aging ship accounted for 28% of the cancellations.
As much as county leaders praise the Tillikum, they still aspire to establish a competing interisland ferry. Paulsen said the goal is to provide an alternative to the state system that provides greater dependability. It’s unclear where the money to launch this new passenger-only service would come from.
Lopez Island author Iris Graville spent one or two days a week riding the Tillikum as the ferry system’s first writer-in-residence before the COVID-19 pandemic. The venerable boat remains her favorite. She described being charmed by 1950s-era touches such as its brass fixtures, elegant wooden slat benches and swivel chairs in front of a throwback mirrored makeup counter in the ladies room.
“She has those classic features that aren’t found in the newer vessels, like the brass railings and trim,” Graville said. “She just has more of a cozy feeling.”
Graville said she will miss the Tillikum whenever it finally retires, yet is also fully on board with the need to acquire cleaner, modern vessels. Like many San Juan County residents, she has her fingers crossed the aging boat will last until a replacement arrives.
“Anybody who knows any of the history of that vessel has to be wondering that very thing, can it really keep going?” Graville said in an interview. “We know there is usually a lifespan and a limit.”
Then and now. At left, Captain Theodore Thorson at the helm of the Tillikum in 1965. At right, Captain Justin McCaughan in the same pilothouse in late September 2026. (Photos  from Washington State Archives (left) and by Tom Banse)
