name: Maryland Matters
title: EPA to give $90M for clean water and restoration projects in Chesapeake Bay watershed
description: The Environmental Protection Agency said Friday it will disburse $37 million to localities to aid Chesapeake Bay pollution reduction and clean-up efforts, with another $53 million in matching funds for 83 projects across the watershed, 32 of them in Maryland.
text:
A living shoreline project on the James River. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Deputy Administrator David Fotouhi announced Friday that the agency will disburse $37 million to localities to aid Chesapeake Bay pollution reduction and cleanup efforts. An additional $53 million in matching grant funds will be awarded to 83 projects across the watershed, 32 of them Maryland-based.
“These awards will empower local towns to implement community level, clean water projects, and they will help fund regional partnerships to keep our soil healthier, restore habitats, and secure our thriving regional economy,” said Fotouhi, who was joined by U.S. Rep. Jennifer Kiggans (R-Va.).
As tiny fiddler crabs scuttled through mud beside an oyster mount that is part of a nearby marshland restoration project, Fotouhi explained that the money would be split between the Chesapeake Small Watersheds Grants Program and the Chesapeake Innovative Nutrient and Sediment Reduction Grants Program.
The former fuels projects that directly support clean water, habitat restoration and species protection. The latter consists of projects that help implement agricultural strategies, stormwater best practices, and other methods that prevent sediment, phosphorus, and nitrogen from ending up in the Bay.
Rep. Jen Kiggans (R-Va.) and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Deputy Administrator David Fotouhi in Smithfield, Virginia. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
Virginia’s chief Chesapeake Bay organization welcomed the collaborative funding opportunity.
“Restoring this vital resource takes collaboration across political boundaries, between federal, state, and local governments. And it takes everyone. Industries, universities, nonprofits, small businesses, and individuals,” Chesapeake Bay Commission Executive Director Anna Killius said. “All of us are empowered with the knowledge and the resources to conserve our waters, our lands, and our living resources that we so care about.”
The grants are awarded once a year through the EPA and are coordinated by the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, a nonprofit chartered by Congress. They are a key to achieving goals identified by federal, state, and local partnerships through the Chesapeake Bay Program.
In comparison to past years, before matching grants the agency awarded $44 million earlier this year and $22 million in 2024.
Small watershed projects that received grants include nature-based stormwater infrastructure across Richmond Public Schools, a process to enhance grazing management practices, living shoreline assessment and design for Leesylvania State Park. A total of 68 projects across the watershed have received awards.
Funding for the nutrient and sediment reduction grants will go towards projects like regional watershed roundtables, and riparian forest buffers and forest cover expansion on private lands and others totaling 16 projects.
The Chesapeake Bay Foundation was one of the organizations to receive a grant from this round of funding. Of their award, $737,000 will help create roughly 5.5 acres of sanctuary oyster reef in the Hampton River. The aim is to produce three million oysters to be planted in other reefs.
“This grant will go a long way toward restoring and preserving oyster habitat in the Hampton River and surrounding areas,” Chesapeake Bay Foundation Virginia Oyster Restoration Manager Jackie Shannon said in a release.
This annual grant comes on the heels of President Donald Trump’s move to repeal Executive Order 13508, signed in 2009 under former President Barack Obama, which directed the EPA to bring state and local agencies together to identify sources of pollutants and ways to reduce sediment and nutrient loads running off into the Bay.
Marsh on the James River. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)
Trump said the significant progress made by states that are part of the Chesapeake Bay Watershed Agreement to reduce Bay pollutants deemed the old order unnecessary.
Leaders in Delaware, Maryland, New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Washington, D.C. recently resigned the agreement.
Trump said the  states “have collectively met 100 percent of their goal for sediment reduction, 90 percent of their goal for phosphorus reduction, and 57 percent of their goal for nitrogen reduction” and revoking the old order cleared up the “lack of clarity (that) has led to harmful economic impacts.”
After Trump revoked Executive Order 13508 in September, Virginia environmental groups including the Chesapeake Bay Foundation and the commonwealth’s two Democratic U.S. Sens. Tim Kaine and Mark Warner said it’s the wrong time to ease up on managing the Bay.
They also said that this move could lead to the breakdown of interstate and interagency cooperation without the EPA at the helm.
When asked about the feared impacts of the president’s action at the funding announcement Friday, Fotouhi said it ensures that “every federal dollar goes directly to improving water quality,” which “removes a more heavy-handed federal approach and empowers state and local communities to continue making that progress.”
The full impact of the rescission of the former order is yet to be realized, according to CBF leadership.
The new watershed agreement comprises four main goals focused on habitat, clean water, healthy landscapes, and more engaged communities, which each of the states will strive to meet over the next 15 years.
Fotouhi emphasized that the agreement is still in place and stated that the new executive order “reconfirmed and reiterated our administration’s commitment to the Chesapeake Bay.”
The full lists of grant awardees can be found here for the small watershed projects and here for the nutrient and sediment reduction grants.

description: The state’s only Alabama House contest with three qualified candidates features two independents at opposite sides of the political spectrum facing an incumbent Republican for a north Alabama House seat. Rep. Ernie Yarbrough, R-Trinity, seeking his second term in the House, faces Trent Ford, a freelance software and website designer, and Angelo Mancuso, a fo[...]
text:
Voters in Lawrence and parts of Colbert and Morgan counties will choose between Trent Ford (left), Angelo Mancuso (middle) and Rep. Ernie Yarbrough (right) to be the Alabama House District 7 representative. (Photos of Ford and Trent courtesy of candidate; Photo of Yarbrough by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector; Graphic by Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)The state’s only Alabama House contest with three qualified candidates features two independents at opposite sides of the political spectrum facing an incumbent Republican for a north Alabama House seat.
Rep. Ernie Yarbrough, R-Trinity, seeking his second term in the House, faces Trent Ford, a freelance software and website designer, and Angelo Mancuso, a former Alabama representative, in the general election next month.
The district includes parts of Colbert, Lawrence and Morgan counties. It has been solidly Republican since 2010.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Multiple messages seeking comment were left with Yarbrough last week. According to Yarbrough’s website, he supports anti-abortion policies, lowering taxes and “medical freedom.”
During his time in the Legislature, Yarbrough has been on the right edge of the Republican caucus. Yarbrough in 2023 sponsored a bill that would have allowed prosecutions of pregnant women for having abortions or attempting one. Yarbrough has also sponsored legislation to expand local law enforcement’s ability to enforce immigration laws and to introduce school vouchers. 
Ford said in an interview Thursday he joined the race because he didn’t “think that our current representative or most of the Legislature was equipped to be able to set proper guidelines in place” for data centers and artificial intelligence. Ford said he decided to run as an independent because he didn’t like “to be told by a national party what I have to say or what I have to do.”
“I believe in trying to go talk to the people and then figuring out what solutions work, and that I don’t think either party would represent me exactly, and that I want to be able to be there for other people too,” he said.
Ford’s priorities include eliminating the grocery tax, implementing protections against artificial intelligence and lowering power bills through nuclear and solar energy.
“Solar panels are actually the cheapest way to generate energy by orders of magnitudes, and you can put in solar panels faster than anything else that scales up,” Ford said. “And then expanded nuclear power would allow us more dependability for people worrying about when it’s not sunny, and if the batteries are low, if it’s been cloudy, all that nuclear power would give us a buffer. So combined, they would create a more robust system.”
Mancuso, a Democratic member of the Alabama House of Representatives from 1998 until 2002, originally sought the Republican nomination for District 7, but was removed by the Alabama Republican Party earlier this year. He said in an interview Friday he’s running because of locals asking him to.
“Patients kept coming in asking me to run, and I was like, ‘I don’t think I want to do this,’” Mancuso said. “I talked it over with my wife. She’s from Courtland in Lawrence County, and we just got to the point where we said these are the things that have to be done. These are the things that are being overlooked, and it just snowballed from there.”
The former representative called the removal a “setup” and accused the Republican Party of limiting voters’ options in the district.
“If you meet the criteria of a party, then you should have the option to run, and if the people who are in that district, who are, let’s say, the Republicans or the Democrats, let them vote. That’s what a primary is for,” Mancuso said.
A message seeking comment was left with the Alabama Republican Party Friday.
Mancuso’s priorities include getting a local trauma emergency room for Lawrence County, improving schools in the district and eliminating the grocery tax and suspending the gas tax.
“What’s happening now is, obviously the price is going higher and higher, and it’s a temporary suspension,” Mancuso said. “This is not something where we’re getting rid of the gas tax because some people say, ‘well, this is the money that’s used for the roads and the bridges.’ I understand that, but we have a lot of families that since there aren’t that many businesses in Lawrence County and in Colbert County, they have to travel.”
Mancuso said that voters should choose him because “I’m the one who has the vision.”
“I’m the one who has the experience. I’m the one who has the knowledge,” he said. “It’s like my whole life has been a preparation for where I am at this moment right now.”
Ford said people should choose him because he can identify with voters.
“I have had a wide range of experiences, so I can identify with a lot of people because I’ve done blue collar and white collar work,” Ford said. “I was raised to believe in public service and to believe in helping people, and even though I haven’t been in public office before, this is how I try to live my life.”
According to campaign finance records, through Sept. 1 Ford raised $12,200 and spent $6,900; Mancuso raised $2,000, loaned himself $138,700 and spent $119,900. Yarbrough raised $77,200 and spent $40,800.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Issue spotlight: North Dakota US House candidates discuss AI regulation, data centers
description: North Dakota’s Republican and Democratic U.S. House candidates agree artificial intelligence is powerful and in need of guardrails, but they differ on the level of accountability for AI products and their parent companies. Republican incumbent Julie Fedorchak said she supports a bipartisan effort in the U.S. House to regulate the expanding industry and hopes[...]
text:
On the left, Democratic-NPL U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer speaks to during the party's state convention on March 7, 2026. On the right, Republican incumbent U.S. House Rep. Julie Fedorchak gestures at supporters during a victory party in 2024. (Photos by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota’s Republican and Democratic U.S. House candidates agree artificial intelligence is powerful and in need of guardrails, but they differ on the level of accountability for AI products and their parent companies.
Republican incumbent Julie Fedorchak said she supports a bipartisan effort in the U.S. House to regulate the expanding industry and hopes accountability measures for AI misuse will come from the process. Democratic-NPL U.S. House candidate Trygve Hammer said AI regulations should be proactive instead of reactive and companies should be held negligent if their products violate the law.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Fedorchak said AI could be the most powerful technology Americans have encountered.
“That’s one of the main reasons why it’s so important for the U.S. to lead the way in the development of this industry and the regulation of it,” Fedorchak said.
Potential regulations
She said many states are already regulating different aspects of AI, and she believes the federal government should follow suit.
“It doesn’t make sense to have a patchwork of 50 different state regulations that these companies have to try to figure out,” she said. “It’s important to remember what we’re doing this for. People have legitimate fears about privacy.”
Fedorchak said she supports the Frontier Act, a bipartisan AI regulation bill in the U.S. House. The bill would establish reporting requirements for AI companies and their products, such as risk assessments, cybersecurity safety for unreleased AI models, response procedures for critical incidents and compliance audits. The legislation includes civil penalties of up to $1 million if the law is violated.
She said it’s important that AI models have a published safety framework in place when their models are released, as well as reporting requirements for critical incidents that could occur.
Issue spotlight: North Dakota US House candidates differ on solutions to affordability

The bill is under consideration by the U.S. House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which includes Fedorchak as a member.
Hammer said, “I think we need to get a handle on it, and we need to be thinking ahead of it instead of reacting to it.”
An international agreement may be needed to curtail AI use in areas affected by war so those products cannot create and approve their own kill orders without a human in the chain of command, he said.
“That’s part of the problem here is that AI will never have a concept of what’s morally right and wrong,” Hammer said. He added AI hacking into infrastructure will also be a problem since the products have learned how to cover their tracks.
A prohibition on self-feeding artificial intelligence, an AI product that learns and grows on its own without human involvement, is something Congress should look into, he said
Holding AI companies accountable
Hammer said he believes AI companies should be held responsible for the products they create. He added he does not want immunity offered to AI companies similar to what internet service providers received during regulation of the internet, which protects online platforms from content posted to websites by third parties.
At the very least, Hammer said AI companies should be able to be prosecuted for negligence based on the use of their products.
He said international outreach, especially with China, on AI needs to occur to put the products and industry on the same playing field.
“Let’s do this thing right and let’s not rush in and create more problems than we solve,” Hammer said. “When you have a bunch of people who only think about the next quarterly earnings report, it’s just not going to get done the right way.”
‘Dumbfounds us all’: Congress struggles with policies rippling from AI development

An international framework surrounding AI issues is something that should be discussed, Fedorchak said, and the world will need to work together “to some extent” to protect against the potential dangers of AI technology.
She said she didn’t have an answer on whether AI companies should be held responsible for the actions of their products in the hands of third parties, but hoped the House committee addressing AI regulations and the companies themselves would be able to find the “right balance.”
“We have to get bipartisan support for what we’re doing, and so if we get too dug in on a particular position on the front end, perfect could be the enemy of good,” Fedorchak said. She added tech companies do have to be held accountable and take down inappropriate AI content posted to their platforms.
“As a mom, I don’t want my daughter having images of her that were doctored up and posted on the internet,” she said.
Federal role in data center construction
Fedorchak said she supports local control for the development of data centers and doesn’t want the federal government getting in the way.
“I don’t think the federal government has a role to play in where they (data centers) are located,” Fedorchak said. “If there are appropriate places on federal land that could host data processing facilities … I’m open to that. There’s good processes in place for siting and permitting this kind of infrastructure already that are proven.”
She added the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act and historical preservation process have blocked the development of all kinds of infrastructure. One of Congress’ priorities is permitting reform to move projects along more quickly, Fedorchak said, but it would not impact local control.
Hammer said he expressed his concerns about the increase in data center construction two years ago in a debate with Fedorchak. He added he worries about abandoned facilities, if the demand for data centers subsides.
Construction of data centers should be a state and local issue with the backing of transparency laws, Hammer said. Companies constructing the facilities need to be upfront with citizens about energy and water use and written plans addressing the order of operations, if an emergency arises demanding a choice between resident needs and the needs of a data center, he said.
“I think we need to make sure it’s the community that wins,” he said. “Congress needs to force transparency and honesty, and restore trust.”
Hammer said a recent social media post from President Donald Trump about communities becoming “backwards and poor” if they don’t allow data centers into their communities is the wrong attitude.
“These people aren’t dumb. They’re not backward. They are just concerned,” Hammer said. “And part of their concern comes from being surprised, and there has to be better outreach.”
Independent candidates Helene Neville and Charles Tuttle are also running for U.S. House.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Kalshi leads prediction markets’ $3 million effort to fight off state regulations
description: As prediction markets have exploded in popularity over the past two years, they have also become increasingly controversial – setting off a lobbying-fueled power struggle for regulation of the platforms. Amid allegations of insider trading, bets on military operations, and deceptive marketing practices, some states are seeking to sue or ban prediction market[...]
text:
NEW YORK, NEW YORK - JUNE 23: A supporter checks the gambling site 'Kalshi" just before State Assembly member, Alex Bores (D-NY) gives a speech to supporters at his watch party at The Freehand Hotel after conceding the congressional race to Micah Lasher who will replace Rep Jerry Nadler (D-NY) in NY's 12th Congressional District on June 23, 2026 in New York City. The former Palantir employee received both support and attacks for his promise to reign in Big Tech and particularly AI if elected.(Photo by Laura Brett/Getty Images)


As prediction markets have exploded in popularity over the past two years, they have also become increasingly controversial – setting off a lobbying-fueled power struggle for regulation of the platforms.
Amid allegations of insider trading, bets on military operations, and deceptive marketing practices, some states are seeking to sue or ban prediction markets.  But the federal government has taken an unusual role in the legal battle, with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission suing states that seek to enforce their gambling laws against prediction-market platforms.
Prediction market companies contend they are offering financial transactions known as swaps – which are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a federal agency – while many states argue they are gambling operations, akin to sportsbooks and casinos. Gambling is regulated by the states.
Several lawsuits addressing whether state law applies to prediction markets have advanced to federal courts, but because judges have split on their rulings, the question is still unsettled and moving towards the Supreme Court.
Although market leader Kalshi argues it should be regulated at the federal level, the company’s lobbying and spending demonstrates a push to gain state-level influence – especially in the states spearheading regulation.
So far in 2026, Kalshi, its competitor Polymarket and the Coalition for Prediction Markets have spent at least $3 million on lobbying and campaign contributions across the federal and state levels.
Online prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket are attracting scrutiny from state lawmakers, who argue the platforms are undermining state gambling regulations. (Photo by Alyssa Chen/Minnesota Reformer)
Kalshi directs political spending to governors and state AGs
State attorneys general are leading the regulatory fight against prediction markets – and the majority are united in the opinion that CFTC regulation should not preempt state gambling laws. In July, a coalition of 44 state AGs signed onto a letter to the CFTC arguing that prediction markets are a “new form of casino.”
But just as attorneys general and prediction markets appear to be battling each other, Kalshi is pouring hundreds of thousands of dollars into the two major political organizations dedicated to electing and supporting AGs.
According to IRS filings reviewed by OpenSecrets, in the first half of 2026, Kalshi gave $147,500 to the Republican Attorneys General Association and $170,000 to the Democratic Attorneys General Association.
Kalshi has also donated directly to some attorneys general – including the super PAC supporting Ken Paxton’s run for Senate in Texas and the campaigns of Vermont’s Charity Clark, Oregon’s Dan Rayfield and Florida’s James Utheimer. In response to the contributions, Rayfield and Clark told local news outlets they are not influenced by political donations. A spokesperson for Paxton’s super PAC told Politico that Paxton “has fought at every turn to hold big corporations accountable.”
The New York Times reported in August that Donald Trump Jr., who serves as a strategic advisor to Kalshi and Polymarket, told Republican state AGs not to fight prediction markets. Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm is invested in Polymarket and he has an equity stake in Kalshi.
The head of Kalshi’s state relations, Blake Bee, was previously director of the National Association of Attorneys General’s Center for Leadership Development, where he worked directly with state attorneys general.
Kalshi also donated $100,000 to the Republican Governors Association and $150,000 to the Democratic Governors Association in the first half of 2026.
“Like many U.S. regulated companies, we support candidates on both sides of the aisle,” Dani Lever, a spokesperson for Kalshi, wrote in a statement to OpenSecrets.
Kalshi hires dozens of new lobbyists, focusing on California and New York

Kalshi has ramped up state-level lobbying in the past several months. As of September, the company has at least one registered lobbyist in 41 states, nearly all of them brought on board since April.
Kalshi appears to be spending the most on lobbying in California and New York, though many states do not require financial disclosure by lobbyists.
In California, Kalshi spent $62,000 on lobbying in the first half of 2026. Disclosure reports reviewed by OpenSecrets show that Kalshi is lobbying on three assembly bills and the “Attorney General’s and Governor’s offices re: prediction markets.”
Kalshi’s California lobbying has so far been handled by Redwood Public Affairs. Redwood’s co-founder and principal was formerly the legislative director and chief of staff for state Attorney General Rob Bonta. On Aug. 12, Kalshi registered another California-based firm, the Weideman Group, to begin lobbying.
In New York, Kalshi recently reported that it would increase its payment to lobbyists at Brown & Weinraub Advisors from $10,000 monthly to $25,000 monthly to work on legislation relating to prediction markets.
Kalshi is spreading its Empire State work around, also committing to pay $25,000 monthly to the Mirram Group in a contract running until July 2027. Additionally, Kalshi has registered Blake Bee as its in-house lobbyist in New York. Bee will lobby the office of the governor and the state assembly through December 2026, according to the registration.
Between its payments to both lobbying groups and Bee, Kalshi is currently projected to spend over $400,000 on lobbying in New York through July 2027.
Through its state-level lobbying efforts, Kalshi may be positioned to deal with a flood of new laws if the Supreme Court rules that prediction markets should be regulated by the states as gambling.
“Most state gambling laws are designed for sporting events, poker, casino games, but they mostly clearly cover gambling in whatever form or packaging,” said Benjamin Schriffin, director of securities policy at Better Markets, a nonprofit that advocates for financial reform. “I don’t think anybody ever conceived of having to pass a law that’s going to prevent people who are watching ‘Survivor ‘at home on a Wednesday night from betting on who’s going to win. So you could see states thinking, ‘We need to clarify our gambling laws for all these new ways that people have now found to gamble on prediction markets.’”
Polymarket has not yet registered any lobbyists at the state level.
Predictions market sites are shown on electronic devices on Feb. 25, 2026. Online prediction market platforms, such as Polymarket and Kalshi, allow people to place bets on wide-ranging subjects such as sports, finance, politics and currents events. (Photo illustration by Scott Olson/Getty Images)
Kalshi continues federal lobbying, spending nearly $1 million in the first half of 2026
As it expands its state presence, Kalshi is also continuing its federal lobbying by spending nearly $1 million through June 30.
In January, Kalshi opened a Washington, D.C., office headed by John Bivona, who served on the Joe Biden’s presidential campaign and as the Department of Homeland Security’s White House liaison during the Biden administration.
In addition to its in-house federal lobbying team, Kalshi has hired six outside firms. Kalshi relies most on Miller Strategies, which it has paid $240,000 during the first half of 2026. Miller Strategies is headed by Jeff Miller, who served as finance chair on President Donald Trump’s second inaugural committee and has grown his shop into the fifth highest-grossing lobbying firm in the first half of 2026.
Kalshi has also reported $120,000 in lobbying expenses to Lincoln Policy Group, founded by former Sen. Blanche Lincoln (D-Ark.). While in the Senate, Lincoln chaired the Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee – the CFTC’s authorizing committee.
As a lobbyist for Kalshi, Lincoln is now arguing directly against stances she took as chair. In 2010, Lincoln said the CFTC should be empowered to “prevent derivatives contracts that are contrary to the public interest because they exist predominantly to enable gambling through supposed ‘event contracts.’” In 2025, Lincoln submitted a public letter to the CFTC arguing that Kalshi should be permitted to offer sports bets in all states.
Kalshi has disclosed lobbying on three Senate bills – the Prediction Market Act, which would create stronger federal regulations on events contracts, the Protect College Sports Act and the National Defense Authorization Act.
The Protect College Sports Act would create federal rules around athlete payment, transfers and conference alignment. Although lobbying disclosures do not specify Kalshi’s stance in its lobbying, the NCAA, which supports the bill, has previously stated its “vehement opposition” to prediction market contracts related to college sports. The Senate passed the bill on Monday and it now awaits action in the House of Representatives.
Kalshi’s lobbying on the NDAA is likely related to sections 1081, 1082, and 1083, which would ban “covered transactions” involving prediction market contracts, prevent Department of Defense personnel from trading on prediction markets, and ban all bets regarding military operations.
In addition to those three bills, Kalshi’s lobbying disclosures also reveal its focus on the CFTC, the Executive Office of the President, the Securities & Exchange Commission and both chambers of Congress.
The director of the CFTC has been explicitly pro-prediction market, both through public statements and the commission’s legal action against states attempting to regulate the platforms.
Brad Lipton, director of the Roosevelt Institute’s corporate power and financial regulation program, said the CFTC suing states is “unprecedented.”
“They’re being super aggressive, and it’s sort of a head scratcher as to why they’re being so aggressive,” Lipton said. “It’s because they’re so committed to helping out prediction markets, is really the only explanation.”
Beyond its corporate spending, Kalshi’s co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara have donated to federal political campaigns and political action committees. Mansour and Lopes Lara have collectively given about $1 million to both Democratic and Republican recipients this cycle, according to FEC filings.
Polymarket has spent $180,000 on federal lobbying in 2026, hiring Advocus Partners. Advocus is a collaborative advocacy group whose members include BGR Group, one of the leading lobbying firms. Polymarket’s lobbyists include Keaghan Ames, a former senior policy advisor at the CFTC.
Coalition for Prediction Markets brings in other other players
In December 2025, Kalshi joined Robinhood, Coinbase, Crypto.com and Underdog – which all offer exchange betting in their apps – to launch the Coalition for Prediction Markets. Polymarket is not a member.
The coalition’s bipartisan leadership includes a pair of former House members. President Sean Patrick Maloney represented New York as a Democrat before serving in the Biden administration, and senior adviser Patrick McHenry was briefly the acting speaker of the House while he represented North Carolina as a Republican.
In July, the coalition named former CFTC Commissioner Brian Quintenz as a senior advisor and has brought on a pair of lobbying firms to work at the federal level. As of its June 30, the coalition had paid $100,000 to four Invariant lobbyists and registered two Determinant lobbyists.
The coalition has also spent $50,000 lobbying in California through Redwood Public Affairs, the same lobbying firm used by Kalshi.
The coalition’s crypto members are some of the biggest political spenders in the current election cycle. Crypto.com’s parent company, Foris Dax, is the largest donor to MAGA Inc., the main super PAC supporting President Donald Trump. Coinbase is the 10th largest political donor in this election cycle.
The coalition follows a pattern of unified advocacy seen in other lines of business, much like that of the sports betting and gambling industry – which has spent millions on lobbying and industry-specific super PACs this year.
Lipton said the current battle for regulatory control of prediction markets is an “existential question” for the platforms, likely motivating their attempts to increase their political influence.
“It’s not at all clear to me that their business model can compete if they are going to comply with state law,” Lipton said. “They’re really trying to create a situation, I think, where they have enough political power to overcome the legal deficiencies in their arguments.”


This article was originally published by OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that tracks money in politics.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Under Trump, immigration arrests and detentions surge in Tennessee
description: Since Donald Trump was sworn into office for a second time, immigration arrests have surged nationwide as his administration carries out an unprecedented mass detention and deportation agenda.  In Tennessee, the number of people arrested and detained began to climb almost immediately after the president’s January 2025 inauguration. In total, the number of im[...]
text:
Federal immigration agents prepare to enter a South Nashville apartment on April 28, 2026. Immigration detentions have surged across the nation and in Tennessee in President Donald Trump's second term. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Since Donald Trump was sworn into office for a second time, immigration arrests have surged nationwide as his administration carries out an unprecedented mass detention and deportation agenda. 
In Tennessee, the number of people arrested and detained began to climb almost immediately after the president’s January 2025 inauguration.
In total, the number of immigrant arrests and detentions multiplied nearly four-fold in Tennessee during the president’s first year in office, compared to the final year of the Biden administration, according to data the Tennessee Lookout analyzed from the Deportation Data Project at U.C. Berkeley and U.C.L.A. The Deportation Data Project obtained the data from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, through Freedom of Information Act litigation. 
At the current pace of arrests and detentions, ICE is on track to arrest and detain an even greater number of immigrants in Tennessee this year.


Tennessee’s Republican leaders have largely applauded the heightened immigration enforcement activities across the state 
Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton, a Crossville Republican, openly talked about working with Trump’s White House to pass a slate of legislation targeting immigrants without legal status, calling it a “model for the nation.” Several laws prevent immigrants without legal status from accessing the limited public benefits that immigrants without legal status are entitled to, such as public health clinic access.
“Tennessee will not become a sanctuary state for illegal immigration,” Sexton said in a news release last touting recent ICE deportations. “We will ensure our public benefits are only for those who are citizens and who come into our country legally.”
Among state Republican actions was establishing a first-of-its-kind Centralized Immigration Enforcement Bureau in Tennessee whose mission is to “oversee state and local collaboration with federal immigration authorities.”
At the same time, immigrant advocates have sprung into action to provide legal services, organize public protests, organize aid to families left behind by the detentions and train volunteers to monitor and document ICE arrests in real time.
“The Trump administration has aggressively imposed a brutal campaign of mass detention and deportation, sparing no one,” Spring Miller, senior director of legal strategy at the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition wrote in a recent op-ed highlighting the impact of ICE detentions on mothers and children. 








Brenda Perez talks to community volunteers at an April 18 training held by Migra Watch on monitoring ICE interactions. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









Community volunteers wait outside the Department of Homeland Security facility in Nashville as they observe vehicles entering and exiting. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)









Ashley Warbington leads chants at a Jan. 10. 2025 protest of Immigration and Customs Enforcement after ICE officers in Minneapolis shot and killed Renee Good. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)






Hundreds of the Tennessee arrests during Trump’s second term stemmed from large-scale, targeted operations highlighted in ICE news releases. 
ICE announced 196 arrests in Nashville during a weeklong traffic stop dragnet in May 2025 dubbed “Operation Flood the Zone,” conducted in partnership with the Tennessee Highway Patrol. 
On May 5, 2025, as part of an immigration dragnet in South Nashville, Immigration agents gather at the Department of Homeland Security's office in Nashville. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Federal immigration agents remove a man from an apartment complex in South Nashville on April 28, 2026. The agents were met by protesters. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)ICE agents arrested 7 undocumented people when they showed up for traffic court in Robertson County. Wo mothers were arrested along with others

Photographs by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout
In May 2026, ICE in partnership with Sevierville police and sheriffs arrested and detained 117 immigrants in east Tennessee in “Operation Smoky Mountain.” In the initial weeks after Trump created the crime-fighting Memphis Safe Task Force in October ICE data shows more than 400 arrests and detentions of immigrants in that city. 


Partnerships between ICE and local police and sheriffs have also driven increasing immigration arrests that have taken place largely out of public view. 
Before Trump retook office, just two Tennessee sheriffs had entered into so-called 287(g) agreements with the federal government to cooperate with the federal government in immigration enforcement.
Today there are more than 120. 


While federal officials have pledged to target the “worst of the worst” in immigration enforcement, data shows the majority of immigrants detained in Tennessee since the beginning of 2025 had not been convicted of any crime. Two-thirds of those detained had either no criminal mark on their record or faced pending charges. 


While immigration arrests and detentions are occurring across Tennessee, Memphis has seen the largest number, followed by Nashville/Davidson County, Knox County, Rutherford County and Hamilton County. 


Gov. Bill Lee greets President Donald Trump during a March 23 event in Memphis at which Trump said the Memphis Safe Task Force was a model for the nation. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Northwest Arkansas growing pains, national concerns top issues at Springdale political gathering
description: Rain and overcast skies didn’t dampen the mood at the annual Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ event Thursday at Springdale’s Shiloh Square as residents, business owners and elected officials networked over plates of fried chicken and shrimp. During election years, the 16-year-old gathering is a popular stop for candidates in a rapidly growing region that’s hom[...]
text:
Guests attend the Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ networking event at Springdale's Shiloh Square on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Rain and overcast skies didn’t dampen the mood at the annual Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ event Thursday at Springdale’s Shiloh Square as residents, business owners and elected officials networked over plates of fried chicken and shrimp.
During election years, the 16-year-old gathering is a popular stop for candidates in a rapidly growing region that’s home to some of the world’s largest companies. And this year’s event occurred as Democrats hope to make gains in a heavily Republican state.
Shiloh Square was humming with chatter and music this year as hundreds packed into the open-air space. Some guests of the Springdale Chamber of Commerce event stood in small groups casually chatting beneath strings of lights hung from the roof. Others sat at round tables decorated with checkered tablecloths and enjoyed dinner served buffet style on paper plates.
Democrats see rare signs of hope in solidly red Arkansas’ midterms

Voters at the gathering said healthcare, immigration and economic development were top of mind for them as they prepare for the midterm election. 
Laura H. Tyler, CEO of Arisa Health, the state’s largest behavioral health provider, said she spoke to Washington County Sheriff Jay Cantrell about the needs for mental health services in jails. 
“That’s not the right place for them, but our nation has by default made them institutions,” Tyler said. 
Arkansas historically ranks low in several healthcare areas and that won’t improve until investments are made, she said. 
“I think we could be very wise with our limited funds here in Arkansas if we would look at how to treat the whole person,” Tyler said. 
Adan Torres of Rogers works for a local health system and said he still has more research to do before heading to the polls, including how Immigration and Customs Enforcement is enforcing the Trump administration’s mass deportation efforts. 
Torres said he wants to learn how candidates will “rein it back in and focus on the right people to deport versus just randomly finding people that are trying to live life.”
President Donald Trump’s national immigration crackdown has received criticism for fatal encounters, wasteful spending and the arrests of people without criminal records.
Guests attend the Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ networking event at Springdale's Shiloh Square on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Springdale Mayor Doug Sprouse (right) speaks with U.S. Rep. Steve Womack during the annual Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ networking event at Springdale's Shiloh Square on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate) Circuit Judge candidate Wendy Howerton speaks with guests at the annual Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ event at Springdale's Shiloh Square on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate) Guests attend the Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ networking event at Springdale's Shiloh Square on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Robb Ryerse, Democratic candidate for Arkansas' 3rd Congressional District, and his wife, Vanessa, speak with a guest of the Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ networking event at Springdale's Shiloh Square on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Washington County Judge Republican candidate Tim Shepard (left) and Washington County Quorum Court member Vladimir Rivera Lopez share a laugh at the annual Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ event at Springdale's Shiloh Square on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Michael Pakko, Libertarian candidate for Arkansas secretary of state, listens to guests at the Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ networking event at Springdale's Shiloh Square on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Guests attend the Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ networking event at Springdale's Shiloh Square on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)
Tricia Shaw of Springdale, who helped hand out koozies on behalf of her employer and event sponsor Flintco, said she “absolutely” plans to vote and one of her biggest concerns is funding for new construction. 
“I want to know that we’re going to continue to keep up with the infrastructure that we need in this area because the growth continues to be monumental,” she said. 
Northwest Arkansas is the ninth fastest-growing metro in the country due to rapid economic growth spurred by companies like Walmart and Tyson Foods being headquartered in the region. The community has also been boosted by investments from the heirs of Walmart founder Sam Walton, including an art museum and medical school founded by his daughter, Alice.
But affordable housing has become an issue for Benton and Washington counties because demand has outpaced the construction of new homes. Construction has also been limited in some towns by limited sewer infrastructure capacity. 
Watermelons and Arkansas politics collide in Hope festival

Concerns about the region’s growing pains were echoed by Robb Ryerse, a Springdale Democrat seeking to represent Arkansas’ 3rd Congressional District. He faces incumbent Republican Rep. Steve Womack and Libertarian Bobby Wilson.
Ryerse, who attended Chickin, Peelin’ & Politickin’ for the first time, said much of his conversations with guests focused on the future of Springdale and how the city has grown. 
“I think it’s really important for us to make sure that no working families get left behind in the process of that growth,” he said. 
Republican state Rep. Chad Puryear said voters in nearby House District 25 are concerned about property taxes increasing in the rapidly growing region. While property taxes are levied at the county level, Puryear said the Legislature would look at “any avenue we can get some tax relief while still funding county government.”
Puryear, who’s facing Democrat Courtney King in November’s election, said he supports continuing to increase the homestead tax credit. Lawmakers raised the credit to $675 earlier this year. 
Fresh off visiting all 75 of Arkansas’ counties, U.S. Senate candidate Libertarian Jeff Wadlin said voters have told him they’re frustrated. 
“They’re obviously frustrated with the cost of living, but they’re also frustrated with the two-party system and that’s why Libertarians like us are in the race to give people a third option and a third option that’s in the middle,” he said. 
Wadlin faces Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton and Democrat Hallie Shoffner in the general election.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Youth vote skews heavily to Democrats in Michigan, swing states, economic issues stay top concerns
description: Democrats have a large advantage among young voters in Michigan across the different races coming to the ballot in November, according to a new poll from the Alliance for Youth Power PAC and YouGov released Monday, which showed “pretty unambiguously good news for Democrats,” as John Ray, a senior political analyst at YouGov Blue, described […]
text:
Line to register to vote and cast a ballot at the University of Michigan, Nov. 8, 2022 | Laina G. StebbinsDemocrats have a large advantage among young voters in Michigan across the different races coming to the ballot in November, according to a new poll from the Alliance for Youth Power PAC and YouGov released Monday, which showed “pretty unambiguously good news for Democrats,” as John Ray, a senior political analyst at YouGov Blue, described in a press call on Friday.
Democratic candidates held large margins in each of the statewide elections surveyed. 61% of respondents said that they plan to vote for Democrat Jocelyn Benson for governor, while 26% said they plan to vote for Republican John James. The margin was even wider in the U.S. Senate race, where 66% of participants said that they plan to vote for Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and 24% said that they plan to vote for Republican Mike Rogers.
Benson and El-Sayed also had higher approval ratings than the Republicans in their respective races, according to the survey.
“The easy read here is that young voters are with Democrats, and the job is done just less than five weeks away. But across all these eight states, we see Republicans top out with not even getting 30 percent, and this generation is hungry for something new,” Dakota Hall, executive director of the Alliance for Youth Action, said. “Young people are looking at who’s making their rent, their groceries, their future harder, and they’ve made a judgment in this moment about who is actually really doing that, and they’ve also made a judgment on who is actually running government corruption and taking a stand against that.”
Even in the Secretary of State race — an election in which around a fifth of voters said that they were undecided, and more than 60% of voters said that for each candidate they had “no opinion” — 55% said that they plan to vote for Democrat Garlin Gilchrist and 25% said that they plan to vote for Republican Anthony Forlini. The race for attorney general, Michigan’s other statewide election, was not included in the survey.
YouGov_AYP_SlideDeck
Across all U.S. House races in the state, gaps by gender and education persist, though across demographics, young voters still skew heavily towards Democratic candidates. In Michigan, men had a 25-point differential between Democrats and Republicans, while women had a 43-point gap. College-educated voters had a 41-point gap in favor of Democrats, while for voters without college degrees, that gap shrank to 34 points.
One key issue where young voters seem to be coalescing is disapproval of President Donald Trump. In Michigan, 78% of voters had an unfavorable opinion of the president while just 19% had a favorable opinion, similar to those in most other battleground states.
Even among previous Trump voters, the president only has about a 65% approval rating nationally for young voters in that camp.
“By really any measure available in the data, Trump’s reputation among young people is very bad,” Ray said.
The poll covered eight battleground states with about 400 respondents in each, with a margin of error of about five percentage points, and surveyed voters ages 18-29. It included voters in Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Nevada, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.
Most of those voters in Michigan are first-time voters who did not cast ballots in 2024 or earlier — 42% are eligible to vote for the first time, while an additional 32% are voting for the first time in 2026 despite being eligible to vote in a previous election.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Only 37% of Michigan’s young voters said that they feel “very prepared” to vote, but another 48% said that they feel “somewhat prepared.” Only 21% said that they feel either “somewhat unprepared” or “very unprepared” to vote in November.
Across the battleground states surveyed, economic issues were the most important to young voters, a finding that also held true in Michigan. Almost half of voters listed inflation or the cost of living as one of their top three priorities in the election, and over 20% of voters said that housing cost and rent, economy and jobs, or corruption in the political system were among their top three priorities.
“Something we are tracking here is that young people, to a unique degree, are also reporting being concerned about corruption in our political system,” Ray said. “Corruption as an issue is rising in many different segments of the electorate. It kind of began to creep up early, a few months into Trump’s second term. Now, actually, it is a top concern for several pieces of the electorate, particularly high currently for young voters.”
Other issues such as climate change and the conflict in Israel and Gaza were among the top three priorities for a smaller share of voters, around 10% each.
Ray also described “broad-based economic pessimism” among young voters about the state of their own personal finances compared with the previous year.

title: Federal grant will help WV State University preserve historic Malden homes
description: West Virginia State University is moving forward with a project to preserve two historic Kanawha Valley homes with the help of a federal grant. The university was recently awarded a $398,000 historic preservation grant from the U.S. Department of Interior National Park Service through a program that helps preserve properties on the National Register of […]
text:
The historic Norton House (left) and Hale House (right) in Malden, West Virginia. West Virginia State University has received a nearly $400,000 federal historic preservation grant to preserve the structures, built in the 1800s. (Photos courtesy of West Virginia State University)West Virginia State University is moving forward with a project to preserve two historic Kanawha Valley homes with the help of a federal grant.
The university was recently awarded a $398,000 historic preservation grant from the U.S. Department of Interior National Park Service through a program that helps preserve properties on the National Register of Historic Places.  
The school aims to preserve two buildings it owns in the Malden Village Historic District in Kanawha County: the Hale House and the Norton House, it said in the news release Sept. 4.
“We are thankful to the National Park Service and to United States Senator Shelley Moore Capito, Congresswoman Carol Miller and former Senator Joe Manchin for their support in helping the university to secure this grant,” WVSU President Ericke S. Cage said in the release. “These historic properties listed on the National Register of Historic Places played a vital role in the history and evolution of the Kanawha Valley’s early salt industry, and we are hopeful this investment will help us to maintain these properties for the benefit of future generations.”
Built in 1938, Hale House was the one-time home of Dr. John Hale, an influential 1800s Kanawha Valley business and political leader. Hale was owner of possibly the largest salt works in North America, supplying the thriving meat-packing center of Cincinnati, according to the university. 
Norton House is the oldest frame house in Malden, built around 1840 by Moses and James Norton, a father and son pair who were bookkeepers for salt makers in the area, the school said in the release. 
Before any restoration work on the houses can begin, the school has hired an architectural firm to complete an engineering report of the structures. The report will help the school determine what next steps will be, said Curtis Johnson, the school’s executive advisor to the president for strategic initiatives and government affairs. Johnson is the lead coordinator on the grant for the school. 
Johnson said the school does not yet know what the full cost to restore the homes will be. The $398,000 amount in the congressional directed spending grant was a guess, he said. 
The homes are in need of repairs that could include foundation, porches, floors, ceilings, doors, roofs, restrooms, windows, HVAC systems and siding, Johnson said.
Leaders of the school — one of two historically black colleges and universities in the state — are getting the engineering report done in order to be the “best steward of the money that we’ve received,” Johnson said. 
“There is concern that the true cost of restoration for these two homes will be in excess of the money that we currently have,” Johnson said. “But again, you can’t really ask for more money in a responsible manner unless you know how much money you need, and have some documentation as to that cost. So this was, I think, a plan with very good stewardship to be able to tackle that next feat.”
The school has hired WYK Associates, Inc, a Clarksburg architectural firm, to do the report, Johnson said. 
He said the school may conceivably open the structures to the public in some manner when they’re restored, but that’s an idea the school still has to flesh out. Those are questions that will be answered at a later date when the school knows what it will cost to fully restore the homes, he said. 
The university acquired the structures under a prior administration. In 2024 and 2023, the school conducted archeological field schools on the Hale House grounds, a spokesman for the school said. 
“I don’t know precisely what the vision was for the prior administration that brought in (the homes) and how that aligns with the current day needs at the university and things,” Johnson said. “That’s the issue, of course. There has to be a lot of focus here on campus with regards to our mission to educate and serve the public here through our land grant mission.
“We are definitely wanting to make sure we honor the history of Malden, as well, and do that in a responsible manner,” Johnson said.
The university expects to have the engineering report by late November, if all goes as planned.

Saginaw City Council voted 8-0 to approve a data center zoning ordinance. Alexander Gustanksi of Mid-Michigan Now reports that the new rules require developers to provide a good neighbor policy,  a water consumption and thermal management report, an electric and natural gas service report and citizen participation measures.

Updates

The Michigan Public Service Commission on Thursday unanimously approved contracts for DTE Energy to supply power to Google’s 1 gigawatt data center, Brian Allnutt of Planet Detroit reports. The data center is expected to come online in December 2027.
Additionally, the Wayne County Commission voted unanimously to override Wayne County Executive Warren Evans’ veto of a $125 million tax break for the Google data center and community benefits agreement tied to the project, Candice Williams reports in The Detroit News.

Legislative Action

State Rep. Reggie Miller (D-Van Buren Township) introduced House Bills 6426 and 6427. The legislation is intended to strengthen legal protections for local governments and require large-scale data center developers to provide up-front disclosure on the facility’s expected energy and water use, infrastructure needs, environmental impacts, ownership information and any expansion plans. The bills were referred to the House Government Operations Committee.

News of Note

Ahead of the University of Michigan’s second town hall discussing its $1.25 billion computing center project with Los Alamos National Lab, U-M Regent Paul Brown joined township residents and labor representatives in speaking out against the facility, Allnutt also reported.
As Michigan’s largest energy companies look into building new natural gas power plants, Lucas Smolcic Larson of MLive examines what role data centers play in driving energy demand in the state.

description: Archaeologists recently removed seven coffins containing human remains and an unknown wooden box from a construction site near the North Dakota governor’s residence, according to the Office of Management and Budget. The archaeologists explored more than 80 areas of interest in September after human remains were discovered in May while construction crews were[...]
text:
Freshly smoothed dirt rests behind a fence outside the North Dakota governor's residence in Bismarck on Sept. 30, 2026, after seven coffins containing human remains were exhumed from the site. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Archaeologists recently removed seven coffins containing human remains and an unknown wooden box from a construction site near the North Dakota governor’s residence, according to the Office of Management and Budget.
The archaeologists explored more than 80 areas of interest in September after human remains were discovered in May while construction crews were installing a new fence around the property.
Brandon Solberg, facilities management director for the office, said in a statement that archaeologists will now review and catalog all remains and items discovered during fieldwork. That analysis is expected to continue into early 2027.
“It’s going to take a while now to do the research and analysis,” Solberg said in an interview last week. 
 


The archaeologists are trying to identify basic information, such as age ranges, and potentially diseases, Solberg said. DNA testing will not be part of the analysis, he said.
The area where the remains were discovered was once part of Bismarck’s first cemetery from 1873 to 1877, OMB said previously. Many of those burials were reinterred to St. Mary’s Cemetery and Fairview Cemetery in the 1880s. 
Remains were also discovered on the Capitol grounds during the 1903 construction of a trolley line near the southwest corner of the property and in 1959 during construction of the previous governor’s residence, according to the statement. 
The office said it has contracted with a local funeral home, and Crisis Care Chaplaincy has volunteered its services to ensure the remains are handled with care. Reinterment at a local cemetery is expected to take place in the spring, Solberg said.
Lawmakers last year approved $2.35 million for security upgrades to the governor’s residence, including the fence and driveway extension. As of Sept. 1, the archaeological work was estimated to cost the state an additional $155,000, according to the Office of Management and Budget.
The office did not provide an update for additional costs after the exhumation work was completed. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Boulder, fossil-fuel companies face off at the Supreme Court in high-stakes climate case
description: Attorneys representing two Colorado local governments are set for a high-stakes legal showdown over climate change Monday at the U.S. Supreme Court, where they’ll ask justices to allow Boulder’s lawsuit seeking monetary damages from two fossil fuel companies to proceed in state court. With help from the Trump administration, the two companies, Suncor Energy[...]
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Attorneys representing two Colorado local governments are set for a high-stakes legal showdown over climate change Monday at the U.S. Supreme Court, where they’ll ask justices to allow Boulder’s lawsuit seeking monetary damages from two fossil fuel companies to proceed in state court.
With help from the Trump administration, the two companies, Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil, have asked the court to step in and quash the lawsuit, which was filed in 2018 by Boulder County and the city of Boulder. The plaintiffs are seeking monetary damages under state tort law “for the substantial role (the companies) played and continue to play in causing, contributing to and exacerbating climate change.”
Monday’s Supreme Court hearing in the case, known as Suncor v. Boulder, follows another unprecedented summer of record heat, extreme drought conditions and destructive wildfire activity impacting communities across Colorado. Boulder’s suit is one of more than 30 similar cases filed to date by state and local governments nationwide as human-caused climate change, mostly the result of fossil-fuel combustion, pushes average global temperatures to dangerous new highs.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“This case is really about who’s going to bear the costs of all of these accelerating effects that we’re experiencing on the front lines here in Colorado,” Chris Winter, an environmental attorney and executive director of the Getches-Wilkinson Center at the University of Colorado School of Law, said in an interview. “Are those costs just going to fall on the shoulders of all of the taxpayers and citizens and our local governments? Or is the oil industry going to be at least partially responsible for their role in contributing to this crisis?”
Exxon and Suncor, a Canadian oil giant that operates Colorado’s only fossil fuel refinery, argue that federal law preempts Boulder’s efforts to hold the companies accountable in state court. The defendants have tried and failed repeatedly to have the case dismissed or removed to federal court, most recently in May 2025, when the Colorado Supreme Court issued a ruling allowing the case to proceed.
Soon after that ruling, however, the companies asked the U.S. Supreme Court, where conservatives hold a 6-3 majority, to step in. Their petition asks the nation’s highest court to rule that federal statute “precludes state-law claims seeking relief for injuries allegedly caused by the effects of interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions on the global climate.”
In February, justices agreed to hear the case, which is set to be among the most closely watched proceedings on the court’s docket for the 2026-27 term, and one of its highest-profile climate change decisions ever. A ruling from the court could have profound consequences for the dozens of other lawsuits seeking climate-related damages from fossil fuel companies, as scientists warn that catastrophic impacts from higher temperatures will continue to accelerate.
The view from aboard a Colorado National Guard helicopter, in which Gov. Jared Polis on Dec. 31, 2021, got a flyover tour of Boulder County neighborhoods destroyed by wildfires the previous day. (Hart Van Denburg/CPR, pool)
In an unusual move, President Donald J. Trump’s administration filed an unsolicited brief in support of Suncor and Exxon’s petition shortly after it was filed, urging the court to overturn the Colorado Supreme Court’s decision, which it called “contrary to the Constitution.” Alongside petitioners and respondents, U.S. Solicitor General John Sauer will be given time during Monday’s oral arguments to represent the Trump administration’s position in support of the companies.
“We’ve seen this administration really bend over backwards to serve the interests of the fossil-fuel industry, and this case is just one of many examples,” Winter said. “A lot of us who watch the court and have studied these issues for a long time are quite troubled by some of the legal arguments this administration has used, to try to undercut the ability of the states to protect (their) citizens, and to insulate the oil industry from liability for its actions.”
Alito’s recusal
In another unusual development, Justice Samuel Alito, one of the Supreme Court’s most conservative members, recused himself from further proceedings in the case last week.
Though the court’s announcement did not explain why, environmental advocates had called for Alito’s recusal because he owns stock in at least two oil companies. He previously stepped aside from a separate environmental case involving the oil industry in January of this year.
Critics say Alito’s abrupt recusal, announced just days before oral argument, raises the question of why he nonetheless participated in the court’s deliberations over whether to take up the case in the first place. Known as granting a writ of certiorari, that process requires at least four of the court’s nine justices to agree to accept a petition. The court does not release such votes publicly.
“We don’t know whether Alito’s vote made the difference, and that uncertainty is precisely the problem,” Alexandra Nagy, organizing director of the nonprofit Consumer Watchdog, said in a statement last week. “The Court is preparing to hear a case of enormous national consequence after one of the justices who participated in granting review concluded days before the hearing that he should no longer participate. If Alito was the fourth vote, this case should be dismissed.”
In their petition, Suncor and Exxon raise the specter of “potentially crushing monetary liability” imposed on fossil fuel companies for what they repeatedly refer to as the “alleged harms” of climate change.
The Suncor oil refinery in Commerce City is one of Colorado’s largest sources of air pollution. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
“The requested damages in any one case could reach into the billions,” attorneys for the companies wrote. “And if claims such as Boulder’s are allowed to proceed, every political jurisdiction in the Nation could bring a similar suit against any subset of the world’s fossil-fuel producers.”
Attorneys for Boulder’s city and county governments say it’s far too early for the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case — which, despite having been filed eight years ago, has not even proceeded to the trial stage amid the protracted jurisdictional challenges made by the companies. Neither the Constitution nor any legislation passed Congress preempts the state’s authority to try the case under tort law, they argue.
“Unwilling to let either the federal legislative or the state judicial process play out, (Suncor and Exxon) have run to this Court at the case’s outset, claiming that something implicit in the Constitution resolves the debate,” Boulder’s attorneys wrote in a response to the court.
“The conservative justices, and conservative line of thinking, usually interprets the Constitution in a way that protects the authority of the states, unless there’s been a very explicit grant of limited authority to the federal government that’s found in the text of the Constitution,” Winter said. “But this case flies directly in the face of that typical way of looking at the Constitution — because there’s nothing in the text of the Constitution that says states are preempted in this field.”

 Catching Our Eye

• We’ve all been there… The Ohio Newsroom’s Kaitlin Thorne digs into “The challenge of growing colossal pumpkins inside Ohio’s prisons”
Behind barbed-wired fences and multiple security checks sits a small patch of land in the center of the Belmont Correctional Institution in southeast Ohio’s Belmont County.
The growing season is over, so it doesn’t look like much now, but just a few weeks ago it was home to a colossal pumpkin weighing 1,700 lbs.
The pumpkin-growing tradition dates back to 2022, when Mansfield Correctional Institution issued a challenge: grow the biggest pumpkin in a prison yard. The Larry Stewart Giant Pumpkin Challenge, in its fifth year, now involves correctional institutions across the state.
• Notes from the underground. The Cincinnati Enquirer’s Sydney Franklin reports, “Cincinnati firms chosen to plan next steps on reviving subway tunnels”
The effort to revive Cincinnati’s abandoned subway tunnels is not over. And some of the world’s leading design and engineering experts have vied to study how to repurpose them, a sign that this could be more than a city daydream.
Over-the-Rhine-based Woolpert Inc. was ultimately chosen to lead the study for $284,073.
City records obtained by The Enquirer reveal that Woolpert and its team have likely been working on the feasibility study throughout this year. The final study is estimated to be done by early 2027.
• Delay tactics. Jonathan Walsh from News5Cleveland reports, “A man has lived in a $4.5 million mansion for 15 years while fighting foreclosure — now he’s facing eviction”
Louis Telerico has been living in a 17,000-square-foot home in Barrington Estates, an exclusive residential area in Aurora, near the 17th green of a golf course.
A foreclosure on the property began in August 2011. Court records show Telerico filed numerous motions over the years, including multiple bankruptcies, appeals, and other filings. The foreclosure took 14 years before the bank finally acquired the property in 2025, then sold it to investment company ERADAL.
At a recent eviction hearing, a magistrate approved the eviction of Telerico. However, Telerico’s attorney, Mark Graziani, indicated the situation may not be fully resolved.
Telerico told News 5 he plans to live in the house until he dies and said he believes he will be able to secure financing.
