name: Maryland Matters
title: Third-party candidates decry exclusion from only debate of the governor’s race
description: There are four candidates on the ballot for governor this fall. There will be two on stage Tuesday for the only scheduled debate of the campaign. To Andy Ellis and Cathy White, that doesn’t seem right. Ellis, the Green Party nominee, and White, the nominee of the Working Class Party, have continued, without success, to […]
text:
Former Prince George's County Executive Rushern L. Baker III (D), right, prepares for a Maryland Public Television debate on Monday. Photo by Bruce DePuyt.There are four candidates on the ballot for governor this fall. There will be two on stage Tuesday for the only scheduled debate of the campaign. To Andy Ellis and Cathy White, that doesn’t seem right.
Ellis, the Green Party nominee, and White, the nominee of the Working Class Party, have continued, without success, to push for inclusion in the debate being held by Maryland Public Television. But MPT says only Gov. Wes Moore, the Democratic nominee, and Republican nominee Dan Cox met the criteria to be on the stage.
“We claim to be living in a democracy, yet they put up all these barriers to having third parties in the first place,” White said last week. “The two-party system is a trap that we’re stuck in, like this ping-pong game, just going back and forth, and we’re all the losers for it.”
According to MPT, which is broadcasting the upcoming debate, candidates must be polling at 10% to be eligible to participate in their broadcast debates. That’s tough to do, notes Ellis, when most polls don’t include candidates besides Moore and Cox in their questions to voters.
“There’s a lot of people who look at Wes Moore and Dan Cox and don’t feel like that represents what they want to vote for and would like to see other choices,” Ellis said last week. “The value of adding those … outweighs any lost time that comes with a few extra questions.”
MPT said in a statement to Maryland Matters on Thursday that its content division, its news and public affairs team, and additional broadcast partners collaborate to organize candidate debates “designed to best serve the public interest of citizens across Maryland.”
The ballot takes shape, as state officials certify a handful of third-party hopefuls for Nov. 3

Its content division and senior leadership team review the political debate guidelines about every four years after an election cycle. According to MPT, When conducting a review, the team considers feedback from residents across the state to determine whether updates to debate or participation guidelines are necessary.
But for now, Ellis and White will likely be watching the debate from home.
Ellis has repeatedly demanded answers from MPT leadership, and said he also obtained signatures from hundreds of Maryland voters in support of all parties being included in the debate, which he also sent to MPT leadership.
But in an email Friday, MPT reiterated its position, telling Ellis he had “failed to demonstrate a significant candidacy” through polling, by “demonstrated voter interest” for previous office, substantial media coverage or “financial resources, sizeable volunteer efforts, or large turnouts at campaign stops.”
White said in a Thursday interview it isn’t fair to her or Ellis to be left out of the debate because they aren’t polling in the same manner as major party candidates, who gain far more funding and traction across their campaigns.
Though White said she has been in communication with Ellis regarding an attempt at debate participation, she hasn’t taken much action and has accepted that MPT won’t allow her to debate. She plans to tune in to Tuesday’s broadcast.
Ellis and White separately detailed their frustration with not being able to participate in an event seemingly meant to help voters make a more informed decision on election day.
After back-and-forth discussion with MPT about his debate eligibility, Ellis requested public records over the summer regarding internal MPT communications with or about excluded candidates, records related to the required threshold, and written debate eligibility policies.
Email correspondence obtained by Ellis shows MPT leaders in discussions about not following their debate criteria when extending the 2026 Republican primary debate invitation to the nine candidates running for the nomination this summer. Only three candidates, not including Cox, showed up for the debate in May.
“Your participation would ensure the people of Maryland get a better picture of their electoral options for Governor this election cycle,” MPT emails to Republican candidates in late spring read.
Trio of GOP candidates for governor — out of nine total — meet in debate

Ellis said he agrees with the MPT’s attempt at including all primary candidates and believes its leaders should be taking the same initiative to include the four gubernatorial candidates for the midterm debate.
Other records obtained by Ellis show MPT leaders coordinating and organizing the 2022 gubernatorial midterm debate details and candidates involved before public polling had even begun. He claims that shows MPT was shutting out third-party candidates and reducing their chances at public exposure from the jump. MPT did not comment on these claims.
Public records cited by Ellis also show that Richard Bodorf, the chair of the Maryland Public Broadcast Commission, which is MPT’s governing body, and his wife maxed out donations to Moore’s campaign, giving up to $6,000 each at times since last fall. That shows MPT’s bias toward Moore is excluding the state’s non-principal parties, Ellis said.
MPT wrote in its statement that the broadcast commission doesn’t have any involvement with the planning or decision making for its debates. Bodorff acted within the law when providing candidate donations to Moore, and was chosen for his role as chair because of his extensive background with the Federal Communications Commission, not because of any campaign contributions, MPT added.
Todd Eberly, a political science professor at St. Mary’s College of Maryland, said in an interview last week that a media organization being in charge of the debate broadcast doesn’t necessarily mean it gives way to viewpoint discrimination. These organizations, as part of the nature of the field, already pick and choose what viewpoints are worthy of attention in their day to day, he said.
Today’s voters might not believe debates are as productive as they used to be, Eberly said, with regulations on how candidates can speak to each other and time limits on their responses. But even though political figures are more virtually connected with voters than ever, Eberly said these debates can still have value.
He noted that third party candidates have shown up on debate stages before, but usually through buckets of funding and political and business connections. These conversations surrounding debates and campaign platforms are just another example of the ever-changing nature of how politics are conducted, he added.
Moderating organizations “still see them [debates] as being worthwhile, but if you don’t get the two main characters to participate, no one is going to watch,” Eberly said. “Viewership of databases isn’t what it used to be and the need for them isn’t what it used to be.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Despite their struggles to be on Tuesday’s debate stage, the third-party candidates agreed that these types of forums are still useful to voters and would boost their exposure.
Even if candidates now might have different avenues to promote their campaign now as opposed to past generations, through social media or news releases, Ellis believes voters want to see candidates engage with one another without a filter. That’s what debates are best at. White also said she believes that not including all candidates blindsides voters, as they don’t get the opportunity to observe the opinions of every candidate in the race.
If he isn’t permitted to participate, Ellis said he does not plan to hold a hold a separate event or mount a protest against MPT, but hopes to to be able to attend the debate and listen in.
“We can talk about why it would be better if we were included, but I’m not going to force myself on to the stage,” he added.
White said she understands her chances of winning against major party candidates are slim, but participating in the debate would allow her to spread her platform and give her party more publicity.
“We’re all on the ballot. We did everything, jumped through all the hoops of fire we were supposed to do,” White said. “Why can’t we all just be in the debate? Are people afraid of ideas? Is this not a democracy? I don’t see what the problem is.”
— Maryland Matters reporter Bryan P. Sears contributed to this report.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Can AI agents produce real news reporting in Rhode Island? A human journalist has some thoughts.
description: Since July, a Rhode Island news site has been publishing stories by authors that don’t exist.  Kelly Lockhart, a housing reporter for Uprise RI, wrote about the widening gap between earnings and housing costs in the Ocean State. Correspondent Adriana Vossari covered the latest votes — on zoning, school procurement, criminal justice for juveniles, and […]
text:
A page on the Uprise RI news site explains how it reports news using AI. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)Since July, a Rhode Island news site has been publishing stories by authors that don’t exist. 
Kelly Lockhart, a housing reporter for Uprise RI, wrote about the widening gap between earnings and housing costs in the Ocean State. Correspondent Adriana Vossari covered the latest votes — on zoning, school procurement, criminal justice for juveniles, and other issues — from the Providence City Council. Debut stories by national politics reporter Ryan MacMahonaghan, labor reporter Eddie Exxe, and other correspondents followed. 
None of them are actual humans. They are, as the site notes, “computing agents — intelligent LLM reporters.” 
They kept up their work with little fanfare until Sept. 17 when Boston Globe media reporter Aidan Ryan reported on Uprise RI’s novel approach to newsgathering in the AI age. 
Other Rhode Island news organizations have tinkered or dabbled with artificial intelligence. The Providence Journal partnered with the AI-powered search engine, Perplexity. The Globe’s RI bureau published an op-ed that included the disclaimer: “The author used generative AI to help draft this commentary.” 
But no outlet, as far as I know, had farmed out entire stories to chatbots before. 
Uprise RI was founded in 2017 by progressive independent journalist Steve Ahlquist and is now owned solely by software developer Greg Brailsford.
Brailsford, who joined Uprise RI in 2020, declined interview requests from the Globe but did tell the paper, via email, that he thought the use of AI personas to report the news would become more common. Uprise RI, he told the Globe, is “a bit ahead of the game.”
This country’s robust freedom of speech gives people wide latitude to speak and publish without prior permission or regulation. But we should discuss big shifts in how our communities are covered. Because journalism is the lifeblood of democracy. And if that process is outsourced to machines — even if, as Uprise RI insists, humans oversee “Editorial standards, judgment calls, and corrections” — that has implications for all of us.  
I was an unpaid contributor to Uprise RI, when Ahlquist ran and edited the site. Alquist left in 2023, and I continue to contribute to his Substack on an unpaid basis. He had nothing to do with this article. I’m writing this as a Rhode Islander, journalist, longtime observer and reporter on local media and someone who frequently gives library talks about media literacy and misinformation. 
First, I want to thank Brailsford and Uprise RI. By going further than any other local outlet in the blending of AI tools with journalism, the site has sparked an important and timely conversation.
In theory, more coverage of local government is a good thing. One of the places hardest hit by the deterioration of local news has been the kind of granular, hyper-local reporting that Uprise RI offers. Go to the site and you’ll find coverage of zoning boards, city councils, and school committees. This is an admirable attempt to fill an existing gap.
But I have thoughts about Uprise RI’s approach.
Transparency, transparency, transparency
The Society of Professional Journalists’ Code of Ethics has a whole quadrant of principles under the heading “BE ACCOUNTABLE AND TRANSPARENT.” This need for transparency in the news-reporting process is even more urgent when non-human technologies are being used.
In Uprise RI’s case, I wish Brailsford had offered an essay at the start of the LLM-reporting endeavor introducing the “reporters,” explaining how the process works and how this serves the public. And, in general, I would love to see the site feature more prominent labeling that the articles are generated by artificial intelligence. Right now, you have to click a “reporter’s” “bio” to see the “Digital LLM Reporter” label. 
One day after the Globe article, Brailsford published a piece, “How a Rhode Island meeting becomes a story,” that explains the site’s process. The site’s “About” page now has a section labeled “Why do our reporters have human names and human faces?” 
I say: Keep going. 
Nothing about using LLMs for reporting is obvious or self-explanatory. I believe prominent labeling and explanation — to an extent not just equal to, but beyond what human-written sites offer — should be a staple of any AI-journalism operation.
Understand: Hesitation about AI is well-earned 
I spoke with Brailsford via direct messages on the social media platform Bluesky. 
“I almost never see journalists who write about AI talk about its benefits, and when they do, it’s a sentence or two, with the rest of the piece being how terrible it is,” he told me. Brailsford insisted he was no AI “defender” but has used AI for over two years and sees its great potential. 
AI may well have miraculous and beneficial applications. But its downsides are glaring. Even if you don’t believe AI is going to lead to mass human extinction, it is certainly going to put lots of people out of work. Chatbots are often trained on the uncompensated lifting of intellectual property. Some of AI’s most visible champions are throwing money at President Donald Trump. Data centers essential to the success of AI are now so unpopular they are one of the few issues that unite our intensely divided country. 
Anyone who aims to blend AI and journalism should be prepared to meet the audience where they already are — skeptical, wary, perhaps even angry — and not where they believe readers should be. 
Rolling out AI tools in journalism is hard, perhaps impossible 
People are used to getting their news from human beings. Journalists are familiar faces on TVs and voices on our radios. They are with us during a community’s darkest moments. In Rhode Island, journalists are our neighbors: people we run into at the coffee shop or grocery store, people whose kids go to our kids’ school.
Moreover, news reporting is an activity that involves some of the processes that make us most human: conversations, sensory descriptions (smells, sounds, feelings), and an ever-evolving application of ethical considerations. To shift this work to robots is not a minor tweak; it fundamentally rethinks what journalism is.
Beyond that, accuracy is paramount in journalism, and AI is a misinformation accelerant. We see this in Google’s frequently erroneous AI-fueled search summaries and the flood of AI-generated images. AI fakes even hindered the manhunt for the Brown University mass shooter last December.
For lots of good reasons, many folks associate AI with fakery and falsehoods. This is a major, perhaps insurmountable, hurdle to getting them to trust AI-reported news.
What if these stories never got told?
In my exchanges with Brailsford, it was clear we approach this issue from very different perspectives. We disagreed about a lot. He did not appreciate it when — since we weren’t speaking face to face, or even via phone — I asked to confirm I was speaking with a human being, not an LLM. 
But he said something that stuck with me.
He told me that, even when Ahlquist worked at the site, Uprise RI never made a lot of money. 
So he doesn’t see using LLMs as a substitute for human reporters; it’s a way to publish stories that otherwise won’t get written. 
“I, for one, want to know this information about the town I live in,” Brailsford, who lives in Cumberland, told me. “I don’t care who writes it. If it’s accurate, then I don’t care if a little child writes it, if a seasoned journalist writes it, or if a machine writes it. I just want to know what happened.”
It’s a provocative idea. One that we should all grapple with. 
As a human journalist, I’m wary of making predictions. But I’m comfortable saying that the issues raised by Uprise RI and its team of LLM “reporters” aren’t going away soon.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Early, in-person voting starts today. Here’s what Mainers need to know.
description: Monday is the first day Mainers can vote early, in-person at town offices for the Nov. 3 election.  That’s in addition to being able to return absentee ballots. More than 70,000 Mainers had already requested absentee ballots as of Friday, with just over 45,000 issued and 793 returned and accepted. Requests so far are not […]
text:
A ballot drop box outside the Caribou Municipal Building. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Monday is the first day Mainers can vote early, in-person at town offices for the Nov. 3 election. 
That’s in addition to being able to return absentee ballots. More than 70,000 Mainers had already requested absentee ballots as of Friday, with just over 45,000 issued and 793 returned and accepted. Requests so far are not a dramatic difference from 2022, said Secretary of State Shenna Bellows. 
“Numbers seem to be down slightly from what we expected after such a high turnout in the primary,” she said, “but that may be due to mistrust of the postal service given the failed attempts by Trump to restrict vote by mail. We’re hopeful to see a corresponding jump in voters choosing in-person absentee voting starting Monday.”
Mainers have the chance to weigh in on a number of state and federal races. The state’s high-profile congressional races could determine the balance of power in Congress. Maine voters will decide who will replace Gov. Janet Mills. And every seat in the Maine Legislature, which has had a Democratic majority in recent years, is up for grabs, as are many local and county positions.
Check out Maine Morning Star’s voter guide for information about the candidates and their positions. 
How to register
To register to vote for the first time in Maine, update information on your existing Maine voter registration, or change your party enrollment, visit maine.gov/vote. 
In order to register, you will need your driver’s license or State ID number, or if you do not have either, the last four digits of your Social Security number and an image of your hand drawn signature. 
Because Maine has same-day voter registration, you can also register at the polls. You can call your town’s clerk’s office if you have any questions about voting.
Beware of partisan voting websites 
There are several websites that look like official election websites but are run by partisan actors. 
Maine.vote is run by Right Vote, a nonprofit tied to a conservative political action committee headed by state Rep. Laurel Libby (R-Auburn). The PAC launched to try to get Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins reelected as part of a broader push to gain more conservative power in Maine’s local and federal offices.
VoteSafe.org is operated by Elon Musk’s America PAC. The website’s privacy policy states that it may collect, share and sell personal information to unaffiliated third parties.
“If you don’t see .gov in the web address, it is not an official state government website,” Bellows said. “If you are being asked to enter personal information like name and email address before you get to an official .gov link, then someone else is getting your private data.”
Ranked choice voting 
Ranked choice voting will only be used in the races for U.S. Senate and Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, general elections for federal offices that have three or more candidates. 
While only two candidates will appear on the ballot in both races, each has at least one declared write-in candidate. 
In the U.S. Senate race, incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic nominee Troy Jackson will appear on the ballot, but there will be a third line where voters can write-in a candidate and then rank all three of those names. There are six declared write-in candidates to choose from. 
In the 2nd District race, Republican nominee Paul LePage, former Maine governor, and Democratic nominee Matt Dunlap, current state auditor, will appear on the ballot, and Mainers could also choose to vote for an independent declared write-in candidate, Gregory A. Ward. 
If a voter writes in the name of someone who isn’t a declared write-in candidate, their vote will go uncounted.
If no candidate receives more than 50% of votes on Election Day, the race goes to ranked choice run-off, where last-place candidates would be eliminated first. Votes for those candidates are then redistributed to a voter’s next choice. That’s repeated until one candidate receives more than 50% of votes.
How do I find out details about where and when to vote absentee?
Hours and location details vary based on the municipality where a person is registered to vote. 
You can find municipal office hours and absentee drop box locations on the Secretary of State’s website.
The Secretary of State also has a tracking system for voters to monitor the status of their absentee ballot.
The deadline to request an absentee ballot or vote in the presence of the clerk is by Oct. 29, the Thursday before the election.
An absentee ballot request must be received by the municipal clerk by the close of business on Nov. 3.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Right to bail: Amendment asks voters to rewrite pretrial detention rules
description: Indiana judges may soon have the ability to deny bail for more defendants they believe pose a danger to the public. Defendants are guaranteed the right to bail under the Indiana constitution except in cases of murder or treason — even when a judge believes the defendant may reoffend while awaiting trial. Hoosiers will vote this […]
text:
Indiana voters have two constitutional questions to weigh in on this year at the ballot box. (Getty Images)Indiana judges may soon have the ability to deny bail for more defendants they believe pose a danger to the public.
Defendants are guaranteed the right to bail under the Indiana constitution except in cases of murder or treason — even when a judge believes the defendant may reoffend while awaiting trial.
Hoosiers will vote this fall on a proposed constitutional amendment years in the making to rewrite these rules, so judges could deny bail to any defendant if the state proves they cannot be safely released.
Supporters say the amendment is needed to detain defendants who repeatedly commit violent crimes while on bail, while critics worry it jeopardizes due process rights for defendants who may spend months in jail without a conviction.
Two successive general assemblies approved the proposed amendment: in 2023 and 2026. Now it goes to the people on the Nov. 3 ballot.
What does the amendment say?
The amendment would preserve the right to bail for all offenses other than murder or treason — unless the defendant poses a “substantial risk to any other person or the community.”
Those offenses would not be eligible for bail if “the proof is evident or the presumption strong” of their guilt. The state would then need to prove “by clear and convincing evidence” no other release conditions would “reasonably” protect public safety.
Defendants are entitled to an attorney and a hearing if the state asks to deny them bail, as well as the right to appeal the court’s decision.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and tools you need to cast your vote.]
A companion bill adopted earlier this year directs courts to consider the evidence against the defendant and nature of the offense — did it involve drugs, alcohol or an act of violence?
Judges should consider the arrestee’s character, health, family ties, employment, financial resources, community ties, criminal history and potential danger to the public.
Courts must also consider whether alternatives to pre-trial detention are suitable.
Evidence produced at a bail hearing cannot be submitted at trial except in impeachment or perjury inquiries.
“The goal is to have the right people in custody for the right reason for the right amount of time,” said Vicki Becker, the Elkhart County prosecutor. “It is not just checking boxes and putting a rubber stamp on things in order to forward different agendas.”
How does bail currently work?
Each county sets its own bail schedule to guide judges as they determine how much a defendant should pay to stay out of jail before trial.
Marion County Superior Court, for example, sets bail at $50,000 for serious felonies, though the defendant may pay far less through a licensed bail bondsman who pays the remaining balance so long as they attend their court hearings.
Murder is not eligible for bail, while defendants charged with misdemeanors or non-violent felonies like marijuana possession are typically released on their own recognizance or without bail.
Aggravating factors like possession of a deadly weapon, inflicting serious bodily injury or a history of felony convictions may result in higher bail.
Bail schedules are advisory, with some counties opting for much higher amounts: In Elkhart County, the schedule calls for $150,000 bail for Level 1 felonies.
Judges can order a defendant back to jail if they’re arrested again or violate the terms of release.
“The purpose of bail right now is to make sure people show up to court,” said Mike Cunningham, a criminal defense attorney in Franklin who opposes the proposed amendment. “That’s it. That’s the purpose.”
Cunningham said judges already have the discretion to order a defendant to wear an ankle monitor or not possess a firearm while on pre-trial release, or set bail high enough to make sure defendants appear for their court hearings.
“We’re in a system that works,” he said.
The Indiana Criminal Justice Institute found 7% of defendants released on bail or their own recognizance statewide last year were rearrested and charged with a new offense while awaiting trial.
Focus on repeat offenders
Rearrest rates vary by county and release conditions: The report found 32% of the 399 defendants released on bail in Allen County last year were rearrested while awaiting trial, while 24% of the 2,200 defendants released without bail were rearrested.

A second public question will also be on your ballot. It would allow judges of city or town courts to live outside the jurisdiction. The exact wording is: “Shall the Constitution of the State of Indiana be amended to permit the judge of a city or town court to reside in: (1) the county in which the court is located; or (2) the bordering county closest to the city or town in which the court is located?”

In Boone County, the rearrest rate was only 4% for the 1,183 defendants released on bail and 0.6% for those released on their own recognizance, though 20% of defendants released under unknown conditions were rearrested while awaiting trial last year.
Dearborn County claimed the lowest rearrest rate at 0.3%, with only 595 defendants released on bail.
An analysis of Indiana Office of Court Services data reviewed by the American Civil Liberties Union of Indiana, which opposes the amendment, found few of these defendants commit new violent crimes while awaiting trial.
Still, Becker said prosecutors became increasingly concerned about bail reforms adopted in recent years, which she said were applied inconsistently across the state, with some counties not prioritizing public safety in those decisions.
“One of the things that was really a catalyst in trying to push legislation through over the last few years to try to balance this out was the fact that so many individuals that were out on bond or that had pending cases were back out in the community without any accountability whatsoever and continuing to commit offenses against other people,” she said, “and it just did not sit well with prosecutors who are much more focused on protecting public safety.”
What evidence would be needed?
While the amendment requires “clear and convincing evidence” a defendant is too dangerous for bail, how judges determine this standard could vary based on available evidence and their own judgement.
Prosecutors may present video, audio recordings or witnesses to the offense, but Becker said the most likely source of evidence will be the court record itself.
“We can articulate the person was under supervision or had a pending case or had other factors that had been imposed by a court,” she said.
The defense would then have the chance to cross-examine witnesses, but Cunningham said attorneys often don’t have access to much evidence from discovery at this stage.
He worries judges may accept weak evidence or that lawmakers may rewrite standards outlined in SEA 2, despite assurances from supporters who say everyone will follow their best judgement.
“When it’s my job to make sure that the government is doing what they are required to do in black and white under the law, I don’t know that it’s going to be like that. And if it’s not, then what does that mean? Does that mean the government is really presenting the evidence necessary to meet their burden, or are they going to start cutting corners? Are judges going to start accepting the least bit of evidence? And then what do you have? You’ve got people sitting in jail based on what — not a whole lot.”
The amendment isn’t limited to serious felonies either.
A 19-year-old charged with misdemeanor reckless driving for driving too fast could be held without bail if the judge or prosecutor “want to send a message,” Cunningham said.
Defendants may in turn feel pressured to plead guilty to avoid weeks or months in jail without trial, he said.
“I’ve heard the phrase ‘sticks and stones may break my bones, but words will never hurt me.’ Not under this new constitution,” Cunningham said. “It can. It can keep you in jail for a long time.”
But Becker said it’s not that simple.
“This does take a person’s liberty away … Everybody just needs to remember that one person’s right ends where another person’s begin,” she said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: A new partnership is helping Indiana librarians meet mental health needs
description: Walk into almost any public library in Indiana, and you’ll find much more than just the books on the shelves. You’ll find reliable internet access, a place to escape the heat, and often, a staff member who has quietly become the first person to which a struggling neighbor turns. Librarians have become a mental health […]
text:
Books at the Danville-Center Township Public Library on July 29, 2026. (Photo by Jack Forrest/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Walk into almost any public library in Indiana, and you’ll find much more than just the books on the shelves. You’ll find reliable internet access, a place to escape the heat, and often, a staff member who has quietly become the first person to which a struggling neighbor turns. Librarians have become a mental health front line, and we should support them in this unexpected role.
That evolution reflects what libraries are designed to be. Public libraries have long been community anchors. They are open, accessible spaces where anyone can walk in and find information, connection, and support. There are nearly three times as many public libraries in the United States as hospitals, making them some of the most widely accessed community hubs in the country. In Indiana, that access matters as one in five Hoosiers live with a mental health condition. 
We must recognize the critical role thrust upon our libraries. Nearly every Hoosier lives within five miles of a library, and 73% live within a mile. Unlike many other institutions, libraries do not require you to spend money to walk through the door. For low-income residents and those experiencing homelessness, that matters.
Many Indiana libraries are already adapting. Allen County Public Library employs social workers, and the Johnson County Public Library offers direct services such as employment assistance and school enrollment help, along with referrals to critical resources like food and housing. In practice, libraries are already functioning as informal access points to community resources.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



However, most libraries are not prepared for what comes through their doors. Library staff report witnessing alcohol use and injection drug use in their buildings, situations far outside the scope of what library training typically covers. Recognizing this gap, The MolinaCares Accord, in collaboration with Molina Healthcare of Indiana, awarded a $50,000 grant to Mental Health America of Indiana to develop mental health training for library staff through the Stanley W. DeKemper Training Institute. The goal is straightforward: give librarians the practical tools to recognize warning signs, de-escalate tense situations, and connect people to appropriate care.
The impact of this investment extends far beyond the library walls. Early detection and intervention lead to better long-term outcomes for those experiencing behavioral health challenges. Many behavioral health needs can be addressed outside a hospital emergency room, yet avoidable emergency department visits occur and cost the country an estimated $8.3 billion annually. In Indiana alone, the economic burden of untreated mental illness is estimated at $4.2 billion. Equipping library staff eases pressure on emergency rooms, first responders, and other systems already stretched thin. Most importantly, it provides needed assistance to the people we serve.
Indiana’s mental health challenges won’t be solved by any single program or organization. But partnerships like this one between Mental Health America of Indiana Molina Healthcare of Indiana can move Hoosiers in the right direction. The people walking through library doors every day are already trusting librarians with more than their book requests. We need to ensure libraries have the resources and training to meet that need and be worthy of their trust.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: FEMA awards more than $4.5M to Rhode Island fire departments
description: Fire departments and other first responder organizations across Rhode Island are getting more than $4.5 million in grants for new equipment, training and emergency response upgrades, federal officials and Rhode Island’s congressional delegation have announced.  Funding comes from the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) Assistance to Firefighters Gra[...]
text:
The Newport Fire Department received FEMA funding to purchase a Lucas CPR device for each of its three rescues. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)Fire departments and other first responder organizations across Rhode Island are getting more than $4.5 million in grants for new equipment, training and emergency response upgrades, federal officials and Rhode Island’s congressional delegation have announced. 
Funding comes from the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) Assistance to Firefighters Grant program, which provides funding to fire departments and emergency medical service organizations for equipment, training and other improvements.
 

 Rhode Island FEMA grant recipients


Providence: $1.85 million for firefighter breathing apparatus and training


Woonsocket: $1 million for a new aerial ladder truck


Coventry: nearly $500,000 for a new ambulance.


West Warwick: $339,932 for equipment and cardiac monitors.


Prudence Island Volunteer Fire Department: $255,015 for new radios


Lincoln’s two fire departments: $157,031 for cardiac monitors, radios and a thermal imaging camera.


Newport: $68,181 for three chest compression system devices


Rhode Island Fire Training Academy: $370,086 for training equipment




“Our firefighters take tremendous risks to serve our communities and we’ve got to have their backs and ensure they have the best equipment, vehicles, and training to safely and effectively do their job,” U.S. Sen. Jack Reed said in a statement.
Providence is getting the largest award, $1.85 million, for firefighter breathing apparatus and training. Rhode Island’s capital has two years to spend the grant once it accepts the award, city spokesperson Carl Austin Miller Grondin wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current. 
Nearly $1.5 million will go toward new self-contained breathing apparatus, or “Air-Paks,” with the city expecting to purchase the equipment within the next few months and put it into service in early 2027. 
“The remaining funds will support Providence Fire Department officers, including lieutenants, captains and chief officers, to obtain various levels of nationally standardized supervisory training,” Grondin wrote.
Woonsocket will get $1 million for a new aerial ladder truck and Coventry nearly $500,000 for a new ambulance.
West Warwick will get $339,932 for equipment and cardiac monitors. The Prudence Island Volunteer Fire Department will receive $255,015 for new radios, while Lincoln’s two fire departments will get $157,031 for cardiac monitors, radios and a thermal imaging camera. Newport will receive $68,181 for CPR devices, and the Rhode Island Fire Training Academy $370,086 for training equipment.
The grant awards were announced separately over the past two weeks, with FEMA providing details in two releases on Sept. 25 and Oct. 2. Rhode Island’s all-Democratic congressional delegation combined the funding allocations into a single announcement Wednesday, Sept. 30.
Rhode Island’s federal delegation and FEMA have been at odds over federal funding for the state, most recently over FEMA’s rejection of Gov. Dan McKee’s request for disaster assistance following February’s historic blizzard, which caused about $19 million in damage and cleanup costs after the state was buried under more than 3 feet of snow.
Four members of Rhode Island’s congressional delegation on Sept. 9 directed the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA to preserve and provide all records related to the state’s request for a major disaster declaration. Spokespeople from 
Asked about the status of the delegations’ request, a FEMA spokesperson wrote in an email Friday to Rhode Island Current that the agency considers factors including the cost of the damage, local impacts, insurance coverage, other federal aid and the state’s ability to pay.
“Major disaster declaration request evaluation factors considered include estimated cost of the assistance, localized impacts, insurance coverage in force, hazard mitigation, recent multiple disasters, programs of other federal assistance, state fiscal capacity and resource availability, uninsured home and personal property losses, disaster-impacted population profile, impact to community infrastructure, casualties, and disaster related unemployment,” the spokesperson said.
FEMA has provided other federal funding to Rhode Island since the delegation’s request, including more than $3.3 million announced Sept. 18 for projects to reduce disaster risks, such as seawall repairs in Barrington and Bristol and flood mitigation work in Providence.
Reed and U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the Disaster Relief Fairness Act in July, which would require the federal government to approve disaster aid when a state meets FEMA’s criteria for assistance. U.S. Reps. Gabe Amo and Seth Magaziner introduced the same legislation in the House in September.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Data centers drive debate in Louisiana’s congressional races
description: As data centers pop up across the country, debate around what role elected officials have, if any, on monitoring and restricting their resource use and development has become part of the political conversation.
text:
State Rep. Mike Echols speaks to the media after qualifying as a candidate for Congress in Louisiana's 5th congressional district. (Photo by Julie O'Donoghue/LAI) As data centers pop up across the country, debate around what role elected officials have, if any, on monitoring and restricting their resource use and development has become part of the political conversation.
In Louisiana, Democrats running for Congress in the 5th and 6th U.S. House districts as well as the U.S. Senate said they were concerned about water and electricity data centers need.
Republican candidates were more inclined to trust the data center industry’s promises not to overuse public resources or pass along operational costs to the public.
State Sens. Stewart Cathey, R-Monroe, who is in the 5th District field, and Rick Edmonds, R-Baton Rouge, a 6th District candidate, could not be reached for this report through multiple phone calls and text messages. State Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, also on the 6th District ballot, declined to answer questions.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Who covers the cost?
Environmental and consumer rights advocates as well as residents living near data center projects have repeatedly voiced concern over the amount of water and electricity the facilities, such as Amazon’s facility in Shreveport and Meta’s expansive campus in Richland Parish, will require.
Pat Forbes, a Democrat running in the 6th District, said his “gut feeling” is that legislation will be required to protect ratepayers. The public will “need to rely on something more than a handshake” for ratepayer protection, he said. Other Democratic candidates generally agreed.
“I know that there needs to be some regulation,” said state Rep. Pat Moore, D-Monroe, who is in the 5th District race.
Republican candidates were generally less supportive of government regulation. State Rep. Gabe Firment of Pollock, state Board of Regents chair Misti Cordell of Monroe, both Republicans seeking the 5th District seat, said they feel assured by data center developers’ claims that water use would be minimal and electricity costs would not affect average households enough to warrant extensive regulation.
Edmonds made similar comments at a debate for Republicans in the 6th District race Tuesday in Denham Springs.
“(T)here are those that say that it’s going to cost the taxpayer more money on their energy costs. I don’t believe that’s true,”Edmonds said. Adding that investment from companies such as Meta would contribute to power access with grid strengthening projects.
Largely breaking from other Republican candidates, state Rep. Michael Echols, a 5th District candidate from Monroe. He said the government should monitor data center water and power use to prevent consumers from being affected.
“It is absolutely a concern, and it’s something that through responsible policy we can monitor and make sure that they’re good stewards of our natural resources,” Echols said.
Protecting ratepayers
Meta and Entergy, which is providing power to its Richland Parish data campus, have signed ratepayer protection pledges promising not to hand down electricity costs to other consumers.  Critics have pointed out that these pledges aren’t legally binding.
When asked whether ratepayer protection pledges were strong enough to guarantee responsible resource use and protection against rising utility costs, all candidates said it was a good first step.
“The data center should pay its own bills. Bottom line. Period,” said Jamie Davis, an Tensas Parish farmer and Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate.
All but Cordell said they would go a step further, generally favoring some form of legislation requiring data centers to cover the cost of their electric use.
“I’m not for extra regulations that would be burdensome on any economic development that would come into our area,” Cordell said.
Congresswoman Julia Lettow of Baton Rouge, the Republican nominee in the U.S. Senate race, cited her vote in favor of the Ratepayer Protection Act as proof of her support for holding data centers responsible for their promises. The federal legislation would have encouraged states to consider large data centers covering all of the costs linked to the power generation and transmission they need.
“If a data center creates the need for major new infrastructure, families and small businesses should not be left footing the bill,” she said in a written statement to the Illuminator.
The Ratepayer Protection Act gained approval in the U.S. House but failed in the Senate by just three votes.
Trust and transparency
Secrecy surrounding big economic development deals in Louisiana, including that of data centers, has become an increasingly charged topic. The use of NDAs by public officials has candidates sharing with their voters whether there is enough transparency in government around the development of major industrial projects like data centers.
Candidates largely agreed that more work could be done in government to increase transparency around data center development. Some were more specific than others on exactly how to do so.
Chauna Banks, a former East Baton Rouge Metro Council member running as a Democrat in the 6th District, said there needs to be “a limit upfront on how many data centers should be in each state.” She added that she is leery of data centers because she has lived in communities that have often been asked to give up things in the name of progress with no reciprocity.
NDA secrecy for major projects hovers over Louisiana’s congressional elections

Banks also said data centers should only be allowed in areas zoned for heavy industrial uses, and that elected officials should “never, ever sign NDAs” unless it is an issue of national security or maybe a trade agreement.
Davis, Echols and Lindsay “Rubia” Garcia, a Democrat in the 6th District race, share similar views on NDAs.
“I recognize that some business information is legitimately confidential. But that cannot become a blanket justification for withholding the assumptions behind demands on public infrastructure or promises used to justify incentives,” Garcia said in a written statement.
Firment countered, saying while officials “need to err on the side of transparency,” they could be useful in the name of economic development and national security.
“There needs to be some balance when it comes to disclosing proprietary information and trade secrets that would potentially put companies at a competitive disadvantage,” Firment said.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Conservationists want Congress to do more to protect New England’s roadless areas
description: As the period for public comment on the proposed rollback of the Roadless Rule draws to a close, some conservationists want Congress to do more.  The Roadless Area Conservation Rule, which dates to 2001, prohibits road construction and timber harvesting in remote areas of national forests across the country. A proposal from the U.S. Department […]
text:
About 235,000 acres of roadless areas are located within the White Mountain National Forest in New Hampshire. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)As the period for public comment on the proposed rollback of the Roadless Rule draws to a close, some conservationists want Congress to do more. 
The Roadless Area Conservation Rule, which dates to 2001, prohibits road construction and timber harvesting in remote areas of national forests across the country. A proposal from the U.S. Department of Agriculture would remove those federal limitations on the allowed uses of roadless areas. 
Most roadless areas, which total more than 58.5 million acres, are concentrated in the West, but not all; within New England, New Hampshire hosts the largest amount, with about 235,000 acres in the White Mountain National Forest designated as roadless.
Jeffrey Swayze, a registered New Hampshire guide and mental health counselor, has become an advocate for the Roadless Area Conservation Rule, which he credits for keeping the White Mountain National Forest healthy, productive and protected. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
The proposal is “the existential threat in the fire-hose assault on our public lands right now,” said Jeffrey Swayze, a New Hampshire guide and mental health counselor at White Mountains Community College in Gorham, who described the potential repeal as “unconscionable.”
Swayze was impressed by the volume of comments that have been submitted on the proposal so far. As of Sept. 30, the total number of comments on the rule’s online docket was more than 522,600; the current comment period runs until Oct. 6. But he said the “chaos” around the proposal, coupled with the strength of the public’s response, called for Congress to act with force to keep the rule intact.
“This is an opportunity for New Hampshire’s congressional delegation to start really speaking up, and this is one thing that I think Congress hasn’t done,” he said. “They talk tough, but they act weak, and I don’t think they’re using the power that they have.”
The Trump administration has defended the rollback, saying the change would free up wildlands for broader use, including by extractive industries, like timber harvesting and mining. The change would leave decisions about roadless area management to local forest managers, the U.S. Forest Service wrote in the proposal.
Critics say the move would jeopardize the most pristine wilderness areas remaining in the country, with broad consequences for people and wildlife. The Roadless Area Conservation Rule was originally implemented to protect sources of clean drinking water and undisturbed soil and air; diverse plant and animal communities; species that depend on large, undisturbed and connected areas of land; and the traditional, cultural and recreational value of remote landscapes, according to the Forest Service.
The New Hampshire chapter of the Sierra Club supports efforts to codify the 2001 Roadless Rule into federal law, said Catherine Corkery, chapter director. That is what the Roadless Area Conservation Act, a bill proposed in 2025 by Washington Democrat Sen. Maria Cantwell, aims to do. By enshrining the rule in federal law, the measure would require an act of Congress to enact future changes, rather than the rulemaking process through which the USDA is currently moving to rescind the regulation.
The Sierra Club was involved in efforts to support the Roadless Rule when it was first proposed in the early 2000s, Corkery said, and within the last few months, thousands of its members and supporters nationwide have submitted comments opposing the rollback. Locally, over 1,000 people attended virtual and in-person “mock hearings” hosted by the New Hampshire Sierra Club chapter, speaking about the importance of roadless areas, she said. 
“We support the rule and the legislation to codify the rule,” she said. 
New Hampshire has designated roadless areas within the White Mountain National Forest, which draws hikers and tourists from far afield. A signpost welcomes hikers to the Great Gulf Wilderness, in the White Mountain National Forest. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Swayze said he wanted to see protections for the White Mountain National Forest’s roadless areas become a more central ballot issue this fall than it had been during primary campaigns.
New Hampshire’s current congressional delegation has expressed support for the Roadless Rule, including through multiple letters sent to the U.S. Department of Agriculture and Forest Service opposing the rule’s repeal. 
Congressman Chris Pappas, who is now a candidate for New Hampshire’s Senate seat, said he would continue to support the rule if elected. 
“Repealing the Roadless Rule threatens the health of our most important lands, forests and ecosystems, and it would disrupt the balanced approach developed 25 years ago with exhaustive input from stakeholders and the public,” Pappas said in a late September statement to the Bulletin. 
He criticized the Trump administration’s attempts to remove the rule as “reckless.” He did not respond to a question about whether he would support efforts to codify the rule in federal law. 
Discussion about the Roadless Rule has leaned partisan both federally and locally. Pappas’ Republican competitor for the Senate seat, John E. Sununu, did not respond to questions about the roadless rule sent by email. New Hampshire’s Republican candidates for Congress, Lily Tang Williams and Anthony DiLorenzo, similarly did not respond to roadless rule inquiries.
Maggie Goodlander, who is running for reelection against Williams to represent New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District, criticized what she said was a chaotic move that could harm New Hampshire’s forests and tourism industry. The timeline given for the repeal, she said, was too abbreviated, with insufficient chances for the public to weigh in. 
In the early 2000s, the roadless rule was implemented after more than 600 public meetings and with written input in the form of more than 1.6 million comments, Goodlander said. Official public meetings were not held on the proposed rescission, on which the public was initially given 30 days to comment before the period was extended by an additional 15 days. 
“That’s simply not a reasonable timeframe or approach to make reasoned and informed choices about rules that could have generational consequences,” Goodlander said. 
She raised concerns about the impact on taxpayers of funding and maintaining new roads in the national forest; the Forest Service is already facing a maintenance backlog, she added. She went on to say she would continue to oppose the closure of Forest Service experimental forests, like Hubbard Brook and Bartlett Experimental Forest in the White Mountains, and oppose reorganization and staffing cuts at the Forest Service. 
However, Goodlander said she did not support the Roadless Area Conservation Act.
“The answer to a chaotic rescission from Washington is not a permanent freeze from Washington,” she said. 
Stefany Shaheen, who is running against DiLorenzo to represent New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District, said she supported the Roadless Rule and opposed its rescission, but she did not comment on whether she would support putting it into federal law. 
Swayze said he believed voters would prioritize New Hampshire’s forest lands this fall.
“These are our lands, and we haven’t been vocal enough about demanding that our federal government manage and steward them in a way that’s responsible,” he said. “… I want the idea that public lands are for sale to the highest bidder to go away.”

name: National
title: Kratom, 7-OH laws diverge amid the spread of potent synthetic products
description: For years, the psychoactive compound kratom has been sold across much of the United States as an herbal supplement, available in powders, capsules and extracts with few of the restrictions applied to controlled substances. But the market is changing. Products containing a potentially dangerous kratom derivative known as concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine, or[...]
text:
Liquid kratom extracts and capsules containing 7-OH are displayed for sale at a smoke shop in Buffalo, N.Y. A growing market is prompting state lawmakers to reconsider how the substance should be regulated. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)For years, the psychoactive compound kratom has been sold across much of the United States as an herbal supplement, available in powders, capsules and extracts with few of the restrictions applied to controlled substances.
But the market is changing. Products containing a potentially dangerous kratom derivative known as concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH, and other chemically modified kratom compounds are increasingly being sold alongside traditional kratom leaf products, prompting state lawmakers and federal regulators to reconsider how the substances should be regulated.
The evolution has put states in the middle of a difficult policy question: how to address concerns about increasingly potent kratom-related products without treating traditional kratom leaf the same way.
At least 31 states regulate kratom, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Some have banned or scheduled kratom, while others have imposed age limits, labeling requirements or restrictions on 7-OH and synthetic compounds. 
During the 2025 and 2026 legislative sessions, lawmakers in 36 states introduced legislation to regulate kratom, 7-OH or synthetic kratom compounds, according to the Rockefeller Institute of Government. Many cities and towns nationwide have adopted sales restrictions.
Kratom faces increasing scrutiny from states and the feds

Federal regulators are increasingly taking a similar approach, targeting certain high-potency and synthetic compounds while leaving traditional botanical kratom outside the latest federal scheduling actions.
The issue gained new attention recently in Mississippi, where local police found the same potent synthetic kratom-derived product while investigating the separate deaths of two University of Mississippi students last month. Authorities have not established that the product contributed to either death, and toxicology results are still pending.
Lawmakers in a growing number of states, including Mississippi, are calling on their legislatures to act swiftly against concentrated 7-OH products, commonly referred to as “gas station heroin.” 
Pennsylvania lawmakers also are considering legislation that would allow registered retailers to sell natural-leaf kratom to people 21 and older while banning synthetic and adulterated products, including those containing more than 0.5% 7-OH. The bill unanimously cleared a House committee last week and now heads to the full House. 
This year, lawmakers in Connecticut, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Tennessee, Virginia, Washington and Wyoming have considered or adopted bans and regulations on kratom and its synthetic variants.
The number of kratom-related reports to U.S. poison centers has also risen sharply recently. An analysis published on the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website in March reported 14,449 kratom exposure reports from 2015 through 2025, including 3,434 in 2025 — about 1,200% more than in 2015.
But this data does not identify whether those exposures involved traditional leaf products or newer concentrated and semisynthetic formulations such as 7-OH, limiting what researchers can conclude about the risks of particular products.



Quotation







It’s easier to become dependent and more euphoric with the 7-OH, and so coming off of it is more dramatic as well.


– Dr. Alta DeRoo, chief medical officer, Hazelden Betty Ford Foundation


Poison centers have logged 3,190 reports involving kratom or its derivatives through June, according to a news release. If that pace continues, the number of reports in 2026 would be nearly 68% higher than in 2025.
Addiction medicine experts and researchers say significant questions remain about the safety and effects of these largely unregulated products, including how they affect people of different ages, what doses may be safe or effective, and whether they have potential therapeutic uses. More research is needed to better understand the risks and potential benefits of kratom and its newer formulations.
“These products are unregulated,” said Dr. Sarah Kawasaki, an associate professor of psychiatry and internal medicine at Pennsylvania State University. “There’s no quality control needed to make sure that what is stated is on the bottle is actually in the bottle.
“What we don’t know, and its accessibility, should scare us all,” Kawasaki added, referring to the lack of research on dosing and effects across different age groups.
The changing kratom market
Kratom comes from the leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tree native to Southeast Asia. Traditionally, the leaves have been chewed, brewed into tea or dried and ground into powder.
The plant contains dozens of alkaloids, including mitragynine and smaller amounts of naturally occurring 7-OH. Those compounds interact with opioid receptors in the brain. Kratom, which is most commonly sold as powder, capsules and tablets, can have stimulant effects at lower doses and more sedating effects at higher doses.
“With kratom, it’s weaker and it’s hitting more than just the opioid receptor. When you go with 7-OH, it’s very targeted at the mu-opioid receptor –– the same receptor that morphine or fentanyl would hit,” said Dr. Alta DeRoo, the chief medical officer of the Hazelden Betty Ford Foundation, one of the largest nonprofit treatment providers for addiction and mental health. DeRoo also is a board-certified addiction medicine physician and OB-GYN.

“It’s easier to become dependent and more euphoric with the 7-OH, and so coming off of it is more dramatic as well,” she said.
Kratom-infused drinks are stacked in a refrigerator at a smoke shop in Howard County, Md. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)
People use kratom or 7-OH for a variety of reasons, according to addiction medicine experts. Some report using it for pain, energy or focus, while others use it in an effort to manage opioid withdrawal or reduce their reliance on opioids. 
“7-OH products are really the first thing in almost two decades that have helped me sleep for more than about a half hour at a time, so they’ve helped me deal with that kind of chronic pain,” said Jeff Smith, the executive director of the Holistic Alternative Recovery Trust, an advocacy group that represents some 7-OH manufacturers. 
Government health officials and addiction medicine experts have also raised concerns about 7-OH’s potential to cause dependence, withdrawal and other adverse effects.
Some newer products in the market may contain concentrated amounts of 7-OH and chemically modified or semisynthetic kratom-derived compounds, including mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15, and MGM-16. These products are sometimes marketed or sold under the broad label of “kratom,” which some experts say creates a challenge for both consumers and regulators.
These types of products also are widely accessible. Concentrated 7-OH products that may also contain other kratom-derived compounds are sold online and at gas stations, convenience stores and smoke shops as tablets, capsules, extracts or shots, drinks, gummies and dissolvable strips. 
Latest regulatory changes
State and local governments have taken increasingly different approaches as the market has changed.
Some have banned kratom, while others have classified it or its components as controlled substances under state law.  Others have focused on sales restrictions, including minimum-age requirements, labeling rules and manufacturing standards. A growing number of states are specifically targeting concentrated 7-OH or synthetic kratom-derived compounds rather than banning traditional leaf products.
A Rockefeller Institute of Government analysis lists three states that ban or schedule non “pure leaf kratom,” 14 states that ban or schedule kratom, 13 with potency limits and 24 with sales restrictions. The categories overlap because states can impose multiple types of restrictions.
A new Tennessee law went into effect in July that prohibits the possession, sale and distribution of kratom statewide, joining the other 13 states that have chosen prohibition rather than regulation. In Massachusetts, Democratic Gov. Maura Healey issued an executive order in August temporarily placing all forms of kratom in Schedule I under state law for one year.
States taking a more targeted approach include Oklahoma, which has set a 1% ceiling for 7-OH as a share of the total kratom alkaloids in a product and bars the sale of products containing synthetic kratom-derived compounds or other contaminants. The state also requires manufacturers to disclose the amounts of total kratom alkaloids, mitragynine and 7-OH on product packaging.
Kratom alkaloids found in cat’s claw tablets linked to multiple overdoses, Utah agencies warn

But some Oklahoma officials say those restrictions do not go far enough. 
Republican state Rep. Tim Turner, a former sheriff and narcotics officer, announced plans in September to introduce legislation targeting concentrated or synthetically enhanced kratom compounds, including 7-OH and MGM-15, during the 2027 session.
“It is time to stop treating this like just another product on a convenience store shelf,” Turner said in a news release. “If companies knowingly manufacture, market, distribute or sell dangerous products that are killing Oklahomans, there needs to be accountability.”
Donnie Anderson, the director of the Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs Control, also said that gaps in state law make it difficult for investigators to pursue suppliers of synthetically enhanced kratom products.
Rhode Island took a different approach this year, becoming the first state to replace a statewide kratom ban with a regulated market for people 21 and older. The state still prohibits products containing synthetic kratom alkaloids or other synthetically derived compounds, including mitragynine and 7-OH.
Mississippi falls somewhere in between. A 2025 law prohibits kratom sales to people under 21 and prohibits products containing certain synthesized or semisynthesized kratom compounds. It also establishes registration requirements and preserves local governments’ ability to restrict kratom.
But state Rep. Lee Yancey, a Republican who has pushed for additional restrictions, has called for lawmakers to revisit the issue in 2027 following the Ole Miss deaths, including the consideration of a statewide kratom ban.
A public health approach
Federal regulators have also increasingly focused on the newer products.
In July, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration announced plans to temporarily place 7-OH above a 0.05% concentration threshold and three related compounds — mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15 and MGM-16 — in Schedule I of the federal Controlled Substances Act. The three related compounds were placed in Schedule I effective Aug. 26 and will remain there through Aug. 26, 2028. The separate 7-OH scheduling action has not yet taken effect. The change does not apply to botanical kratom containing naturally occurring 7-OH below the threshold.
“We support what the feds are doing,” said Matthew Lowe, the executive director of the Global Kratom Coalition, an industry advocacy group representing kratom businesses and consumers. “It’s the right thing to do from a public health perspective.”
The New York Times also reported in June on efforts by kratom industry groups to build relationships with Trump administration officials and influence federal policy. The industry has sought to distinguish traditional kratom leaf from newer, more potent 7-OH products, while pushing for tougher restrictions on those synthetic products.
“This is pretty much overblown by the critics of kratom, who are saying that some in the industry are trying to buy their way in to get a policy that they’re pursuing, when in fact both sides are doing that,” said Mac Haddow, the senior fellow on public policy at the American Kratom Association, one of the nation’s leading kratom industry groups.
The authors of the CDC analysis found that 233 deaths were associated with kratom exposure reports between 2015 and 2025. In 184 cases, or 79%, more than one substance was involved. Opioids were detected in 62% of the deaths, while benzodiazepines, stimulants and alcohol also appeared in some cases. Multiple-substance exposures were more likely to result in hospitalization and serious medical outcomes than exposures involving kratom alone.
But the researchers could not determine whether people had used traditional leaf kratom or concentrated or semisynthetic products such as 7-OH. They also could not determine which substance was most responsible for a medical outcome or death when multiple substances were involved.
John Puls, a Florida psychotherapist and addiction specialist, said clinicians treating kratom or 7-OH dependence often approach detox similarly to opioid withdrawal: After assessing what a patient has been using and how much, providers may use a short taper of buprenorphine, commonly known by the brand name Suboxone. 
Kellen Russoniello, the director of public health at the Drug Policy Alliance, said the organization shares public health concerns about 7-OH and other kratom derivatives but opposes criminalization as the response.
Russoniello said safety information and a regulated market could instead give consumers more reliable information through product testing, accurate labeling and limits on active ingredients.
“In a sensibly regulated model, the consumer would have much more information by being able to read the bottle and see what’s in it, what percentage of certain substances are in there,” he said. “It’s a much better approach for protecting the consumer.”
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.
