name: Delaware
title: Delaware human trafficking summit seeks to turn awareness into coordinated action
description: Two-day Dewey Beach gathering brought community leaders together Thursday before more than six hours of training Friday focused on recognizing victims and improving Delaware’s response. By George Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News. DEWEY BEACH, Del. — Delaware leaders spent two days this week examining how the state identifies and responds to human trafficking, begi[...]
text:
The Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors held its inaugural Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit on Thursday, Oct. 1, and Friday, Oct. 2, at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach, 1301 Coastal Highway.
Two-day Dewey Beach gathering brought community leaders together Thursday before more than six hours of training Friday focused on recognizing victims and improving Delaware’s response.
By George Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News.
DEWEY BEACH, Del. — Delaware leaders spent two days this week examining how the state identifies and responds to human trafficking, beginning with a closed-door executive roundtable Thursday and continuing Friday with an all-day summit for health care workers, social workers, law enforcement, advocates and other professionals.
The Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors held its inaugural Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit on Thursday, Oct. 1, and Friday, Oct. 2, at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach, 1301 Coastal Highway.
Thursday’s program was an invitation-only executive roundtable that brought leaders and decision-makers together to discuss Delaware’s response to trafficking. Friday’s public and professional summit ran from Noon to 4 p.m.. It included keynote presentations, professional education, survivor perspectives and discussions involving medical providers, mental health professionals, law enforcement and direct-service workers.
Marcia Ferranto, president of the Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors, said the organization wanted the event to do more than raise awareness.
“Human trafficking affects Delaware communities, but too often it remains unseen or misunderstood,” Ferranto said. “We need residents, business leaders, educators, health care professionals, faith communities and policymakers to understand the warning signs and recognize that each of them can play a role in prevention.”
The two-day format reflected that goal.
Thursday concentrated on the people in positions to influence policies, organizations and systems. Friday focused more directly on the professionals and community members who may encounter trafficking victims but not immediately recognize what they are seeing.
The invitation-only roundtable brought together senior leaders from health care, law enforcement, government, social services, victim advocacy, education, behavioral health and community organizations. It also included political and public-sector leaders representing multiple levels of government, including federal homeland security officials, representatives of the governor’s office and county leaders.
Organizers said it was the first time Delaware had convened such a broad group of high-level decision-makers specifically to focus on human trafficking as a shared statewide challenge. The potential benefit is significant: stronger relationships among agencies, clearer referral pathways, more consistent training, better coordination when victims are identified and a greater chance that warning signs seen by one institution are connected with information held by another.
The coalition billed the gathering as Delaware’s inaugural statewide Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit. National experts and Delaware professionals participated as speakers, moderators and presenters.
A full day of training
Friday’s program began at 7:45 a.m. and continued until 4 p.m.
Nemours Children’s Health offered six continuing education hours for nurses and six continuing education credits for social workers participating in the program. The stated audience included nurses, social workers and others interested in human trafficking education.
Presenters included retired special victims detective Kevin McNeil; survivor, author and speaker Marti MacGibbon; Jennifer Cooper, BSN, RN, SANE-P; Andrea Repine, MSN, APRN, CPNP; attorney Shea Rhodes; Jose Alfaro; Jeanne Allert; Dana Kaplan, MD; and Heather LaRocca, LCSW.
The educational program was designed to help participants recognize behavioral, physical and situational indicators of trafficking, understand gaps in identifying victims and develop cross-disciplinary teams to support survivors.
Training included discussion of warning signs such as a victim lacking control of personal possessions or identification, inconsistencies in a person’s account, signs of branding or other physical indicators and behaviors that could suggest someone is being controlled.
The program also addressed the underrepresentation of male and LGBTQ+ trafficking victims in national data and how those gaps can affect the ability of professionals to identify victims.
Victims may already be in the system
A central message emerging from the summit was that trafficking victims frequently encounter institutions that could help them without ever announcing that they are being trafficked.

A nurse may treat an injury.
A teacher may notice chronic absences.
Police may encounter someone during a domestic dispute.
A social worker may see unstable housing.
A nonprofit organization may encounter someone unable to meet basic needs.
Those individual encounters may appear unrelated unless the people involved understand the larger patterns associated with exploitation.

Ferranto said that makes education across professions particularly important.
“Trafficking does not happen only somewhere else; it is affecting people here in Delaware,” Ferranto said. “When the public understands what exploitation looks like and knows how to respond, we become better able to protect vulnerable people, support survivors and make Delaware a much more difficult place for traffickers to operate.”
The summit’s professional education program specifically emphasized multidisciplinary, trauma-informed and survivor-centered responses rather than expecting a single agency or profession to identify and solve the problem alone.
Trafficking does not always begin with kidnapping
Presenters also challenged one of the most common public perceptions of trafficking — that victims are usually abducted by strangers and physically imprisoned.
That can happen, but speakers said trafficking frequently develops differently.
Victims can be manipulated through relationships, housing, employment, financial dependency, drugs, threats or promises of security.
The process may occur gradually through grooming rather than through a single dramatic event.
Someone who appears free to leave physically may believe leaving would result in violence, homelessness, withdrawal, financial ruin or harm to someone else.
That psychological control can make trafficking difficult for family members, employers, medical professionals and even victims themselves to recognize.
Why health care workers matter
Medical professionals were an important part of Friday’s program because health care may provide one of the few opportunities for someone outside a trafficking situation to interact privately with a victim.
The summit included training aimed at nurses and other medical providers on recognizing trafficking indicators and responding in ways that do not further traumatize patients.
Jennifer Cooper served as course director for the continuing education program, with Andrea Repine and Suzanne Rouleau among the planners.
The program emphasized that professionals need to know not only what to notice, but also what to do next.
Its learning objectives included establishing cross-disciplinary teams capable of supporting trafficking survivors.
That means a nurse identifying a possible victim needs to know who to call. Police need to understand available survivor services. Social workers need relationships with medical and behavioral health providers. Community organizations need to know where safe housing and other assistance can be found.
From executive discussion to front-line training
Holding the executive roundtable Thursday and the professional summit Friday created two levels of discussion.
One focused on leadership and institutional response. The other focused on people likely to encounter potential victims in their daily work.
For Ferranto and the coalition, connecting those levels is a major part of the effort. Delaware already has law enforcement agencies investigating trafficking, hospitals caring for vulnerable patients and nonprofit groups assisting survivors.
The challenge is ensuring those organizations understand what others are doing and know how to connect victims with the appropriate help.
The summit’s emphasis on building cross-disciplinary teams suggests organizers see coordination as an essential next step rather than treating trafficking solely as a criminal justice, medical or social-services issue.
The test comes after the summit
The event ended Friday afternoon, but the larger question is what happens next.
Participants returned to hospitals, police departments, schools, nonprofits, government agencies, and community organizations with a common set of questions:

Are staff members trained to recognize trafficking?
Do they know what to do when they suspect it?
Is there a clear referral process?
Do organizations know what services other groups provide?
Are victims being identified early enough?

And when someone is ready to leave an exploitative situation, does Delaware have the housing, treatment, and support necessary to help?
Those are questions the Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors hopes the two-day gathering will continue to push beyond a conference room in Dewey Beach.
The coalition, formerly known as Meet Me at the Well Delaware, works in education, advocacy, survivor support and outreach and connects trafficking survivors with services including housing, employment and treatment.
Friday’s summit represented its most visible statewide effort yet to bring the different parts of Delaware’s response together.
The next measure of success will be whether those relationships produce lasting changes in how Delaware recognizes trafficking and helps the people caught in it.

name: Delaware
title: Human trafficking is not what many Delawareans think it is
description: Two-day Dewey Beach summit brought together government leaders, law enforcement, health professionals, survivors and advocates while challenging common assumptions about how trafficking begins and who can become a victim. By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE news. DEWEY BEACH, Del. — A two-day human trafficking summit in Dewey Beach brought together government[...]
text:
The Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit, organized by the Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors, began Thursday with an invitation-only executive roundtable and continued Friday with an all-day public and professional program at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach for over 150 people.
Two-day Dewey Beach summit brought together government leaders, law enforcement, health professionals, survivors and advocates while challenging common assumptions about how trafficking begins and who can become a victim.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE news.
DEWEY BEACH, Del. — A two-day human trafficking summit in Dewey Beach brought together government leaders, law enforcement, health care professionals, survivors, advocates and community organizations this week to examine how Delaware identifies and responds to trafficking — and to challenge some of the public’s most common assumptions about what the crime actually looks like.
The Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit, organized by the Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors, began Thursday with an invitation-only executive roundtable and continued Friday with an all-day public and professional program at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach for over 150 people.
One of the clearest messages to emerge from the summit was that trafficking often does not begin with kidnapping, physical restraint or a stranger forcing someone into a car.
Jennifer Cooper, a Forensic Nurse Coordinator from Nemours Children’s Health and one of the summit organizers with the coalition, and fellow nurse Andrea Repine, Pediatric Nurse Practioner from Nemours led a “Human Trafficking 101” session focused on separating myths from reality.
“Most people think, when they think trafficking, that there’s a pimp involved,” Cooper said. “Human Trafficking involves a third party trading sex for value and can involve a boyfriend/girlfriend, family member, or employer and others”  She also pointed out “When it comes to minors, you don’t need that third party.”
Trafficking also does not necessarily involve an exchange of cash.
“It doesn’t have to be an exchange of money,” Cooper said. “It could be that they want food.”
That can mean a vulnerable young person exchanging sex for a place to sleep, food, transportation or something else of value.
Not always kidnapping either!
Cooper and Repine told participants that trafficking often develops gradually through grooming, manipulation, dependency, fraud or coercion.
A victim may never be kidnapped.
There may be no locked room.
And the person doing the exploiting may be a boyfriend, girlfriend, employer, acquaintance or someone who initially appeared to be helping.
Cooper described the session as an effort to explain “what trafficking is” by “breaking down the myths versus the reality.”
The distinction becomes particularly important when children are involved.
That means exploitation of a minor does not require a traditional pimp or third-party trafficker.
A person can be trapped without being locked up
Opening keynote speaker Kevin McNeil, a nationally recognized victim advocate, brought both law enforcement experience and personal experience to the discussion.
McNeil is a retired police officer and a survivor of trafficking and sexual abuse. His presentation, “Stuck in Traffic,” focused on how someone can feel trapped in a trafficking situation even when no physical barrier prevents that person from leaving.
The analogy began with something familiar: the frustration of sitting in traffic with nowhere to go.
For a trafficking victim, however, the barriers can involve fear, financial dependency, threats, homelessness, addiction or emotional attachment to the person doing the exploiting.
That type of psychological control can make trafficking considerably harder to recognize than the popular image of someone being physically held by a stranger.
Substance abuse can deepen the problem
Marty McGibbon brought another survivor’s perspective to the conference.
A therapist, author, comedian and trafficking survivor, McGibbon addressed the intersection between substance abuse and trafficking. She returned later in the program to discuss mental well-being, self-care and trauma-informed approaches for people working with survivors. Pasted text(20260818-140439)
Her presentations reinforced another theme of the summit: Trafficking often overlaps with other problems rather than occurring by itself.
A victim may also be dealing with addiction, homelessness, previous abuse, financial instability or an unhealthy relationship.
Those vulnerabilities can become tools for someone seeking control.
Cooper previously described the intersection between substance abuse and trafficking as “a huge problem, particularly here in Delaware and the surrounding area.”
Vulnerability matters
Presenters stressed that traffickers often exploit vulnerability rather than targeting one particular type of person.
A teenager without a stable place to live may be vulnerable to someone offering housing.
Someone struggling with addiction may become dependent on the person supplying drugs.
A worker may rely on an employer for transportation, housing or access to personal documents.
A person seeking affection or security may become emotionally dependent on someone who later begins exploiting the relationship.
Those situations do not automatically mean trafficking is occurring.
But understanding how dependency can turn into control can help families, teachers, medical professionals and others recognize when something may be wrong.
Why Delawareans should care
The summit’s message was not that every troubled teenager, unhealthy relationship or difficult workplace situation involves trafficking.
For people whose image of human trafficking still involves strangers, kidnapping and locked rooms, summit speakers offered a more practical starting point:

It was that trafficking can look remarkably ordinary from the outside.
It can look like a teenager suddenly depending on an older boyfriend or girlfriend for a place to stay.
It can look like someone working for an employer who controls transportation, identification or money.
It can look like a young person exchanging sex for food, shelter or something else of value.
And it can involve someone who technically can walk out the door but believes there is nowhere safe to go.

For parents, teachers, neighbors and other Delawareans, the goal is not to become investigators. It is to better understand what exploitation can look like so they recognize when something does not seem right.
Almost 700 victims connected to 330 human trafficking cases in Delaware since 2007, with 29 cases of trafficking in 2025. Advocates caution that these figures represent only reported and identified cases. The actual number of victims is believed to be significantly higher because many victims never come to the attention of authorities or service providers.delaware
Look for vulnerability, dependency and whether someone is using those vulnerabilities to control another person.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Whatever the motivation, Republican’s endorsement of Democrat deserves points for facts and reason
description: Since South Dakota’s Republican lame-duck Secretary of State Monae Johnson oddly endorsed the Democrat campaigning to replace her, voters reasonably might wonder: Is she for real? Even though she has been viewed at times during her tenure as just politically eccentric and confounding, this partisan betrayal was a core taboo, akin to political treason. Instea[...]
text:
Monae Johnson waits to welcome potential voters at an October 2022 meet-and-great in a Rapid City coffee shop, during her campaign to become South Dakota's secretary of state. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Since South Dakota’s Republican lame-duck Secretary of State Monae Johnson oddly endorsed the Democrat campaigning to replace her, voters reasonably might wonder: Is she for real?
Even though she has been viewed at times during her tenure as just politically eccentric and confounding, this partisan betrayal was a core taboo, akin to political treason.
Instead of taking this act of apparent partisan infidelity at face value, the current toxic divisiveness in American politics leads us to wonder whether Johnson’s decision was a genuine, evidence-based reversal of her previous MAGA-centric stances, an act of political revenge, or a calculated tactic to undergird an unstated future political ambition.
South Dakota’s top election official, a Republican, endorses a Democrat to succeed her

After all, like proverbial rats fleeing a sinking ship, more and more Republican candidates in the midterm elections this fall — and non-candidates like Johnson — seem to be running full speed away from the hard-core MAGA base and its election-denying messiah, President Donald Trump, to whom they’ve heretofore slavishly stuck like glue.
Even our own junior Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota — a sometime MAGA critic, to be fair — who is up for reelection to a six-year term in November, purposely decided to forgo the unusual 2026 Republican Midterm Convention on Sept. 9 in Dallas to instead confer with voters at coffees and meet-and-greets in 14 different South Dakota counties, according to The Hill, an influential Washington, D.C.,-based political news organ. 
The Hill article noted that Rounds, “who may face a tougher-than-expected challenge in a Republican-leaning state, said his time is better spent meeting with constituents in South Dakota” than gracing the vanity convention.
Still, questions abound about Johnson’s apparent stark betrayal of her political party.
Whereas she campaigned for secretary of state in 2022 refusing to clearly admit Joe Biden won the presidential election in 2020, making the conspiracy-theory concept “election integrity” a centerpiece of her platform, and releasing information that “revealed whether those on the state’s voter rolls were seeking government assistance such as food aid” (she apologized for that “accident”), she now says she’s changed her tune.
After the state Republican convention in June, where MAGA-aligned, hand-ballot-counting proponent Heather Baxter defeated her for the secretary of state nomination, Johnson announced in September she was endorsing the Democrats’ candidate, Terrence Davis, over Baxter. She stressed, “I cannot remain silent when I believe the integrity, stability, and professionalism of this office is at stake.”
Johnson wrote in a Sept. 19 letter published by South Dakota War College, a Republican blog, that she now believes:
“South Dakota deserves a Secretary of State who will strengthen confidence through performance rather than provocation; who will support election officials rather than burden them for political effect; who will protect voter access and election security without pretending those goals are enemies; and who will treat the office’s employees, voters, candidates, and business owners with dignity.”
In other words, much the opposite of what she originally ran on.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Whatever her real motivations, she gets points even at this awkward late stage for seeming to apply facts and reason to the 2026 election equation. Indeed, rather than parroting partisan political gospel, whether or not it actually makes any sense, the sacred motivator of every candidate and elected official should be identifying truth and presenting it fairly to voters. Which is to say public officials should always apply thoughtful, objective skepticism with good faith to societal problems, instead of knee-jerk, visceral bias.
“How tightly should you hold your beliefs?” Massimo Pigliucci, the K D Irani Professor of Philosophy at City College of New York, recently asked in Aeon, a digital magazine of ideas, philosophy and culture. “You face the question several times a week without noticing. Hold them too loosely and you don’t stand for anything, hold them too tightly and you become the sort of person no argument can reach.” 
“Most of us swing between the two and have no vocabulary for the ground in between,” he added in his fascinating essay. “A Roman lawyer [Marcus Tullius Cicero, 106-43 BCE] worked one out … and it is still the best answer available.”
Pigliucci noted that uber-skeptic Cicero believed, “a genuine sceptic, confronted with compelling new evidence, updates (beliefs) — whereas the contrarian does not: they shift goalposts, raise new objections, or ignore what they cannot explain.”
Monae Johnson’s intent in her political about-face might be noble. But who can really be sure in American politics these days?

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Proposed Trump administration changes would gut vital Head Start regulations
description: Head Start works comprehensively. The harm of the proposed rule does not come from any one of the above changes alone, it comes from the compounding impact of removing services and protections for the most vulnerable children and families.
text:
IN THE SPRING of 1965, President Lyndon Johnson announced the launch of a new initiative: Head Start, a program designed to support poor children’s readiness for kindergarten by not only offering them time in classrooms but by addressing their health and well-being and partnering with their families to improve their circumstances. Our nation responded to that vision. Just a few months later, communities across our Commonwealth and across the country welcomed children into Head Start centers.
Sixty-one years later, 28 Head Start agencies across Massachusetts continue to uphold that vision – that vulnerable children deserve the highest quality early education and wraparound supports to grow and thrive. The Head Start statute and regulations codified the early vision for the program and expanded it over time to serve children from birth until kindergarten. Now, that national commitment is at risk because of a recent proposal that would dismantle Head Start’s federal standards. 
In August, the Trump administration released a proposal to gut Head Start regulations and threaten the quality, scope, and services of Head Start. The proposed rule eliminates quality early learning standards; removes standards for critical wraparound services for children and families, including health and mental health services; reduces access and eligibility for children from families experiencing homelessness, children with disabilities, and foster children; and threatens learning outcomes for dual language learners.  
A child cannot learn if she is hungry. A family cannot focus on school readiness if they are facing eviction. A teacher cannot meet a traumatized child’s needs if her classroom is too large, her training is inadequate, and she has no classroom supports. These facts have been the basis of Head Start’s design for 61 years, and now that design is at risk. 
The federal proposal is framed as reducing federal burden and giving local programs greater flexibility. Massachusetts Head Start programs welcome meaningful flexibility. We already design services around the needs of our communities. But rather than addressing the real challenges facing Head Start — including rising operating costs, workforce shortages, and years of inadequate funding — the proposal punishes programs, families, and young children. It hands programs fewer resources and fewer protections at the same time, and it removes many of the evidence-based standards that best serve children and families.  
I see the difference those standards make across Massachusetts’s 28 Head Start agencies. Together, our programs serve more than 10,000 young children and families in ways that best meet the needs of their local communities, including full-day classrooms, home visiting models, and partnerships with early learning programs and public schools. 
Head Start programs enroll the most vulnerable children in their communities, who often need more than the basics that a licensed child care program provides. Head Start programs offer early education alongside health and dental care, developmental screenings, mental health support, nutrition, disability services, and family supports.  
Parents are partners and leaders in their children’s education and in the governance of their programs. And because the services are so customized to those who need them, the harms of the proposal will be felt most deeply by some of the most vulnerable families in our Commonwealth. 
In Massachusetts, 16 percent of Head Start children experienced homelessness during the 2024–25 program year—an 82 percent increase from just two years earlier. Yet the proposed rule would make it harder for families experiencing homelessness to access Head Start by requiring families to provide documentation proving their homelessness status, documentation that many families cannot produce. For a family already living in crisis, it can mean losing access to the very program designed to help them stabilize. 
The same is true for children who speak a language other than English at home. Sixty-four percent of Massachusetts Head Start children come from homes where English is not the primary language, the highest proportion of dual language learners in Head Start of any US state. 
Decades of research tell us that young children learn best when taught by bilingual educators who speak their home language. The proposed rule abandons that research, requiring all education and family services to be conducted in English while eliminating standards supporting bilingual personnel and culturally responsive services. 
Again, the impact is cumulative. These changes would mean less effective communication with families, weaker family engagement, and fewer opportunities for children to learn in ways that reflect how they actually experience the world. 
The proposed changes also threaten the people who make Head Start possible: its workforce. Massachusetts Head Start programs employ more than 4,000 people. These educators, family service workers, health professionals, bus drivers, and other staff build relationships that children depend on. But the proposal would increase class sizes, remove the ability for programs to invest in their workforce’s education and professional development, eliminate staff wellness and break requirements, and reduce key supports, including behavioral health and bus monitors.  
The federal analysis estimates that nearly 40,000 Head Start jobs could be lost nationally. Our standards should encourage recruitment and retention in our programs, not threaten it. 
Head Start works comprehensively. The harm of the proposed rule does not come from any one of the above changes alone, it comes from the compounding impact of removing services and protections for the most vulnerable children and families. The answer to Head Start’s challenges is not to expect less of it. It is to invest in the people and resources that allow it to deliver on its promise. 
I am grateful that in Massachusetts, our elected leaders know the value of Head Start and we have the full support of the Healey-Driscoll administration, the state House and Senate, and the Massachusetts congressional delegation in opposing the proposal. Public comment in the Federal Register on these devastating proposed changes is open until October 6. 
My organization has submitted comments – and urges others to do so as well – imploring the Trump administration to withdraw the proposed rule and protect the promise of Head Start for the next 61 years. 
Michelle Haimowitz is executive director of the Massachusetts Head Start Association, which serves as the voice of Head Start programs in Massachusetts.

name: Delaware
title: University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens Start Conference Play with Loss
description: The Liberty Flames (4-1, 1-0 CUSA) defeated the University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens (2-3, 0-1 CUSA), 30-6, on October 2.   NEWARK, DE — UD needed a spark. The Blue Hens trailed, 20-0, a little more than halfway through the third quarter and as the offense jogged on the field, a switch was made at quarterback. Braden Streeter took ... Read More
text:
Blue Hen quarterback Braden Streeter throws a pass against Merrimack in the University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens first game of the season. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder.
The Liberty Flames (4-1, 1-0 CUSA) defeated the University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens (2-3, 0-1 CUSA), 30-6, on October 2.
 
NEWARK, DE — UD needed a spark. The Blue Hens trailed, 20-0, a little more than halfway through the third quarter and as the offense jogged on the field, a switch was made at quarterback. Braden Streeter took over for the first time starter EJ Archfield Jr. 
Streeter threw three passes on his first drive. The first was a completion that lost a yard, the second fell incomplete and the third ended up in the hands of Flames’ linebacker Deuce Spurlock. Spurlock returned the interception to Delaware’s nine-yard line. The Flames ended the drive with only a field goal, but any chance of a comeback was dashed by the turnover. 
Liberty defeated the Blue Hens, 30-14, Friday night. 
“I do think that we just played against a good football team who beat us pretty good. I don’t know that it had to be the kind of game that it was,” head coach Ryan Carty said postgame. “If we’re being honest and if it was an honest assessment it was so it is what it was, they beat our butts, but I think if we played a little cleaner, that would have been a pretty darn good ball game.”
Streeter got other opportunities behind center in the game’s final 22 minutes and led Delaware to its first score of the game. Freshman Tyler Bell led the Blue Hens’ final scoring drive at the end of the fourth quarter. The touchdowns were scored by Donovan Lewis and Matthew McKinley-Daniels.
Delaware played three quarterbacks throughout Friday nights’ action choosing to give Archfield Jr. the starting assignment in his first ever collegiate game. Archfield finished the game with ten completed passes for 137 yards and a fumble. The fumble occurred on a run which would’ve given the Blue Hens a first down and positioned them in the red zone on their second drive of the first half.
It’s the first time this season UD’s lost a fumble.
“It’s a tough situation to go in there against one of the better teams in our conference, you know, in his first time seeing any action in the game and, you know, not just first time starting, it was the first time since high school getting in a game,” Carty said. “I think he did an admirable job.” 
The offense never found a rhythm after that, crossing mid-field once between the turnover and Streeter’s touchdown drive. UD’s offense finished the game with 359 total yards and two conversions on 13 third down plays.
Despite the score, Delaware’s defense put together a respectable performance against Conference USA’s (CUSA) top scoring offense. 
The Blue Hens defense held the Flames to field goals on their first two drives and forced a punt on Liberty’s third drive, despite being on the field for over half the first quarter. The Flames continued to wear down the Blue Hen defense in the second quarter and scored their first touchdown on a 56-yard run by junior Kam Davis. Liberty’s second touchdown was scored by senior running back Peyton Jones. Jones’ three-yard touchdown run completed a 12 play, 98-yard drive by the Flames offense that sent the Blue Hens into halftime trailing by 20.
The Delaware defense performed better in the second half and allowed only ten points. The defense held Liberty’s running game to 83 yards in the second half following the first half in which the Flames rushed for 199. The Blue Hen defense finished the game giving up 440 yards of total offense.
“We obviously didn’t play to our standard,” senior defensive tackle Dominick Brogna said postgame. “We got to go watch film, we got to lock in on the small details, the communications, the adjustments, the rotations, everything and we need to get it changed.”  
The Blue Hens have 11 days to correct their mistakes and prepare for a road matchup against their second CUSA opponent, the Middle Tennessee Blue Raiders. It’s unclear which of Delaware’s quarterback options will get the starting assignment, but it is unlikely to be Nick Minicucci whom coach Carty says is “week-to-week”. 
“I was kind of out of answers on the back end, and at that point, I wanted to see what everybody can do, and kind of give a chance to everybody and see, you know, if we could evaluate that and then continue to leave it up for competition,” Carty said. “Where we go from here is gonna be us as coaches, you know, in that room and hopefully somebody pulls away with it when they get the opportunity too and proves that they’re the guy if Nick is out for a long time.”
Delaware’s game against the Blue Raiders is Tuesday, October 13. The game will be played in Tennessee and be nationally televised on CBS Sports Network. The game starts at 7:00 p.m.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Immigration insights: Tears and action follow ICE raids  in southwest Kansas
description: DODGE CITY — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrived in southwest Kansas on Sept. 22 and departed three days later, leaving fear, uncertainty and anger.  Many in the Hispanic and Latino communities in Dodge City, Garden City and Liberal, where most ICE activity was located, returned to work this week. But their fear persists […]
text:
Dodge City protesters gather at Wright Park on Sept. 25, 2026, to march to U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann's office. They were protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions in the community. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)DODGE CITY — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrived in southwest Kansas on Sept. 22 and departed three days later, leaving fear, uncertainty and anger. 
Many in the Hispanic and Latino communities in Dodge City, Garden City and Liberal, where most ICE activity was located, returned to work this week. But their fear persists and they aren’t yet leaving their homes or returning to regular activities, multiple immigrants said. 
The fear was contagious. In Manhattan, about 225 miles east of Dodge City, social media posts blasted warnings of possible ICE agents on Thursday because of a large presence of law enforcement vehicles in a store parking lot. It turned out to be a training session for local police, according to a store employee. 
Here are a handful of glimpses into the lives of Kansans affected by the raids. 
 
Viridiana Boron, volunteer
Viridiana Boron spent several days last week delivering meals to Dodge City families whose members were scared to leave home because ICE was in the area. 
Her mother and sister cooked meals for about 200 people, and Boron delivered them, she said. 
“I was the one that was on the street and watching everything, watching all the suffer the families was having,” she said, pausing to apologize for her English. “I saw the reality, the truth. They were scared. They were sad. They were worried. I saw families with no water.”
Boron started crying. 
“It was something that I’ve never seen in my life,” she said. “How can people not have heart and just do things like that? Because I mean, there I know could be a lot of immigrants over here that are like criminals, but a lot of people that I saw, they were not criminals. They were people working hard for their kids.”
This week, many people she knows have returned to work, but they aren’t eating out or shopping as the fear lingers, Boron said. 
Boron came to the United States at age 24, receiving a visa because she and her family were threatened in Mexico. She has since married and is a legal permanent resident. Despite knowing she had the correct documentation, she was scared during the ICE operation. 
Others who stayed home also had documentation, she said. But they have seen instances where it didn’t matter, and ICE agents stopped cars to check paperwork just because someone looked Hispanic or Latina, Boron said. 
The affect on the community was “huge,” she said. It was difficult explaining to her 11-year-old son why people were scared because he didn’t understand the difference a paper could make, Boron said.  
“We are all the same,” she said. 
Priest Mercado, 15, attends a Dodge City march on Sept. 25, 2026, to protest the presence of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents detaining immigrants in his community. He said that he doesn’t believe families should be torn apart. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Julie Barraza, volunteer and activist
Julie Barraza smiled at everyone approaching the table she set up at a downtown Dodge City protest on Sept. 24. She patiently answered questions about a petition to reform the country’s immigration system. 
“I was born and raised here, and I’ve never seen such a cloud over the town,” she said during a break. “The first morning, they (ICE) were waiting for me to get out of my car, and I didn’t know what was going on. I didn’t get out of my car.”
Barraza drove on to work at Rattlesnake Grill. She said ICE agents came in to eat but employees didn’t realize they were with ICE because they wore regular clothing. 
“Once we figured out they were ICE agents, because a customer had alerted us, I stepped out and decided to tell them to leave, and they refused,” she recalled. “I was scared, but I still did it.”
The agents did get up and leave, Barraza said, adding that several restaurants in town refused to serve agents and others closed because there weren’t employees to work. 
 
Patrick Lopez, immigrant and educator
Patrick Lopez stood in the midst of a Dodge City protest on Sept. 24, holding a sign and nodding to people he knew. He was there, he said, to “show solidarity with people who are being persecuted by ICE.”
 “I’m here to defend my immigrant brothers and sisters. I’m here to stand up for them, and I hate that they have to live in fear right now,” Lopez said. “I can’t sleep last night. I’m offended as an American. I’m embarrassed as an American. I’m indignant. I can’t believe that this is happening right now.”
While acknowledging the economic costs to town — restaurants closed, businesses slowing or stopping work — Lopez said they weren’t what made him toss and turn at night. 
“I also wish that people remembered the human rights effect,” he said. “People’s families should be protected. I don’t care what the issue is. You can’t destroy people’s families like that and hopefully get away with it.”
He tried unsuccessfully to reach a friend who drives a cab and worried that he was detained. 
“He works every day, and that’s the thing. The people that ICE is after are hardworking people around town,” Lopez said. “Many of them are putting their kids through school. They’re just trying to make a living.”
Dodge City protesters gather at Wright Park on Sept. 25, 2026, to march to U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann’s office. They were protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions in the community. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)
Sarahí Aguilera, therapist and immigrant
Sarahí Aguilera is a licensed social worker, and she works as a mental health therapist. Advocating for the immigrant community, she said, is at the foundation of her personal and professional life. 
She knows the challenges well. Aguilera is part of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, which allows young people who arrived during specific time periods to apply and work in the country. 
DACA has been under fire during President Donald Trump’s administration, she said, but she was fortunate that her permit didn’t expire when the program was temporarily halted. Since then, it has been a “consistent uphill battle” to keep the program active, Aguilera said.  
Other family members weren’t so lucky. Aguilera’s sister had just been to an immigration appointment after turning 15, which is the age that people can apply for the DACA program, Aguilera said. 
“We had started her paperwork. She had been approved. She had gone to her biometrics. I lived at Wichita at the time because that’s where I was getting my education,” she said. “And she got approved. She just never received her work permit.”
It was frustrating because when the family looked her up in the system, it said she was approved, Aguilera said. But she never physically received the approval that would allow her to receive her driver’s license or continue her education. 
Her sister eventually married and is in the process of acquiring her documentation, Aguilera said. The experience reminds her how difficult it is to go through the immigration process and how different it is for each person, she said.  
“Especially seeing me and believing she was going to have the same opportunity,” Aguilera said. “It really impacted her mental health and her motivation to further her education and just work on herself.”
Aguilera volunteers with New Frontiers, a nonprofit organization that works with young people in southwest Kansas to create a grassroots movement focused on political, social and economic power. 
The group has a rapid response team that becomes active when events like ICE raids in the area occur, she said. Volunteers watch for ICE agents and try to verify information before releasing it to the community. 
“Fear already does a lot to someone,” Aguilera said. “So fear and the wrong information — we want to make sure that we’re just prepared and grounded with what information we’re trying to share.”
Fear of the unknown is a problem for southwest Kansas immigrants, Aguilera said, along with how overwhelming information coming out could be. 
While ICE was in the area, she saw about four clients because most were afraid to go out. Typically, her schedule is full every day. 
Aguilera said she understands why some people are critical of immigrants who don’t have documentation. 
“There is so much misinformation. I believe as a society we need to do a better job of understanding what the immigration process looks like,” she said. “Of understanding what are the barriers, what are the circumstances? Because there is not a system that is going to work for all of us.”
DACA recipients, for instance, don’t have a pathway to citizenship unless they marry or their jobs petition for them, Aguilera said.
Whatever a person’s belief system, she said, she hopes people are careful with their words. 
“I do think it’s important to be mindful of the comments and what they can do to the mental health of someone overall,” she said, adding that people are easily influenced by social media and political figures, who she believes often don’t understand the process either.
Does she think significant immigration reform is likely? 
“My heart wants to say that it’s hopeful. My uncertainty and anxiety that I’ve experienced for the past 10 years wants me to have a different answer,” Aguilera said. “I do believe people are opening their eyes. I believe we are getting a lot more information and more attention. Although I think we are creating great awareness and sharing information and education, I don’t believe we will see the impact and the change we want to see until people get out and vote.”

title: Buddy Guy celebrated at Radio City Music Hall with a sold-out ‘Buddy’s Got the Blues’ show
description: Bobby Rush, left, and Buddy Guy perform at Buddy's Got the Blues during a 90th Birthday Concert Celebration at the Radio City Music Hall in New York, Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Charles Sykes/Invison/AP)
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
NEW YORK (AP) — Two months past his 90th birthday, Buddy Guy is still up for a little bragging, a lot of cursing and a long night of partying.
The blues great was celebrated Thursday night with a sold-out show at Radio City Music Hall in New York, where a lineup of guest musicians and a house band led by Rolling Stones drummer Steve Jordan had the audience on its feet for much of the three-hour-plus “Buddy’s Got the Blues” concert.
Guy himself was only on stage part of the time, but his name was heard throughout, and his spirit always present. One of the last of the Chicago bluesmen who thrived in the mid-20th century, Guy has become so much the ideal of the genre that musicians didn’t need to perform his songs to summon his legend.
John Mayer, with an ache in his voice on Otis Redding’s “I’ve Got Dreams to Remember,” and Eric Gales and Joe Bonamassa jamming on the Jimmy Reed standard “Baby What You Want Me to Do,” seemed as fitting as Susan Tedeschi and Derek Trucks reviving an old Guy-Junior Wells favorite, “Messin’ with the Kid.”
But no one was going to top the guest of honor. Guy, wearing a dark cap, dark pants and a polka dot shirt, opened the show with a long, raunchy acoustic workout of John Lee Hooker’s “I’m in the Mood” and only seemed to get friskier after bringing out his electric guitar.
He leered and joked with longtime friend Shemekia Copeland on a duet of “Rock Me Baby,” left no doubt about the meaning of “to buzz all night long” in Slim Harpo’s “I’m a King Bee” and carried on a lot more when joined by one of his few contemporaries, Bobby Rush, just a month away from his 93rd birthday. Everyone came on at the end for an all-out, self-fulfilling “Got My Mojo Workin.’”
Guy is still making plans. His team announced this week that he has a new album out next year, produced by Jordan and featuring multi-instrumentalist Ivan Neville, bassist Willie Weeks and others who played at Radio City Music Hall.
Guy didn’t seem at first to have a lot on his mind Thursday besides the next double entendre or the next profanity. “Help me f—k up this song,” he liked to call out. But the tributes offered by the younger performers and the presence of Rush, who testified that he would have walked from Mississippi just to be here, left him moved and near tears.
“I didn’t think this many people would be coming out for a 90 year old man,” Guy said, after confiding he didn’t have the strength to blow out that many “f—kin’ candles” on the cakes brought out at the end. “This is the greatest day I ever had in my life.”

title: Jeffrey Mullins sentenced for role in fatal Hartford shooting
description:
Mullins is one of three people involved in the botched robbery that turned fatal in August 2025.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Jeffrey Mullins sentenced for role in fatal Hartford shooting.
text:
Jessica Lemay (left on Webex screen) gives her victim impact statement during the sentencing of Jeffrey Mullins (center) for his involvement in a fatal shooting last August. Photo by Alex Ebrahimi/Valley News

This story by Alex Ebrahimi was first published in the Valley News on Oct. 1, 2026. 
WHITE RIVER JUNCTION — One of three individuals involved in a botched robbery turned fatal shooting in Hartford has been sentenced to six to 10 years, suspended to six months in prison with 10 years of probation.
Jeffrey Mullins, 47, was arrested along with Michelle Mullins, 49, and the alleged gunman, Demetrius Drew, 31, of New Haven, Connecticut, in connection with the death of David Labrecque, 65, of Canaan, New Hampshire, who was shot and killed outside a home on Verna Court on Aug. 21, 2025.
Labrecque died to save the life of his girlfriend, Jessica Lemay, who survived but suffered gunshot wounds to the hand and abdomen. To this day, Lemay, who planned on marrying Labrecque, has a bend in her ring finger as a result of the attack.
“(Labrecque) was the hero that day,” Lemay told the court at Jeffrey Mullins’ sentencing hearing in Windsor Superior Court on Thursday. “Since the shooting, my life has been permanently altered.”
On top of her physical injuries, Lemay said in her statement to the court, she struggles to cope with psychological trauma which is “not in the past, it’s ongoing.”
Both Mullinses were initially charged with aiding in the commission of first-degree murder, which carries a penalty of up to life in prison, and a charge of accessory to attempted assault and robbery, with a penalty of up to 10 years. 
Both Mullinses are now avoiding those potential penalties.
In a November 2025 plea agreement, Jeffrey Mullins agreed to plead guilty to felony accessory to attempted assault and robbery, with a sentence of six to 10 years suspended to six months and 10 years of probation.
On Thursday morning, Windsor Superior Judge Elizabeth Mann accepted and ordered the sentence, which also includes around three months of credit for time already served.
Michelle Mullins admitted guilt to the same lesser charge in a May plea agreement, also stipulating a sentence of six to 10 years suspended to six months, but with 12 years of probation.
For Lemay, the punishment doesn’t fit the crime.
“It’s insane that you get more time in the state of Vermont for drugs than you do for being involved in not only murder, but an attempted murder of a second person,” Lemay said.
The state has agreed not to refile the dismissed charge of aiding in the commission of first-degree murder for both Mullinses unless they fail to comply with court-sealed cooperation agreements ahead of the trial of the alleged gunman, Demetrius Drew.
“The state recognizes that (the plea agreements don’t) capture the harm caused,” said prosecutor Nicholas Battey, in response to Lemay’s victim impact statement. “Of course, the person the state is charging with killing David Labrecque and almost killing and seriously traumatizing (Lemay) is Demetrius Drew.”
Lemay’s anger, Battey added, is understandable and “appropriate,” but he said the state’s objective is to seek the “maximum justice it can for the person most responsible for the harm.”
“It just seemed an unacceptable risk to not get the cooperation of the co-defendants in this case,” he said, justifying the plea deals.
Jeffrey Mullins’ defense attorney, Jordan Handy, assured the court that his client is determined to help with the conviction of Drew.
“From day one, as soon as this all occurred, (Mullins) was immediately wanting to participate in putting Demetrius away behind bars and make sure that that is the end result here, because that is nothing that my client was ever interested in being involved in,” Handy said.
In a statement of his own to the court, Jeffrey Mullins expressed remorse over the incident.
“I couldn’t be more sorry,” he said. “Not a day goes by where I don’t regret everything that happened.”
While one ongoing case of three comes to a close with Mullins being transported in handcuffs to Southern State Correctional Facility in Springfield on Thursday, Lemay said the wounds inflicted in August 2025 remain open.
“Every time this case is brought up, I’m revictimized,” she said in her statement at the beginning of Mullins’ sentencing.
The scheduling of Jeffrey Mullins’ presentence investigation, which culminates in a report prepared by a probation officer detailing a defendant’s criminal history to assist a judge in final sentencing, had been delayed due to his prior incarceration in New Hampshire in Grafton County Jail in connection with a separate misdemeanor criminal trespass case from March 2023.
Michelle Mullins, whose change of plea hearing was also previously delayed, is scheduled for a sentencing hearing on Nov. 13 at 9 a.m.
Drew is not expected to go on trial until next year. In July, he wrote to the court requesting a new arraignment and bail hearing and the impeachment of a witness due to perjury.
“I have to carry the full weight that the system hasn’t finished addressing,” Lemay told the court Thursday.
She said she has been forced to relive the incident over and over, leaving her “drained and empty.”
“My entire world flipped upside down in a matter of two minutes and they all three had a part in it,” she said. “But that doesn’t matter, does it?”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri students need more than a semester of financial literacy
description: As a high school teacher and parent, I see many things to change about our educational system, from funding and curriculum to choice.  A strengthened focus on financial literacy while re-thinking foreign language requirements should be also at the top of any reform list. Most American universities and colleges desire one or more years of […]
text:
(Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)As a high school teacher and parent, I see many things to change about our educational system, from funding and curriculum to choice.  A strengthened focus on financial literacy while re-thinking foreign language requirements should be also at the top of any reform list.
Most American universities and colleges desire one or more years of foreign language (Spanish, French, German, etc) from applicants along with the requisite number of core courses (math, science, etc).  Highly competitive universities strongly suggest or require two or more years of foreign language.
There is no doubt that studying foreign language offers many benefits to students.  However, to my knowledge no major American universities requires financial literacy — the language of money — from would-be students.
It seems our country is at an inflection point.  One major American political party – the Democrats – is wrestling with a large insurgency of young Socialists who want to radically re-order the economic structure of our nation.  Some young Republicans and conservatives are also captivated by this messaging.
“Capitalism” is increasingly becoming a four-letter word for too many Millennials and members of Gen Z.  Yet, this should not be surprising as today’s young people lived through the wreckage of the Great Recession, and then too many of these souls followed up by burying themselves deep in student loan debt and then flocking to expensive locales like New York City.
Is it any wonder that many young Americans feel like the system is rigged and willingly gravitate to voices who promise forgiveness of debt and “free stuff?”  Have our K-12 schools failed kids?   I think so.
Here in Missouri and most other states, we require a semester of financial literacy for high school graduation, but that is not nearly enough.   Unlike conjugating the verb “to be” in Spanish or French, our students will speak the language of money every day of their adult lives but our curriculum priorities do not reflect this reality.
Again, foreign language is not be dismissed, but as an educator I think we need to re-shift our resources.  Many K-8thgrade students receive a smattering of foreign language instruction (a day or two a week, or a quarter), but then they are expected to take year-long courses in foreign language in high school to satisfy university requirements. This seems backwards.
The minds of elementary and middle school students are more plastic and open to new things like learning a foreign language.  High school foreign language teachers should be shifted to younger grades to immerse these younger children in foreign languages as the Europeans do.  If a child really enjoys Spanish, French, or German, they should be afforded the opportunity for advanced classes in high school that may lead to various employment opportunities.
Most teenagers will get their first job, earn a driver’s license, and be engaged in a myriad of financial activities during their high school years.  This should be the time for kids to truly learn about our financial system, but educators barely giving it a passing glance. High school students should study finance for a year, or longer.
High schools have core graduation requirements for a reason: Because kids need certain knowledge to be considered educated and ready for the next steps in life.  Could you imagine, however, if our high schools only required a semester of math instruction for graduation?  How about a semester of science or history to wear a cap and gown?  Parents would be outraged, and university presidents would be lobbying for change.  Yet, we are collectively silent regarding our current financial literacy requirements — one semester or a half credit — and then wonder why so many kids are getting into trouble with money.
Financial literacy requirements need to be increased for high school graduation and admission to any American university as well as any trade school or enlistment in the United States military.
To encourage this important shift, universities need to do their part by mandating financial literacy as a core requirement for applicants (right up there with math, science, English, and history) while seeking evidence of foreign language in K-8th grade transcripts.  Also, state departments of education can increase the pool of qualified financial literacy teachers by accounting for the professional and personal financial experiences of interested educators.
Kids need to learn about money, and our schools need to offer this support.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nine-year dry spell ends Tuesday when state treasurer resumes unclaimed property auction
description: LINCOLN — Stored in a secure spot in a Haymarket District satellite office of the Nebraska state treasurer are abandoned safe deposit boxes filled with items that once were treasures to someone.  Now the public will have a shot at buying pieces of unclaimed property ranging from a diamond ring, a 1961 Topps No. 2 Roger […]
text:
The Unclaimed Property Division of the Nebraska State Treasurer is in Lincoln's historic Haymarket District. Stored in secure area here are  abandoned safe deposit boxes to be up for bid during a seven-day online auction on eBay starting Oct. 6. (Courtesy of Nebraska State Treasurer)LINCOLN — Stored in a secure spot in a Haymarket District satellite office of the Nebraska state treasurer are abandoned safe deposit boxes filled with items that once were treasures to someone. 
Now the public will have a shot at buying pieces of unclaimed property ranging from a diamond ring, a 1961 Topps No. 2 Roger Maris baseball card and a 1934 $500 Federal Reserve note.
Diamond ring up for bid. (Courtesy of Nebraska Treasurer’s Office)
Starting at 8 a.m. Tuesday, a seven-day online auction on eBay will be held to sell the property whose owners likely died and whose heirs have not come forward. The contents were turned over to the treasurer and have sat unclaimed for at least a decade. 
The lineup will be available for viewing when the auction goes live on opening day.
By law, the state treasurer is to conduct a sale of unclaimed property every five years. The last auction was held in 2017, Treasurer Joey Spellerberg confirmed, and items have accumulated.
Spellerberg, who was appointed to his office last November, said he was uncertain of the reason for the gap. He noted a pandemic and turnover in the office during that time. John Murante served from 2019 into 2023 and Tom Briese served from 2023 through 2025.
Murante and Briese promoted the return of unclaimed property in another way, encouraging the use of the NebraskaLostCash.nebraska.gov online lookup.
Spellerberg said his overall goal is to return unclaimed property to original or rightful owners. Multiple efforts were made over several years to locate owners of the items to be auctioned, he said, but were not successful.
“The auction gives these items a new home while preserving the proceeds for their rightful owners,” Spellerberg said, noting that the money from a sale will be waiting if an owner or heir comes forward in the future.
Sports cards up for bid. (Courtesy of Nebraska Treasurer’s Office)
Items to be auctioned have been appraised, he said. Proceeds from individual sales will be recorded in the original owner’s name and held in that name until claimed by rightful owners.
Among items to be auctioned: the white gold diamond ring; a mesh 4.5-ounce purse marked 14-karat gold; a 1917 ladies watch with 14-karat gold band; a 49-piece sterling silverware set; a 1995 Sports Illustrated Huskers National Champions special edition; a 1924 peace dollar; Morgan silver dollars; a 1986 Denver-minted dime with mint error, double struck; a 1929 $100 bill U.S. currency, Federal Reserve of Minneapolis.
Since Nebraska’s unclaimed property law took effect in the late 1960s, the state has returned more than $317 million to rightful owners, the Treasurer’s Office said. One in five Nebraskans has unclaimed property, with money waiting to be claimed in all 93 Nebraska counties.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Steve Erdman: Nebraska must overhaul tax system to prosper
description: I read with interest John Cannon’s recent commentary in the Examiner. As noted in his information, Cannon is the director and lobbyist for NACO  —  the Nebraska Association of County Officials. During my eight years in the Legislature, I cannot recall a single instance in which NACO supported any property‑tax‑relief legislation I introduced to provide […]
text:
State Sen. Steve Erdman of Bayard testifies on behalf of Legislative Bill 16 and a pair of constitutional amendments to create and codify the EPIC option consumption tax Wednesday, July 31, 2024, in Lincoln. (Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)I read with interest John Cannon’s recent commentary in the Examiner. As noted in his information, Cannon is the director and lobbyist for NACO  —  the Nebraska Association of County Officials. During my eight years in the Legislature, I cannot recall a single instance in which NACO supported any property‑tax‑relief legislation I introduced to provide property tax relief in Nebraska.  
One of the most significant bills I sponsored — and which ultimately passed  —  was the damaged‑property bill. This law allows property owners to have their valuation reduced when their property sustains at least 20% damage before July 1 of any year. That provision has saved Nebraska taxpayers millions of dollars over the last six years. Yet NACO opposed it, worried about potential revenue losses for counties. Their position consistently prioritizes government collections over the taxpayers who actually fund those budgets — the people who sign the front of the check, not the back.
Research shows the average household in South Dakota pays $12,300 annually in all taxes. In Nebraska, that number is $16,346 — a 33% higher burden on Nebraska families. Despite this, Cannon argues that “property taxes offer something especially valuable: stable, locally controlled and locally invested funding.” In practice, that means government buys whatever it wants and sends taxpayers the bill, with little regard for whether families can afford the increase.
He also claims that shifting funding to sales or income tax would introduce “budget volatility.” But when a household’s income drops, property taxes do not drop with it. Property tax is a mandatory tax — one you must pay whether you have the revenue or not. Sales tax, by contrast, is voluntary. You pay it only when you have the money to make a purchase. Sales tax is collected from those passing through or visiting Nebraska. Consequently, they help fund our government. 
The state has already removed most community‑college funding from property taxes, and those institutions continue to operate with local control. It works.
Our state constitution is clear: “The Legislature shall provide for the free instruction in the common schools of this state…” (Nebraska Constitution, Article VII‑1)
Education funding is the responsibility of the state — not property owners.
Property taxes also penalize homeowners for unrealized gains. When your property value increases, you are taxed on that increase — even though you have not sold the property or realized any income. Yet when your 401(k) increases in value, the government does not tax that unrealized gain. Shouldn’t similar principles apply?
Cannon also warns about volatility in sales and income tax. When economist Art Laffer (the most renowned economist in the nation) visited my office, he made a different point: States that rely on sales tax perform better in good times than states that don’t — and they perform much better in bad times than states that don’t!
Cannon says broadening our economic base is a good idea. I agree. But he offers no plan. The real path to economic growth is to eliminate property tax entirely and give Nebraskans the freedom to decide how much tax they pay and when they pay it.
Since 1967, Nebraska’s property valuations have increased 400%. Total tax dollars collected have increased 267%, while the mill levy has decreased 46%. The numbers speak for themselves. Houston, we have a problem.
Nebraska’s current property‑tax system is broken. It needs structural reform — not excuses, not fear‑based arguments, and not continued reliance on a tax that punishes homeowners, farmers, and families year after year.
Thank you for reading.

name: Daily Montanan
title: A River Runs Through It Act offers hope for the Blackfoot Valley
description: For more than two decades, people in Seeley Lake, Ovando and Lincoln have worked through one of the hardest questions in Montana: How do we care for public lands in a way that respects the many different people who depend on them? There has never been just one answer. These lands support timber jobs and […]
text:
The Bob Marshall Wilderness (Photo by Victor Albert Grigas | Via Wikimedia Commons | CC-BY-SA 2.0).For more than two decades, people in Seeley Lake, Ovando and Lincoln have worked through one of the hardest questions in Montana: How do we care for public lands in a way that respects the many different people who depend on them?

There has never been just one answer.

These lands support timber jobs and rural economies. They provide places to hunt, fish, hike, ride horses, mountain bike, snowmobile and use off-highway vehicles. They hold some of the wildest country left in the Lower 48 and support some of the most iconic wildlife. And they surround communities that live with the realities of wildfire and forest management every year.

That is why the proposal now called the A River Runs Through It Act matters.


 

  Who wrote this? 

The following people joined together to write this guest commentary. They are:

Jack Rich, Rich’s Montana Guest Ranch, Seeley Lake
Barb Cestero, Montana State Director for the Wilderness Society, Bozeman
Bill Cyr, Lincoln resident and retired Department of Natural Resources and Conservation forester, DNRC
Russ Ehnes, President, Montana Trail Vehicle Riders Association, Great Falls
Jim Stone, Rolling Stone Ranch, Ovando






Earlier this month, Rep. Ryan Zinke announced legislation based on long-running, locally developed efforts that grew from negotiation among Montanans who often began with very different ideas about public lands.

The resulting legislation will manage different parts of the landscape according to these diverse interests. It creates designated areas for forest restoration, adds to the Bob Marshall and Scapegoat Wilderness, and expands motorized and non-motorized recreation areas. It would also resolve the status of wilderness study areas near Helmville and Ovando that have been debated for decades.

This only happened because people representing conservation groups, the timber industry, outfitters, hunters and anglers, snowmobilers, trail riders, local governments and businesses kept coming back to the table. Finally, we stood together in Smoke Elser’s historic Missoula barn with Zinke to introduce this combined proposal – merging an updated Blackfoot Clearwater Stewardship proposal with the Lincoln Prosperity Proposal into the A River Runs Through It Act.

We are grateful to Congressman Zinke for carrying our hard work forward in Washington, D.C.

Zinke is delivering on the promise he made to make public lands a priority. He stood with us as we rejected a plan to sell millions of public lands last summer. Now, he’s trying to codify permanent protections that will help keep Montana the state we love for future generations.

Our leaders in Washington have long argued that decisions about public lands should reflect the knowledge and experience of the people who live, work, and recreate here. This bill gives them exactly what they’re looking for.

At a time when national politics is increasingly defined by division, the River Runs Through It Act offers a different example: People with competing interests and a shared love of the land staying at the table long enough to find common ground. And to even become friends.

That Montana way of solving problems has conserved the landscapes and way of life that make us proud to live here. Much of our beloved Bob Marshall Wilderness came into being because members of both parties representing Montana in Washington responded to similar calls to protect a place that is synonymous with our state.

Now, Sens. Steve Daines and Tim Sheehy, and Rep. Troy Downing have the chance to join us and Congressman Zinke to carry on that tradition. This is their chance to show Washington there’s a better way forward than partisan mudslinging by advancing the plan we’ve built for future generations in the Blackfoot River.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Public can comment on SNAP changes for candy, soda purchases in North Dakota
description: The public can now comment on planned changes to what North Dakotans can purchase with federal food assistance after the state postponed implementation of its Healthy Choice Waiver. The public comment period opened Sept. 15 and will be open until Oct. 15. Comments can be submitted through the Federal Register website. The waiver, which the […]
text:
Candy sits on the shelves at a retail store in Bismarck on Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The public can now comment on planned changes to what North Dakotans can purchase with federal food assistance after the state postponed implementation of its Healthy Choice Waiver.
The public comment period opened Sept. 15 and will be open until Oct. 15. Comments can be submitted through the Federal Register website.
The waiver, which the state applied for in 2025, would bar North Dakotans from using their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits to purchase most candies, energy drinks and sweetened beverages. 
The waiver was expected to take effect Sept. 1, but was postponed to Nov. 1 at the request of federal officials in an Aug. 25 letter asking for additional time to post a public notice about the waiver and assess public comments.
The request was likely connected to a recent federal court case challenging the waivers of five other states, said Rebecca Askins, director of the Economic Assistance section of the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services.
North Dakota grocers prepare for new SNAP restrictions amid uncertainty

“Part of that suit … is, in essence, requiring that this waiver is going to go through this process in the Federal Register,” Askins said. 
The public notice allows anyone, including stakeholders and members of the public, to share their thoughts on the waiver. The notice says the Food and Nutrition Administration, which oversees SNAP, is “particularly interested in comments regarding the state’s implementation and operation of the demonstration project.”
But Askins said she doesn’t know whether those comments could then be used to change North Dakota’s program, given that the state has already spent time and resources preparing to implement the waiver in its current form, which was approved by the USDA at the end of 2025.
“At this stage, it’s too early to know whether those comments would result in changes to North Dakota’s current waiver structure,” Askins said.
Four comments have been submitted as of Thursday. Of those comments, which do not include names, one was in favor and three were against the waiver.
“This is a great first step in cleaning up the unhealthy choices, we as a culture have enabled. Public funding assistance shouldn’t enable these bad habits,” one commenter wrote. 
But other commenters said they had concerns about the policy and its impact. 
“I have diabetes, and I have personally experienced episodes of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). When blood sugar drops, a person may need a fast-acting source of carbohydrate immediately,” the commenter wrote. “For a SNAP recipient who has very little cash outside of SNAP, having more than one practical option available matters.”
What does this mean for retailers?
A spokesperson from the U.S. Department of Agriculture told the Monitor that despite the delay, there will still be a 90-day grace period beginning Nov. 1. During that grace period, retailers will not face disciplinary action for failing to update their systems.
Askins said that even if the deadline hadn’t been postponed, the department was “fairly confident” that within the 90-day period, most or all retailers were going to be in compliance with the new rules.
North Dakota postpones ban on using food assistance for soda, candy

John Dyste, president of the North Dakota Grocers Association, said he’s hopeful that retailers will be able to make the needed changes before the deadline. But he said it’s been a struggle for many grocers and other retailers thus far.
“For the retailers to implement this program is not a simple process. It’s very involved. You’re taking whole categories of food that have been considered SNAP-eligible, and now, all of a sudden, they’re not,” he said. 
He added that the changes aren’t always intuitive.
“An example I was given was marshmallows. Mini marshmallows are eligible, but large marshmallows and colored marshmallows are not eligible,” he said. 
To help retailers sort through their products, the state paid a research firm to create a list of items that would no longer be eligible for SNAP. 
Dyste said his members have told him that the list includes barcodes for around 23,000 items, but many of them don’t match retailers’ codes for the same products. The list also doesn’t include products from grocers’ house brands.
That means that even with the list, retailers are still tasked with making sense of the new restrictions and how they apply to their products. 
So far, 106 retailers have requested the list, according to Askins, who said that accounts for about 65% of SNAP retailers in the state. She said the list is only available to retailers upon request because some of its content is confidential.
Some grocers who have reached out to the state for guidance haven’t received much help, Dyste said.
“My understanding is (that) when they contact the SNAP program, basically, what they’re told is that ‘You have to figure it out on your own.’ The recommendation is to go to your POS (point-of-sale) provider,” he said, adding that the service comes at a cost.
HHS hosted a series of webinars over the summer to explain the changes to retailers. At one of the webinars, an attendee asked whether there would be financial support to help stores pay to update their systems. 
An official initially said that the department was pursuing funding for that purpose, but another official cut in to say that, given the then-approaching Sept. 1 deadline, grocers should not count on additional funding. 
In the Aug. 27 news release announcing the postponement, Askins wrote that, “The new timeframe also allows HHS to expand support for this initiative.” But she told the Monitor that support does not include financial aid for retailers.
The department is exploring the possibility of doing more webinars between now and November, Askins said, adding that she doesn’t expect additional webinars or any other changes to increase the cost of implementing the waiver, which was initially projected to be $3.5 million to $4 million.
