title: URI students, faculty and staff now ride free on RIPTA buses under new agreement
description: University of Rhode Island (URI) students, faculty and staff can now ride public buses for free with their school IDs under an agreement announced last week between the university and the Rhode Island Public Transit Authority. URI will pay a flat $135,000 fee to join RIPTA’s U-Pass program, allowing members of the university community to […]
text:
Rhode Island Public Transit Authority bus 69, which serves the University of Rhode Island's Kingston campus, waits at a stop in Galilee. URI students, faculty and staff can now ride public buses for free with their school IDs now that the school has joined RIPTA’s U-Pass program. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)University of Rhode Island (URI) students, faculty and staff can now ride public buses for free with their school IDs under an agreement announced last week between the university and the Rhode Island Public Transit Authority.
URI will pay a flat $135,000 fee to join RIPTA’s U-Pass program, allowing members of the university community to board buses statewide at any time, including nights, weekends and university holidays, without paying the typical $2 fare. The agreement, signed Sept. 18, runs from Oct. 1 through Aug. 31, 2027.
Before joining the U-Pass program, URI students paid half price for RIPTA’s monthly bus passes, a discount arrangement that had been in place for at least two decades.
More than half of URI students commute to campus, according to the university. 
“We recognize that public transportation is an important service for many members of the URI community — not only as a way to get to and from campus, but also for their day-to-day transportation needs,” Ellen Reynolds, URI’s vice president for student affairs, said in a statement.
Other Rhode Island colleges and universities have also used RIPTA’s U-Pass program, with arrangements varying by school. Brown University, Rhode Island School of Design and Roger Williams University began participating in 2007, according to data provided by the bus agency.
At Roger Williams, all first-year students receive 10 free RIPTA rides during both the fall and spring semesters.
Bus rides are free for all students at Brown University, Bryant University, Providence College, Rhode Island College, Rhode Island School of Design and Salve Regina University. 
Students at the Community College of Rhode Island can purchase monthly RIPTA passes for half the usual $70 price, while Johnson & Wales University students can purchase semester passes for $200 during the fall and spring and $80 for the summer.
URI and RIPTA will meet quarterly to review ridership and the status of the U-Pass program, according to the agreement. URI officials said expanding access to public transportation can help the Kingston campus free up parking spaces, and help relieve traffic congestion.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: GOP pumps $8 million into Kansas to prop up flailing Roger Marshall. We have a race on our hands.
description: National Republicans are racing to the rescue of U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, diverting millions of dollars in advertising from North Carolina to Kansas. At least, that’s what the Friday reports from Semafor, The Associated Press and Politico indicate. The Senate Leadership Fund political action committee has reserved more than $8 million in ad spending right [[...]
text:
Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton and Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall debate Sept. 12, 2026, at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)National Republicans are racing to the rescue of U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, diverting millions of dollars in advertising from North Carolina to Kansas. At least, that’s what the Friday reports from Semafor, The Associated Press and Politico indicate.
The Senate Leadership Fund political action committee has reserved more than $8 million in ad spending right here over the next month, defending Marshall from a surprisingly robust challenge by Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton. The incumbent senator’s flat-footed campaign hasn’t helped.
We can learn three quick lessons from this news.
First, Marshall indeed is in trouble. Real trouble. Terrible, terrible trouble. Of the “capital T and that rhymes with P and that stands for pool” variety. In past columns, I’ve wavered over defining the race — on one hand, Marshall has flailed like an octogenarian on a Slip ‘N Slide, on the other, Kansans haven’t sent a Democratic senator to Washington since 1932.
Eight million smackers have a way of settling that argument. Marshall needs help, and the resources he has on hand don’t cut the mustard.
Second, national Republicans haven’t written off Kansas. A worse sign for Marshall would have been if the GOP decided to send no money whatsoever. (Ask North Carolina’s Michael Whatley how that feels.) Political junkies, reporters and everyday folks should keep watch over the next few weeks to see whether all that money reaches the airwaves.
If D.C. bigwigs see the race slipping away from Marshall, they might re-recommit those dollars to yet another state. We won’t know that for at least a couple of weeks though, or until after the Nov. 3 elections.
Third and finally, we are all experiencing a national environment as hostile to Republicans as any that I can remember since 2006. I had recently resettled in New Hampshire that year, and I remember copyediting stories about shocked Democrats elected to offices they barely campaigned for.
The country had turned so negatively against President George W. Bush that Democrats made gains across the board. With Republicans investing serious dollars in Kansas this fall, it’s clear enough that would-be voters need persuasion to stick with them.
Who knows how this all shakes out next month, when everyone makes their final choices. But Kansans can enjoy one hell of a contest in the meantime.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. title: P-funk praises Eric’s ID Law, Moore names new judges, more in political notes
description: OK, "Eric's ID Law" is popular, but you've arrived when Faith Evans and P-Funk's George Clinton are in your corner, Gov. Wes Moore names enough judges to form a softball team and Montgomery County seeks police advisory panel members, in political notes.
text:
Eric and Linda Carpenter-Grantham pose for a picture Thursday with Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller (D) at Andrews Federal Credit Union in Prince George's County, where an event was held to celebrate the one-year anniversary of Eric's ID Law. (Photo courtesy of Eric Carpenter-Grantham)Almost 31,000 people have applied to get butterfly logos added to their driver’s licenses and identification cards to indicate a hidden disability in the year since Eric’s ID Law allowing the logos took effect.
That feat was marked Thursday by Eric Carpenter-Grantham, the law’s namesake, his mother, Linda, and 148 others at a celebration at Andrews Federal Credit Union in Prince George’s County. Attendees included Gov. Wes Moore’s mother, Joy Thomas Moore; Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller (D); Comptroller Brooke Lierman; and Del. Kym Taylor (D-Prince George’s), one of the two main House sponsors of the legislation when it passed last year.
And support also came from R&B singer Faith Evans, who spoke in support of the law in a video, sporting a yellow T-shirt with a picture of Eric’s ID on it, and from George “Dr. Funkenstein” Clinton of Parliament Funkadelic, in a blue T-shirt with Eric’s ID on it. His favorite song by Clinton: “Atomic Dog.”
When asked if they ever envisioned tens of thousands of people asking the Motor Vehicle Administration for the butterfly logo, Linda Carpenter-Grantham said no. “Only by the grace of God,” said Eric , who has high-functioning autism.
The logo is designed to alert police and other emergency responders to the developmental or intellectual disabilities that are not immediately noticeable. The decal can be placed on driver’s licenses, MVA-issued identification cards, even moped operator permits.
The law also requires that the state Police Training and Standards Commission, in consultation with the State Police and other stakeholders, “implement training concerning interactions with individuals who have a nonapparent disability.”



It could be closer to becoming law in Washington, D.C., where the Eric’s ID Amendment Act of 2026 is set for a third reading Tuesday before the D.C. City Council. The bill would let applicants for a driver’s license, permit or identification card “to designate a butterfly as the nonapparent disability.” One of its sponsors was Council member Janeese Lewis George, who won the Democratic nomination this year for mayor.
Because of Eric and Linda’s continued push for other states to adopt similar laws, Eric was nominated to participate a grand marshal in the Disability Pride Parade in New York City on Oct. 18.
Back in Maryland, the Carpenter-Granthams said more public outreach and programs are needed for individuals with hidden disabilities. Linda said she would like libraries, grocery stores and businesses to incorporate an Eric’s ID program, letting individuals with hidden disabilities to wear a butterfly lanyard if they wanted to, for example.
“A person with an individual disability or a disability could ask for a butterfly lanyard and for the people who work there would be able to assist them in a grocery store,” she said. “That way a person with a hidden disability could not only be helped, but also that person who works there would be educated and learn how to interact with that person.”
Even though some training is still needed to educate people with hidden disabilities, Eric remains thankful for all the support received. “It’s truly a blessing,” he said.
Judges appointed
The governor announced the appointments of nine — count ’em, nine — judges Friday to district and circuit court vacancies in Montgomery County and Baltimore City Circuit Court.
Sean Richard Delaney, James Burke Miller and Jocelyn Lang Williams will serve as judges in Baltimore City Circuit Court.
In Montgomery County, Keith Joseph Rosa and Carlotta Ann Woodward were nominated to the circuit court bench, while Jason Brian Abbott, Rolando Julio Aleman, Howard Ray Cheris and Seth Bradley Zucker were nominated to the district court.
“As judges, I know that their expertise and experience will continue to be of great service to the people of Maryland in their new roles as judges,” Moore said.
Delaney has been an assistant U.S. attorney in Baltimore for the past 12 years as a member of the office’s Fraud and Public Corruption Section. He was previously a trial attorney in the Department of Justice Tax Division. Delaney received his law degree from Boston College Law School.
Burke Miller is chief of the Felony Trial Division in the Baltimore City State’s Attorney’s Office and lead attorney for the Archdiocese of Baltimore Abuse work group. Before that, Burke Miller worked in the Medicaid fraud control unit of the Maryland Attorney General’s Office and as a prosecutor in Prince George’s County. He received a law degree from University of Baltimore School of Law.
Williams has been an administrative law judge at the Maryland Office of Administrative Hearings for the past eight years. Before that, she was a staff attorney and supervising attorney in the Baltimore office of Maryland Legal Aid. Williams received her law degree from Penn State’s Dickinson School of Law.

Rosa is a partner and co-founder of the Bethesda-based law firm Goitein Rosa, with a practice focusing on civil litigation, including family law. Previously, Rosa served as a special magistrate for the Montgomery County Circuit Court and as an associate. Rosa received his law degree from Florida State University College of Law.
Woodward has been a prosecutor in Montgomery County for the past 14 years and currently serves as chief of the juvenile division and primary prosecutor of animal cruelty cases. Woodward was an associate at Cordier Law Offices before opening her own practice. Woodward received her law degree from University of Baltimore School of Law.
Abbott currently works as general counsel for Prince George’s County Executive Office’s Public Safety and Homeland Security. Abbott previously served as principal deputy state’s attorney for the county and as chief of the strategic investigations unit in the county’s State’s Attorney’s Office. Abbott received his law degree at Columbus School of Law at Catholic University of America.
Aleman is an associate attorney with Salvado, Salvado & Salvado in Rockville. Before that position, he was associate general counsel for the Maryland-National Capital Park & Planning Commission and held two clerkships Cumberland County, Pennsylvania. Aleman received his law degree from Penn State’s Dickinson School of Law.
Cheris is the lead partner and managing member of Armstrong, Cheris and Page in Rockville, which he joined after 17 years as a private practitioner concentrating on civil and criminal litigation. Cheris also worked as a contract attorney for the Montgomery County Public Defender’s Office. Cheris received his law degree from American University’s Washington College of Law.
Zucker served his entire legal career as a prosecutor with the Montgomery County State’s Attorney’s Office. Zucker currently serves as chief of the collateral review unit and the conviction integrity unit. He previously served as a trial prosecutor in the circuit, district and juvenile courts. Zucker received his law degree from William and Mary Law School.
Picking the police for the police
Montgomery County is looking for applicants for upcoming openings on the Advisory Commission on Policing — formerly the Policing Advisory Commission — which advises the county council on police-related legislation and policy and seeks community feedback.
The three-year posts are unpaid, but some expenses are covered. The commission is required to meet at least six times a year, more if needed to complete its work. Each council member appoints a board member and the county executive names two, a youth member (25 or younger) and a young adult (age 26-35) member. Applicants must work in the county, or represent an organization that does, and should reflect the geographic and demographic diversity of the county, with an emphasis on those disproportionately impacted by inequities. They should also have a “keen interest and/or expertise in policing matters, and want to deliberate on policy guidelines affecting departmental operations to help identify unintended consequences and develop safeguards to mitigate them.”
Applications are due by 5 p.m. Nov. 2. Late applications will not be accepted. To apply, send a letter expressing interest and a (four pages or less) resume listing professional and civic experience, home address, telephone number and email address, via email to Council President Fani-González at council.clerk@montgomerycountymd.gov, or by postal mail to Fani-González, County Council Office, 100 Maryland Ave., Rockville, Md,, 20850. All interviews and interview materials will be open to the public.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: How many Republicans will vote for a Black man for governor?
description: “Although slavery may have been abolished, the crippling poison of racism still persists, and the struggle still continues.” — Harry Belafonte, 2010 With U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds one step closer to the Governor’s Mansion, Republicans in general and MAGA in particular face a choice: Will they vote for a Black man to be Florida’s chief […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., speaks to reporters at the U.S. Capitol on Oct. 9, 2023. (Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)“Although slavery may have been abolished, the crippling poison of racism still persists, and the struggle still continues.” — Harry Belafonte, 2010
With U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds one step closer to the Governor’s Mansion, Republicans in general and MAGA in particular face a choice: Will they vote for a Black man to be Florida’s chief executive or opt out and open the door for Democrats?
Now that Donalds is in a competitive race in a Republican-heavy state, there are distinct rumblings in GOP-land about whether the party — and especially the far-right conservative, white nationalist faction — will ever vote for a Black man.
There are no simple answers because this is, after all, Florida. Little is black and white, issues are mostly colored grey, coated in nuance and subtlety.
President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Donalds turbocharged his campaign, offering the impetus that has guaranteed wins for a significant number of MAGA Republicans seeking office this election season in other parts of the country.
Racial bias is a key ingredient of the state’s distorted DNA. In its 181-year history, the Sunshine State has never voted for a Black governor, male or female, Democrat or Republican, not because there were never any competent, qualified Black candidates. Only three states have elected Black governors. 
Time will tell whether Donalds can scale this obstacle.
 Historic milestone

A Donalds election as Florida’s first Black governor would represent a historic milestone, but there’s a significant divide among Black people in Florida and even among political observers. Black Westchester publisher Damon K. Jones captured their dilemma in an Aug 20 op-ed.
“He is poised to become Florida’s first Black governor. But this moment is not being celebrated in quite the same way among Black Floridians and Black political analysts nationwide,” Jones explains.
“The rift illuminates how America talks about race and representation more than it highlights anything about Donalds himself. For others, the criticism stems not from Donald’s race, but instead his political beliefs and what they see as his race being exploited by a party which they feel willfully works against Black political and economic interests when it comes to issues like voting rights, criminal justice and civil rights enforcement.”
People who believe this see celebrating a “first” as a hollow gesture in the face of policy positions that person espouses, and they argue that having a representative without unity on key issues is not the type of progress praised in these situations, Jones added.
“Some of the criticism goes a step further by accusing the GOP — whether intentionally or not — of attempting to downvote fraud claims, weakening criticism of the GOP’s positions on race-centric policies by electing Donalds, a Black person, who can help defend their policies,” Jones writes.
 Primary results

Donalds’ primary win prompted conversations about the viability of his general election campaign. It didn’t take long for political pundits like 610WIOD’s Manny Munoz and comedian and television host Bill Maher to say the quiet part out loud.
“It’s not me suggesting that maybe Byron Donalds didn’t get votes because he’s Black. Republican primary results tell the story,” Munoz wrote in an Instagram post following Donalds’ win.
“You look at the map of the Republican primary results last week and the map alone will tell you. Byron Donalds lost 17 counties across Florida. In 16 of the counties, 92% of the voters are white. In counties which were more diverse, Byron Donalds won 39 of the 40 counties. But he lost in rural, Northern, MAGA counties.”
In these counties, Munoz explained, Donalds won 42% of the primary vote “despite tens of millions spent on advertising and the fact that he had the overwhelming endorsement of President Trump before he was even an official candidate,” Munoz said.
Maher told Donalds on HBO’s “Real Time with Bill Maher” (and replayed on Fox News) he believed race played a sizable element in Donalds’ inability to cross the 50% threshold. 
“You did lose the ‘Redneck Riviera’ badly,” Maher said, referring to Donalds’ losses in Calhoun, Columbia, Dixie, Gilchrist, Hamilton, Hardee, Holmes, Jackson, Jefferson, Lafayette, Levy, Liberty, Madison, Suwannee, Taylor, Union, and Washington counties — rural areas where roughly 94% of Republican voters are white, the Redneck Riviera, which is the Panhandle. “I think there are people there who still would not — you’re a Republican, you’re a Trumper — they should love you and they don’t. I think there is still racism.”
Donalds countered: “Let’s talk a little bit about the Panhandle. There are counties we did incredibly well in that we won. There were some counties that we fell a little short in, that’s OK. The No. 1 thing overall, we closed out 48% of the vote in Florida. Eight hundred thousand votes [is] a long way to becoming the nominee.”
 Taking issue 

Donalds argued race isn’t a factor.
“Florida really has become the microcosm of what we all want,” Donalds said. “It’s a meritocracy. And it’s about the best person with the best views, the best skills, the best talent moving forward to represent your state or to represent a district in your state, and Florida exemplifies that.”
Still, in the Trump-DeSantis era, the Black presence in the federal government, business, commerce, and education is diminishing; so is access to jobs, education, and other opportunities, while discussion of race and racism in schools, the marketplace, and wider community is being curbed.
Voting rights advocate Jasmine Burney-Clark criticized DeSantis as Black Floridians have watched him and his MAGA cronies dismantle their political power.
“Florida has 28 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives. After this year’s elections, and barring the November general election results, we are staring at the possibility that just one of those 28 seats will be a Black access seat, also known as a ‘majority-minority district,’” writes Burney-Clarke, founder of Equal Ground Education Fund and Action Fund.
 Black progress?

Democratic State Sen. LaVon Bracy Davis considers Donalds an adversary of Black progress.
Her evidence?
Donalds voted against the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act and “when asked whether he would support the Harry T. and Harriette V. Moore Florida Voting Rights Act, legislation that I am proud to sponsor, Byron Donalds said NO,” Bracy Davis writes. “That legislation is named for two Black Floridians murdered after dedicating their lives to registering Black voters and fighting for our political power.”
He is also a staunch supporter of ICE-led deportations; said he would use state funding as leverage to compel local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement; is a strong supporter of AI data centers; told FOX49 he would keep Florida’s abortion restrictions in place rather than make them more or less restrictive; wants the state to support pregnancy resource centers and community pregnancy clinics; opposes legalizing recreational marijuana; and wants Florida to repeal the post-Parkland restriction preventing people younger than 21 from purchasing long guns.
 Bumpy ride

Donalds had been hoping for a smooth ride on the Trump train into the governor’s office, but things aren’t going as planned.
Trump is enjoying record disapproval numbers — with a net approval rating of -29, Newsweek reports — dogged by a deeply unpopular war against Iran he started that is dragging on into its seventh month. The war and Trump’s tariffs have jacked up the cost of gasoline and grocery staples, producing deep anger among the electorate and tarnishing the Republican brand and MAGA conservatives like Donalds closely aligned with Trump. 
That has produced what The Independent calls “a surprisingly competitive race,” with Donalds, a three-term congressman, and the Democratic candidate, former U.S. Rep. David Jolly, in a dead heat, separated by one percentage point in one poll, according to Florida Politics.
Meanwhile, Donalds tried to leap off the good ship Trump and put as much distance between himself and the embattled president as he can. Last week, news outlets report, Donalds scrubbed most Trump references from his website.
“Donalds has long tied himself to Trump, but on Sept. 22 he erased nearly all references to the president on the website, an indication that the campaign might see the leader of the Republican Party as a drag in the tight race against Democrat opponent David Jolly.” News of the mass deletion was first reported by the Miami Herald. 
Trump’s endorsement of Donalds once dominated the website, but it has now been relegated to a separate page under endorsements, although it still includes a photo of the president and the candidate. There are two other minor references to Trump, as well, the story said.
Donalds, a member of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, castigated the news media for hyping what he called a non-story, insisting the move represents a shift toward the electorates’ priorities including affordability, the cost of insurance, and property tax relief.
Trump meanwhile, defended Donalds while characterizing the coverage as “Another Fake Story.” He also said two rallies were still scheduled in Florida to support the campaign. 
“If Florida thought the story that Byron ‘dropped’ me was true, he would lose the Election, and that would be a terrible thing because he’s going to be a fantastic Governor!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Curtis Bay Energy will end incineration of medical waste under agreement with state
description: State officials hailed the news that the troubled Curtis Bay Energy facility will stop burning medical waste at its South Baltimore site in order to settle a Maryland Department of the Environment lawsuit charging the company with repeated air pollution violations.
text:
Plumes of smoke rise after an explosion at the CSX Curtis Bay Coal Terminal in 2021, just one of the industrial facilities in the Curtis Bay area that residents say place an undue environmental and health burden on them. (Photo by Baltimore Firefighters IAFF Local 734)State officials were hailing the announcement that the troubled Curtis Bay Energy facility will stop incinerating medical waste at its South Baltimore site in order to settle a Maryland Department of the Environment lawsuit charging the company with repeated air pollution violations.
Curtis Bay Energy is one of the largest medical waste incinerators in the country. Under the proposed consent decree, filed Wednesday in Baltimore City Circuit Court, the site will continue operating as a medical waste transfer station, but at sharply reduced levels. Curtis Bay’s current permit allows the company to accept 62,050 tons of waste a year, and burn as much 150 tons a day. That would be cut to no more than 20,000 tons a year, with no incineration, under the settlement.
The company also agreed to pay $600,000 in penalties that will be divided between MDE’s clean water fund and its clean air fund. If there are any pollution violations while the shift away from incineration is under way, the company agrees to pay $5,000 to $7,000 per day per violation.
“This a major win for a community overburdened by pollution,” Maryland Environment Secretary Serena McIlwain said in a prepared statement. “We won’t accept operations that put public health and safety at risk and leave our most vulnerable communities paying the price.”
Attorney General Anthony Brown, whose office negotiated the settlement, said that “the burning of medical waste has forced Curtis Bay residents to inhale smoke and other emissions” for too long.
South Baltimore medical waste incinerator will pay one of largest environmental fines in state history after improper disposal

“This agreement shuts down the incinerator for good, improving air quality for a community that has carried the weight of industrial pollution for generations,” he said in the joint statement with McIlwain.
The changes will take place no later than 90 days after the company submits, and the state approves, an application to change its permit from an air quality permit, allowing it to burn medical waste, to one acting as a transfer station for that waste, which would be subject to steam sterilization.
The consent decree, if accepted by the court, would end a 2024 lawsuit in which MDE charged the company with six counts of air quality violations. The state has added seven more charges since then. As part of the settlement, Curtis Bay Energy “denies the factual and legal assertions in the Complaint” and the additional pollution charges.
The deal comes three years after previous owners of Curtis Bay Energy pleaded guilty to criminal charges of improper disposal of biohazardous materials, and paid a $1 million fine, one of the largest in state history. It also paid $750,000 then into a fund to pay for environmental improvements in the community around the plant.
The Curtis Bay area is dotted with scores of industrial sites, including a CSX coal transfer facility, that residents say place an undue environmental burden on the area.
Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City), whose district includes Curtis Bay community, said the settlement and the end of incineration there comes after “years of violations and continued concerns from residents.”
“Curtis Bay residents …. documented what they were seeing in their own neighborhood, worked with scientists to track emissions, and kept pressing for action. Their photos and videos ultimately became part of the evidence behind the State’s enforcement case,” he said in a statement posted to social media.
He thanked state officials for the deal but said he was “especially grateful to the residents and community organizations … who refused to let these concerns be ignored.”
“Curtis Bay has carried the burden of industrial pollution for generations. This agreement is a meaningful result for a community that has fought for years,” his statement said.

title: Donald Trump tells Mobile rally to ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’
description: MOBILE — President Donald Trump told a crowd of roughly 8,000 supporters Friday night to vote like he is on the ballot in November. “Can everybody just close your eyes and pretend I’m on the ballot?” Trump asked the crowd. Mobile was the president’s second stop in a month-long campaign for Republican congressional candidates across […]
text:
President Donald Trump dances at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama, on Oct. 2, 2026.  The president is visiting several red states in support of GOP nominees about a month ahead of midterm elections in November. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)MOBILE — President Donald Trump told a crowd of roughly 8,000 supporters Friday night to vote like he is on the ballot in November.
“Can everybody just close your eyes and pretend I’m on the ballot?” Trump asked the crowd.
Mobile was the president’s second stop in a month-long campaign for Republican congressional candidates across the country. Supporters lined up at the Mitchell Center on the University of South Alabama’s campus hours before doors opened. The building was roughly 75 percent full by the time Trump took the stage.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Alabama is a Republican state, and Alabama’s 1st Congressional District – which Mobile falls in under a new map – is rated solidly Republican by Cook Political Report. The neighboring 2nd Congressional District, where incumbent U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile faces state Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, the GOP nominee, is considered more competitive. 
Trump said Friday he came to Alabama, and plans to go to other Republican states, to pay his respects to the people who love him. 
“Oklahoma and Alabama, I’m here to say hello,” he said. “I’m here because sometimes even though you don’t have to come here, you’ve got to pay respect to the people that have loved me every year.”
Trump’s approval rating has fallen across the country – and in Alabama – since the beginning of the Iran war in February and the subsequent increase in gas prices. He told attendees the war will end sometime after the midterms. 
“They’re never going to have a nuclear weapon,” he said. “As soon as it does end, oil prices will come tumbling down.” 
Trump-endorsed Alabama Republican nominees opened for Trump, including gubernatorial nominee and U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who walked on stage to Lynyrd Skynyrd’s “Sweet Home Alabama.” 
U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Alabama (left), the Republican nominee for governor of Alabama, shakes hands with President Donald Trump at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama on October 2, 2026. The president is visiting several red states in support of GOP nominees about a month ahead of midterm elections in November. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)
Tuberville pledged to invest in workforce development as governor. 
“We’re going to use our hands. We’re going to teach people and our kids. We’re going to teach them education, and we’re going to teach them how to live a life, to do things with their hands and make decisions,” Tuberville said. 
Trump touted the Senate’s bipartisan passage of the Protect College Sports Act, and urged Alabamians to elect Tuberville as governor. The senator coached football at Auburn University from 1999 to 2008. 
“We’re going to pass something that brings sanity to college football. The Senate passed it, and we had a lot of help, bipartisan help. Can you believe it? Shocking,” Trump said. 
The president also reiterated his endorsements of U.S. Rep. Barry Moore, R-Enterprise, the nominee to replace Tuberville; Jerry Carl, the nominee for the 1st Congressional District; state Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, the nominee for the 2nd Congressional District; John Wahl, the nominee for lieutenant governor and Florida gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds. 
He also endorsed Katherine Robertson, the party’s nominee for Alabama Attorney General. He mentioned Republican U.S. Reps. Robert Aderholt of Haleyville, Dale Strong of Madison and Gary Palmer of Hoover, but said he did not need to “waste time” on them because they are “so far ahead.” He did not mention Republican nominee for the 7th Congressional District Ammie Akin, who is challenging U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Selma, or U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Saks. 
At the party’s midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, last month, Trump promised to give every U.S. adult citizen $5,000 if Republicans held the House and Senate. He doubled down Friday evening with a caveat: the money must be spent in the U.S.
“The Trump dividend is approximately $1 trillion, but we have a record-setting $21 trillion that’s being invested in our country in just 15 months,” he said. “When you spend it and recirculate it in our country, it costs us far less than it sounds.”
The nonpartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget warned last month that Trump’s plan would cost about $1.2 trillion, and “explode” the nation’s deficit.
He criticized Democrats throughout his 90-minute speech, often referring to them as “dumocrats.” He also touted policies on economic development, immigration and lowering taxes.
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones, who held a counter-event in Mobile Friday evening, accused Trump of coming to Mobile to soothe his ego.
“We were going to Mobile anyway, but then all of a sudden Trump started trolling me,” Jones said at a town hall. “I don’t think it’s about Tommy Tuberville. I think he is campaigning, not for a candidate, I think he’s campaigning to get the Mobile Bay bridge named after him.” 
Attendees were not allowed to bring their own signs, but signs were provided to them in the lower level of the area echoing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Signs read “No Tax on Overtime,” “No Tax On Tips,” “No Tax on Social Security” and “Lower Prices.” 
President Donald Trump speaks at the Mitchell Center at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, Alabama on October 2, 2026. The president is visiting several red states in support of GOP nominees about a month ahead of midterm elections in November. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)
Trump also criticized the “fake news media” which led to boos from the crowd directed at the press pool. 
“Our nation is doing better now than ever before. But the fake news media right back there … refuses to talk about our ranks and the numbers, so I have to do it myself,” Trump said. 
Each opening speaker urged attendees to vote Republican in November, and to spread the word. 
“We need each and everybody in this room to go out and vote, and get their neighbors, their family, and their friends to go vote,” Marques said. “We win if everybody in this state votes because we are a Republican state.”
Trump is expected to travel to Ohio over the weekend and Nebraska on Monday. He said he will attend the football game between the University of Alabama and the University of Georgia in Tuscaloosa on Oct. 10.

title: Candidates for Utah’s 3rd Congressional District clash on national monuments, nuclear energy
description: Candidates vying for Utah’s 3rd Congressional District made their pitches for what will be the largest district in the state, clashing over environmental issues, nuclear energy, forest management and the boundaries of Utah’s recently reduced national monuments.  Republican Rep. Celeste Maloy, going into her second general election candidacy, now for an updat[...]
text:
Celeste Maloy, left, listens as Kent Udell answers a question during a 3rd Congressional District debate at Utah Tech University in St. George, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (Pool photo by Jud Burkett special to The Tribune)Candidates vying for Utah’s 3rd Congressional District made their pitches for what will be the largest district in the state, clashing over environmental issues, nuclear energy, forest management and the boundaries of Utah’s recently reduced national monuments. 
Republican Rep. Celeste Maloy, going into her second general election candidacy, now for an updated district, faced Democratic nominee Kent Udell, a mechanical engineer in a debate held Friday at Utah Tech University in St George, moderated by Bob Evans from FOX 13 and broadcast by PBS Utah.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Maloy has represented Utah’s District 2 since late 2023. After the state’s congressional maps changed this year, she’s competing for the 3rd Congressional District’s seat, the home of Utah’s five national parks as well as posh ski resort cities, miles and miles of rural lands eyed by eager energy developers, and national monuments with controversial borders.
“I was standing in the Oval Office when the announcement was made about reducing the monument boundaries. So obviously, I support that decision. It was made by listening to elected officials from Utah,” Maloy said during the debate.
Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante are probably two of the most controversial monuments in the nation, Maloy said, because of the way they were created — by the executive branch.
Celeste Maloy answers a question during a 3rd Congressional District debate at Utah Tech University in St. George, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (Pool photo by Jud Burkett special to The Tribune)
“Congress should be making those decisions, and when Congress declares a national monument like Cedar Breaks, they tend to be uncontroversial.”
But, for Udell, the previous, larger boundaries, established by Democratic administrations “worked out great,” he said.
“To throw that out the window to disrupt our tourist industry, to disrupt our system, for what? A handful of sagebrush rebels and mining companies? No, that’s public land, and that needs to be protected for everybody,” Udell said, adding that if elected, he would work to get the former boundaries established by law.
Kent Udell answers a question during a 3rd Congressional District debate at Utah Tech University in St. George, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (Pool photo by Jud Burkett special to The Tribune)
Another point of contention between the candidates was on the country’s energy strategy. When Maloy thinks about the oil and gas industry in Utah, she thinks about substantial jobs for rural Utahns. When she thinks about other energy sources, she sees big potential for nuclear power.
Udell criticized that nuclear power is one of the most expensive energy resources in the country.  
“We have better options. We have wind and we have solar,” he said. “So who is pushing this? Well, it seems like it is a bunch of entrepreneurs that are keeping the prices of their stocks up.”
For Maloy, the interest of entrepreneurs in a technology is a good hint to determine whether investing in it will pay off, she said. The resource would also be reliable and capable of being turned on and off on demand.
“It’s going to be the energy source of the future that doesn’t disappear. That isn’t controversial,” she said. “It’s going to power the AI future that we are going to have. AI is here. We’re going to be using it. We have to have the power to power it.”
Apart from that, Maloy said, a lot of jobs in rural Utah are in mining, oil, gas and in the future, in nuclear energy — “things that my opponent just said he doesn’t care about,” she said.
“I want to do regulatory reform and make sure that we are removing federal barriers to bringing those jobs to rural Utah. I’ve talked to people in the basin who have the training, they have the know-how,” Maloy said. “They just need the federal red tape out of the way so that they can be out producing the energy we need in this country.”
But Udell contested the notion that he doesn’t care about nuclear energy.
“I think it’s got a place. Carbon-free power. That’s great, but we don’t jump into that without having proven that it is going to work and it is going to be safe and it is going to be decreasing our energy costs,” he said. “And until that is proven, I am not in favor of it. Just hold back and make sure that we’re not being forced into buying a timeshare that we don’t want.”
Celeste Maloy, left, and Kent Udell shake hands at the conclusion of a 3rd Congressional District debate at Utah Tech University in St. George, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (Pool photo by Jud Burkett special to The Tribune)

description: Gov. Kay Ivey dismissed five of the Alabama Educational Television Commission’s seven members Friday evening. Commissioners Pete Conroy, Ferris Stephens, Les Barnett, Bebe Williams and William Green were removed from the AETC. Commissioners Tijuanna Adetunji and Logan Glass remain on the board. A message seeking comment was left with Ivey’s office Friday nig[...]
text:
Members of the Alabama Educational Television Commission listen to a speaker during a meeting on July 21, 2026 in Birmingham. Gov. Kay Ivey removed five members of the AETC Friday night. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Gov. Kay Ivey dismissed five of the Alabama Educational Television Commission’s seven members Friday evening.
Commissioners Pete Conroy, Ferris Stephens, Les Barnett, Bebe Williams and William Green were removed from the AETC. Commissioners Tijuanna Adetunji and Logan Glass remain on the board.
A message seeking comment was left with Ivey’s office Friday night.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The story was first reported by Al.com. The move to dismiss the members came days after a survey conducted by the board showed support for Alabama Public Television continuing its relationship with the Public Broadcasting Service. 
Last October, Stephens and Barnett, two conservative members of the board, brought the idea of disaffiliating from PBS. Barnett accused PBS of being “anathema” to President Donald Trump, and said they had “made themselves the enemy of what I stand with, and so I do not like them, and I don’t follow the philosophy of feeding the beast.” 
The moves prompted public backlash from donors. The following month, the board voted to maintain PBS programming.
Conroy, who served on the board since 2018, said in an interview Friday night he received a letter announcing his dismissal earlier in the day. The new board was the “ultimate goal” for the station, and Conroy said he’s “looking forward to serving APT in whatever way I can.”
A message seeking comment was left with Green Friday night. 
APT Executive Director Wayne Reid said in a text message Friday night the station would have a full statement on the removals Monday and “Alabama Public Television looks forward to welcoming the new commissioners and working together with the Commission to build on APT’s longstanding service to the state.”
The dismissed commissioners also served on the Alabama Educational Television Foundation Authority. Reid said the new commissioners will replace the ones on the foundation board as well.
Under HB 220, sponsored by Rep. Chris Pringle, R-Mobile, Ivey has the authority to remove members of boards she has appointing authority over. Ivey signed the bill into law in April. It went into effect Oct. 1.
The governor last November urged the governing board of APT to pause before voting for disaffiliation and suggested surveying public attitudes before taking that step.
New appointments have been made available on the APT website and include:

Wallace Gilberry for the 1st Congressional District, replacing Les Barnett
Ric Smith for the 3rd Congressional District, replacing Pete Conroy
Neil Lamb for the 5th Congressional District, replacing Bebe Williams
Sally Smith for the 6th Congressional District, replacing Ferris Stephens
Samory Pruitt for the 7th Congressional District, replacing William Green

Conroy said he was optimistic for the future of APT’s governing board.
“There’s a really good new appointee up from the Huntsville area, and he’s a scientist, and he’s well respected, so I’m optimistic about at least one of these appointees,” Conroy said.
In April, the AETC voted to survey Alabamians on their attitude towards APT’s programming. The survey was originally to be conducted by McLaughlin & Associates, a national survey company that has worked with several Republican candidates, including former Attorney General Jeff Sessions and U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville.
The contract with McLaughlin fell through in late August and in a specially called September meeting for the AETFA, members voted to conduct the survey with Cygna, a polling firm that mainly works with Republican candidates, including U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville’s gubernatorial campaign.
Conroy condemned the actions taken by the board in the interview.
“I think we always need to listen to the people,” Conroy said. “And ultimately, it was the weird survey that ended up pointing us in the right direction. But when you listen to people, they’ll remind you what path you need to stay on.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Gov. Kim Reynolds signs law allowing $1.4B in tax incentives for steel mill project
description: Gov. Kim Reynolds signed into law Friday a measure changing a state’s economic development program that could provide nearly $1.4 billion in tax incentives for a $15 billion steel mill project planned in southeast Iowa. “Today, we advance the most consequential economic development project ever to come to our state,” Reynolds said. The governor signed House[...]
text:
Gov. Kim Reynolds signed into law a measure that would allow the state of Iowa more tax incentives for a steel mill project being considered in southeast Iowa after lawmakers passed the bill in a special session Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Gov. Kim Reynolds signed into law Friday a measure changing a state’s economic development program that could provide nearly $1.4 billion in tax incentives for a $15 billion steel mill project planned in southeast Iowa.
“Today, we advance the most consequential economic development project ever to come to our state,” Reynolds said.
The governor signed House File 2801 just hours after lawmakers approved the proposal during a special session Friday, convened for the sole purpose of considering the legislation. The Iowa House approved the bill in a 75-17 vote, and the Senate approved the bill in a 28-19 vote. The proposal would modify the state’s Major Economic Growth Attraction (MEGA) program to include further incentives for businesses within rural areas, a targeted change to benefit the Mesabi Metallics project planned in Lee County.
At a news conference Monday, President Donald Trump announced the steel plant was a $15 billion project. When operational — with a goal of 2030 — the steel mill is estimated to create 1,750 permanent jobs paying an average of $48 per hour, alongside 6,000 temporary construction jobs as the facility is built, state and business officials said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rep. Matt Rinker, R-Burlington, said the project would be a major victory for southeast Iowa and was the culmination of years of work from local, state and federal officials alongside Mesabi Metallics.
During his time at the Burlington City Council and as a state legislator, Rinker said he has thousands of conversations with members of his community about what was needed to bring success to the area. He told the House, “I’m proud to say that what everyone has been asking for has finally arrived.”
“Our vote today isn’t just about a change to something that already exists, or just about incentives for a steel plant, or just about bringing a new industry to Iowa,” Rinker said. “It’s about mortgage payments, grocery bills, dance lessons. It’s about infrastructure and public safety. It’s about opportunities for Iowans and growing our communities while also supporting them at the same time. It’s about thousands of new homes. It’s about the revitalization of a region of our state that has experienced its fair share of tough times.”
Iowa Rep. Matt Rinker, R-Burlington, spoke in support of legislation making changes to the state’s Major Economic Growth Attraction program to allow the Iowa Economic Development Authority to provide tax incentives to a proposed $15 billion steel mill project in Iowa during a special session Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
As she signed the measure into law, Reynolds thanked “everybody who helped pave the way for this moment,” including local southeast Iowa leaders, companies and workers who advocated for the business to locate in Iowa.
“We don’t do this without you, so thanks for being bold and believing in this state and believing that in America we build things, and we are really going to build things right here in Iowa,” Reynolds said. “And then again, I just want to thank Mesabi Metallics for this opportunity. And we really truly look forward to a very long partnership with them and what this means for our state.”
Sen. Dan Dawson, R-Council Bluffs, who voted against the bill, called it the “largest corporate giveaway in the state of Iowa’s history.”
He also warned the change to the tax incentive program for Mesabi Metallics would influence any future negotiations between the state and companies considering bringing their facilities to Iowa, “because the ceiling now becomes the floor.”
“Incentives are supposed to make a good deal better, not a bad deal good,” Dawson said. “So to all my colleagues, I know you’ve been put in a difficult position. And you’ve been put into position by people and entities who, frankly, do not care. If they did, you wouldn’t be jammed with this bill in front of you today.”
The bill would allow the Iowa Economic Development Authority to authorize a tax credit for a business up to 10% of the business’ qualifying investment in a rural county — an increase from the 5% tax credit currently allowed under the MEGA program for projects representing $1 billion or more in capital investment.
According to analysis from the nonpartisan Legislative Services Agency, the net impact of changes to the MEGA program’s Investment Tax Credit made by the bill would result in estimated revenue decreases to the state’s general fund of $575 million from fiscal year 2029 through 2041 — on top of the $575 million that would come under the current MEGA program structure. The MEGA program’s sales and use tax refunds and withholding tax credits are not changed by the legislation, but under the current program, Mesabi Metallics would be eligible to claim $215 million in tax incentives from FY 2028 through 2041.
IEDA Director Debi Durham said this investment will provide greater benefits for Iowa through later revenue to the state, as well as an expansion of jobs and economic value to the region.
“The state’s portion on the deal that is before you today (is) a 1 to 5.6% return,” Durham said. “So that means for every dollar that we invest as a state, that we get that return back. And when you think of manufacturing, it is the largest part of our gross state product — there is a multiplier of jobs attached to manufacturing, anywhere from three to five jobs will follow. When you happen to talk about a (project) as complicated as this, and as many investments, the investment being made, it is a 5-to-1 job ratio as well, meaning, for every job that they hire, there’s a follow-on job that will occur in our economy.”
Rep. Carter Nordman, R-Adel, floor manager for the bill in the House, said the change is not an increased tax incentive for the MEGA program — created with wide bipartisan support in 2024 — but a way to combine the two 5% MEGA program investment tax credits that IEDA can currently offer. The IEDA has not previously awarded any MEGA program tax incentives.
“The reality is we are not reinventing the wheel here,” Nordman said. “All we are doing is modernizing and combining two existing incentive programs into one, so Iowa is not on the sidelines, but actively competing on the national and global level for large projects. When creating those incentives of packages a couple years ago … this body could never have imagined the possibility of a $15 billion investment landing here.”
Iowa Sen. Dan Dawson, R-Council Bluffs, spoke in opposition to legislation passed by the Iowa Legislature in a special session Oct. 2, 2026 making changes to a state economic development program to provide more tax incentive for a steel mill project in southeast Iowa. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Dawson said this was a fundamental misunderstanding of the original intent of MEGA program — a measure Dawson said he helped negotiate when it was approved in 2024.
“To be clear, the intent was never 5% plus 5% equals 10%,” Dawson said. “And that the intent was never that we throw the entire farm into one basket, and it could be a ‘one and done’ proposition. We wanted to see this spread throughout Iowa.”
Durham told lawmakers increasing the tax credit to 10% was necessary for Iowa to bring the steel plant to Iowa.
“We basically do have to be competitive in the marketplace,” Durham said. “So, we look at deals all across the country with this type of industry, and I will say 10% is is a national average of what these businesses are getting.”
Supporters say MEGA program change needed to compete against other states for steel mill
The IEDA director said the states of Arkansas and Kentucky were also competing for the steel mill project, with Arkansas being “our biggest competitor.”
Dawson said Senate Republicans were told Arkansas lawmakers were expected to call their own special session to create an offer providing “cash up front” to the company by modify their state’s recycling tax credit and funding the tax credit change by borrowing against the Arkansas teacher pension fund. He said officials who knew about the Arkansas proposal told him Arkansas officials walked away from these negotiations, “because the companies seemed to lack equity and could never locate where the equity would come from and the paperwork that they provided to the state.”
“While I respect Governor Reynolds’ deep desire to bring a MEGA site to the state of Iowa before her term ends, because she wasn’t willing to walk away from this deal, it’s my belief she negotiated against herself,” Dawson said. “Because Arkansas, I do not believe, was ever actually at the table seriously. And by negotiating against herself, she negotiated against the Iowa taxpayer.”
Durham also emphasized the bill is written to ensure the state will not provide tax incentives to the Mesabi Metallics if the project is not completed. The measures states the tax credit will not be issued to a business until the business begins operations, or until “a designated portion of the project” has been placed in service, and until at least half of created jobs — which must meet a qualifying wage threshold — associated with the project or a designated portion have been added to the payroll. The legislation also states the 10% tax credit will be remitted over the course of a decade.
Some Democrats had questions about portions of the bill which allow the tax credit to be transferred to another person or entity. During the House subcommittee meeting on the bill, Jacoby shared concerns from a constituent that the state would not be able to claw back tax credits “against the buyer if the project goes wrong” — a statement Durham said was incorrect.
“We will have not only oversight into the transferability, we will have approvals over the transferability, and so that is not correct,” Durham said. “We will be fully protected even with the transferability.”
Opponents express concerns about Mesabi Metallics past
Iowa GOP leaders have praised the planned steel mill, with Reynolds saying, “this opportunity will fundamentally change the economic trajectory of our state and the entire region for decades to come.” But others are cautious about the project, saying there are concerns about Mesabi Metallics’ commitment to finishing and opening the plant given the company’s history as it also seeks to open an iron ore mine in Nashwauk, a city in the Minnesota Iron Range.
The mine has not yet officially started operation. The project began in 2008, under the India-based Essar Group’s company Essar Steel Minnesota, the Des Moines Register reported. The Essar Group was founded by brothers Sashi and Ravi Ruia, and expanded to include the Minnesota company as well as a Essar Steel Algoma in Canada.
Essar Steel Minnesota filed for bankruptcy protection in 2016, blocking the Minnesota governor’s attempt to revoke its mineral lease. Investors took control of the company and rebranded it as Mesabi Metallics in 2017 and came out from bankruptcy protection, before Essar Group took over the project again in 2019 under its new name.
Marshall Singer, a local activist from Des Moines, shared these details about Essar Group during subcommittee meetings on the proposal. Singer also highlighted Essar Group and associated companies had received loans from a VTB, a Russian state owned-bank, according to the Guardian. VTB has been sanctioned by the European Union and other countries following the start of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022.
“Iowa’s economic incentive law bars the state with providing tax credits and refunds to a business tied to a foreign adversary,” Singer said. He also added, “This will cost every taxpayer $866, and this is irresponsible when we are running a $1.4 billion dollar deficit.”
Joe Broking, president and chief executive officer of Mesabi Metallics, the company seeking to build a $15 billion steel mill in Lee County Iowa, spoke to lawmakers about the project at a subcommittee meeting Oct. 2, 2026 as lawmakers considered a bill making changes to a state economic development program to allow the state to offer a more substantial tax incentive package than currently allowed. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Joe Broking, president and chief executive officer of Mesabi Metallics, addressed some of the comments by Singer about the Minnesota project and Essar Group. He said “there was a global commodity price collapse that happened in 2015, and there were hundreds of companies globally that went through restructurings,” not just Essar Steel Minnesota.
He also said the delays of the mine construction were in part due to “certain activities by a competitor to try and stop development on the Iron Range.” Broking’s comments referenced allegations that fellow steel company Cleveland-Cliffs committed antitrust violations. Mesabi Metallics sued the company for in 2025 in a pending case.
Additionally, Broking said Mesabi Metallics has “completely rebuilt all of those relationships” with Minnesota public officials, including Gov. Tim Walz, state legislators and the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources. He also added Mesabi Metallics has “invested close to $3 billion to complete this project, and we’re about to start it now.”
“And Essar Group and the Ruia family have been a fantastic partner, an absolutely wonderful partner,” Broking said. “They’ve met that commitment the entire time. They’ve invested $2 billion of their family money to complete this project, and like I said earlier, we are on the precipice of doing this.”
Answering questions from Sen. Tony Bisignano, D-Des Moines, Durham said she believed the company would be able to complete the Iowa project. Durham said based on the company’s “capital stack,” financing from the Export–Import Bank of the United States and what it has been able to accomplish in Minnesota after “missteps,” she felt confident supporting the project.
“When you see where they are today, and when you see what their business plan is, and when you see the people that are coming in and supporting them, I absolutely have no hesitation to say that they will (do) what they say,” Durham said. “And if they don’t, then we’re going to hold them accountable. But I believe that this project is a good project for the state of Iowa, and I do believe that they have the ability to pull it off.”
But several lawmakers said they were not as confident as Durham in the project’s viability. Bisignano criticized how Republican leaders and the company brought about the legislation, saying it was concerning that many state legislators did not know about the proposal — or the steel mill project in general — a week before the special session. As Trump and many state leaders have touted the project as the “biggest thing to come to state of Iowa,” Bisignano said there should be more time for legislators and the public to review the project and MEGA program changes.
“This should be one of those occasions where — if this is the biggest thing to come to the state of Iowa — that we as a group ought rejoice, with no suspicions, with full knowledge, with defendability when we go back home and we’re asked, ‘why are you giving away a billion and a half of my tax earnings,” Bisignano said. “… I would love to embrace a job creation, of 1,700 jobs with good wages and good benefits that’s going to help a small community that’s been struggling. Who wouldn’t? … Again, we failed. We failed to be transparent with the public, and so they also could rejoice in something like this coming to the state of Iowa.”
Timing of special session, budget impacts questioned
Bisignano also questioned the timing of the special session, which came just shy of a month before the Nov. 3, 2026 general election. Iowa is situated to play a key role in deciding control of Congress with several competitive U.S. House races, in addition to contentious elections for U.S. Senate and Iowa governor. This is a major change from previous recent elections where Republicans saw decisive victories. Heading into the midterms, all members of Iowa’s federal delegation are Republicans, and there are GOP majorities in both chambers of the Iowa Legislature.
There were also questions about the Trump administration’s presentation of the steel mill plan. At the White House announcement, U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick said, “I think this deal is done” when a reporter asked if the project was contingent on approval of state or local tax breaks.
Sen. Janet Petersen, D-Des Moines asked Durham “why are we here and putting more of their taxpayer dollars on the line” if the deal was finalized.
“Senator, I was surprised by that comment as well, because this is not a done deal,” Durham said. “As we said, you have to pass legislation. It still has to go through the final negotiation. So, I don’t know why that that was stated. I can’t speak to that.”
Nordman said he believed the comments made in the Oval Office were “more about the Minnesota mine rather than the plant itself.”
While the measure was approved by both the House and Senate Ways and Means committees, the two chambers had differing views of the bill. The House committee approved the measure with bipartisan support — a 20-5 vote — while the Senate committee only narrowly passed the measure with a 10-8 vote as all Democrats, alongside Dawson and Sen. Jason Schultz, R-Schleswig, voted against the measure.
The majority approval from Senate Ways and Means only came after two Senate Republicans — Sens. Jeff Taylor and Dawn Driscoll — were replaced on the committee by Sens. Tim Kraayenbrink and Dan Zumbach, who voted in favor of the bill. Taylor voted against the the measure on the Senate floor.
When the Iowa Senate debated the measure, Senate Democrats introduced two amendments calling for certain protections for labor unions and organizations to be codified in the legislation. Both proposals failed.
Schultz said during debate he was voting against the legislation, saying, “I’m worried about paying for it, I’m worried about our budget, I am worried about the the situation we’ll find ourselves in in January.” He said the Republican trifecta at the Iowa Legislature chose to the state income tax in previous sessions with the understanding “that the key to tax cuts is controlling spending.” 
“As we go through, and I look back on my years in the legislature, for all of this time, tax credits have been counted against revenue as an expenditure,” Schultz said. “As we authorized additional tax credits, they were against the tax plan, as I see it, and puts us in a difficult situation where we are spending — in advance — revenue.”
Iowa Rep. Dave Jacoby, D-Coralville, said the package amounts to a cost of roughly $3,000 per household.
“What I do want Iowans to know is this: Today is not a ribbon cutting,” Jacoby said. “… We do not have men and women in hard hats and carrying lunch buckets, ready to go to work. This truly is a concept plan right now, a concept plan with many questions. … But sadly, this is a concept that is sorely needed in our great state of Iowa.”
Jacoby said he was voting in support of the bill with the hope that “this plan is real.”
