name: Connecticut Mirror
title: New England not likely to see nuclear power revival any time soon
description: Many leaders across New England are looking to nuclear as a possible solution to the region's energy needs, despite many obstacles.
text:
The long-anticipated renaissance of American nuclear power is unlikely to get its start in New England. 
Lack of demand from data centers, high costs for labor and materials, unseemly battles with neighbors and — perhaps most importantly — uncertain financial options are all pushing developers of new nuclear technologies elsewhere, particularly to the Deep South and Midwest. 
But as leaders across the region face rising demand for electricity and few options for delivering that power on-demand without fossil fuels, many are beginning to turn to nuclear as a possible solution, albeit one that is years or even decades away.
On Wednesday, officials from all six New England states gathered at the University of Massachusetts in Lowell for a summit on the revival of nuclear power in the region. The event was hosted the National Governor’s Association and featured scientists, clean-energy advocates and industry representatives, along with state officials.
The summit was born, in part, out of a public letter signed by the governors off all six states in March. The letter called for greater regional collaboration to keep New England’s remaining nuclear stations operational and to identify potential locations for expansion.
The location was symbolic for two reasons. The Merrimack River, which flows through the center of campus, was itself the power source that fueled the region’s early industrial rise. UMass-Lowell is also home to one of the few operating university research reactors located in the United States. 
“It’s been a while since there was a new energy and a new opportunity like this,” said Emma Cimino, the acting commissioner of the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection who led a small delegation of state officials at the summit. 
“All of our states have had some association with nuclear,” she added. “I think we’re all sort of hoping that leads to a little bit more openness to especially some of these new technologies that may not be these big, hulking, kind of traditional nuclear facilities that maybe conjure fears in people’s minds.”
As recently as 1990, New England was home to eight operating nuclear power plants with a combined output of over 7,000 megawatts of electricity. The cost of maintenance on those aging plants, combined with competition from cheap natural gas, contributed to a succession of closures over the next several decades that whittled the number of plants to two: Millstone Nuclear Power Station in Waterford and Seabrook Station in New Hampshire.
Together, Millstone and Seabrook’s three reactors have an output of nearly 3,300 megawatts, or about one-quarter of all the electricity produced in New England. 
Efforts to restart commercial production of nuclear power elsewhere in the country have been repeatedly stalled by technical problems and cost overruns. Only two new reactors have entered service in the U.S. in the last decade, both at Georgia’s Vogtle Electric Generating Plant. 
The Vogtle project was completed in 2024 at a total cost of over $30 billion and several years behind schedule.
Strategic challenges
Proponents of nuclear power have pinned much of their hopes on the development of a new generation of small modular reactors that can be built from standardized designs to help lower costs. Dozens of companies are vying to complete designs, and early prototypes are under construction in Tennessee and Wyoming.
For similar projects to get underway in New England, however, developers and state officials say they need to figure out a way to address some of the region’s unique political and economic barriers to nuclear power.
Massachusetts, Maine, Rhode Island and Vermont all have restrictions in place that require voter or legislative approval to construct any new nuclear reactor. In Massachusetts and Maine, that approval is also contingent on the federal government finding a long-term solution to the seemingly intractable problem of storing radioactive nuclear waste.
Connecticut lawmakers partially repealed the state’s own nuclear moratorium in 2022, allowing for the development of a new reactor at the Millstone site. Two years later, the legislature went one step further, allowing any city or town to hold a vote on whether to host “advanced” reactor technology.
So far, no municipality has exercised that option.

A dry cask storage facility for spent nuclear fuel on Millstone’s property on October 2, 2025. Credit: Shahrzad Rasekh / CT Mirror

Ed Lyman, the director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists, dismissed the notion that nuclear power offers a realistic solution to New England’s rising energy needs over the next decade.
In addition to old fears about safety that make it difficult to site nuclear facilities within a densely populated region, Lyman said that much of the current interest in nuclear is being driven by startups and unproven technologies that have yet to show they can be cost-competitive with other sources of power.
“It’s the industry’s own problems in strategic planning and … coming up with ways to realistically finance these things instead of a lot of hot air and hoping that if they generate enough steam or generate enough heat about this that investors will come,” Lyman said. “I think we’re still in that that space where it’s mostly being driven by hype and PR, and not by fundamentals.”
Another hurdle in New England’s quest for new nuclear power is the fact that each of the states, with the exception of Vermont, have adopted deregulated energy markets that generally prohibit public utilities — such as Eversource and United Illuminating — from owning their own power plants while also selling power to customers. All of the region’s existing reactors were built by utilities prior to deregulation.
Dominion Energy, the Virginia-based company that owns Millstone, has focused its development of small modular reactors in states with fully regulated electricity markets, which provide a more direct path to recouping upfront costs from ratepayers.
Dominion is also in the process of being sold to NextEra Energy, which would create one of the world’s largest power utilities. NextEra is the owner of Seabrook Station, raising concerns from some New England officials that the sale would give the combined company a monopoly over nuclear power in the region. Earlier this week, Connecticut Attorney General William Tong filed a formal opposition to the merger with federal regulators.
“Right now, we’re just focused on the continued safe operation of Millstone,” Dominion spokesman Ryan Frazier said in a statement Thursday. “Until the merger closes, Dominion and NextEra will continue to operate independently. Beyond that, no decisions have been made. Both companies are proven, high-quality nuclear operators.”
Neil Nissan, a spokesman for NextEra, said in a statement that the company has a “dedicated team” exploring new nuclear technologies, including small modular reactors, but has not announced any plans for expanding Seabrook Station. 
“NextEra Energy continuously evaluates opportunities to meet growing energy demand across the country, including in New England,” Nissan said.
Cimino, of DEEP, said Wednesday that one of her key takeaways from the conference was the need to understand developers’ concerns about New England’s energy markets and develop new financing and risk management structures to help attract investment.
“I think that that’s something that we, individually as states, and collectively need to drill in on as we continue to explore this technology,” Cimino said. 
At the federal level, officials and Congress are continuing to search for locations that could serve as interim storage sites for spent nuclear fuel until a permanent repository can be built. Currently, the spent fuel from nuclear power plants, including decommissioned plants, is stored on location in concrete casks. Earlier this year, Department of Energy signed agreements with six states to further explore the development of spent-fuel recycling or disposal facilities. (One of those states, West Virginia, dropped out of consideration in September).
“With renewed investment and support for nuclear power as a clean energy source, there is an opportunity to reuse spent fuel and significantly shrink the volume of material that requires disposal,” U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney, D-2nd District, said in a statement this week. “There is still much work to be done, but Congressional support is strong to move the spent fuel initiative that has occurred over multiple administrations.”
Raising hands
At Wednesday’s summit, Cimino participated in a panel featuring representatives from the six New England states. Each expressed an interest, to some degree, in either hosting a new nuclear facility or providing financial support to make such an expansion happen.
One area that garned a lot of interest was the town of Waterford, which has hosted Millstone since the 1970s.  
Waterford First Selectman Robert Brule also attended the summit to spread the word that his town is open to new nuclear development. He said he met with three different developers who are seeking potential locations to build advanced reactors. (Brule declined to name the developers, citing the preliminary nature of their discussions).
Part of the reason for his town’s interest, Brule said, is the need to make up for shrinking tax revenues from Millstone, which experienced a decline in property values following deregulation. Prior to deregulation, Millstone made up about 64% of the town’s overall tax revenues, according to The Day of New London. That figure has since fallen to around one-third of revenues.
In order to fill that gap, Brule said, the town had previously explored hosting a large data center that would draw about 300 MW of electricity directly from Millstone. That plan fell apart due to public opposition and difficulty executing a host-fee agreement, and Brule told the Connecticut Mirror on Thursday he had no plans of reviving the data center project as long as he is in office.
“We’d rather produce the energy now than produce a project that sucks up the energy,” Brule said.

Acting DEEP Commissioner Emma Cimino (far left) participates in a panel on the future of nuclear energy with officials from other New England states at the University of Massachusetts, Lowell, on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Credit: JOHN MORITZ/ CT MIRROR

Brule said Waterford benefits from having residents who are familiar with the realities — and potential risks — of living next to a nuclear power plant. Town officials also undergo regular emergency preparedness training and are in frequent contact with Dominion, he said. As for other potential locations in Connecticut, Cimino said that DEEP has been “laying the ground work” to engage with local officials and community members about their interest in nuclear development.
The 2024 law that allowed municipalities to volunteer to host a new reactor also set aside $5 million in state bonds to establish “site readiness” funding program. That fund can be used to help pay for things such as preliminary technical or environmental studies, community engagement initiatives or other expenses deemed necessary by DEEP.
“There’s about 40 criteria that you got to go through” to determine if a particular location is suitable for a nuclear power plant, according to Jeff Semancik, the director of DEEP’s radiation division. Those criteria include having an adequate footprint, ground seismology and access to large quantities of water.
“We kind of know if a site had nuclear before that’s probably pretty good,” Semancik added. “We don’t know in some of these other sites if it would fit, and so I think [the fund is] kind of helping to do it.”
Cimino said that funding should be available for grants sometime within the next six months. 
Another enthusiastic response at Wednesday’s summit came from Vermont, formerly home to the 650 MW Vermont-Yankee Nuclear Power Plant, which closed in 2014. Workers are in the midst of disassembling the old plant, a process that is expected to be completed next year. At that point, Kerrick Johnson, the commissioner of the Vermont Department of Public Service, said the site will become a “ready-made asset” for new nuclear development, with existing access to transmission lines, rail networks and community that is familiar with living next to a reactor.
“The community agrees, we and our department agree, the state, our governor [Phil Scott] agrees, and the region, initially, agrees,” Johnson said. “The collaborative role we can serve — as Vermont has traditionally served — is to go first.” 
Johnson added that he hopes officials in surrounding states are driven by the urgency to tackle region-wide challenges posed by climate change, electrification and rising power costs.
“You start now, you’re talking about 2032, 2035,” before anything is finished, he said. “So you’ve got to start now.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Overhaul of Head Start could endanger CT children, advocates say
description: Changes would allow bigger classes, no longer require degrees for many staff and require programs to be taught in English, among other things.
text:
Advocates and legislators condemned the proposed overhaul of a federal early childhood program — changes they said would endanger programming that serves thousands of Connecticut children.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in August announced sweeping changes to Head Start, a federal program that serves low-income children up to age 5. According to a recent report by the Connecticut Office of Early Childhood, 4,847 children and pregnant women participated in 34 federally funded Head Start programs in the state during the 2024-2025 school year. 
The proposed rule would allow for larger class sizes, no longer require degrees for many staff, loosen federal requirements for serving children with disabilities and require education programs to be taught in English. If the changes are approved, Head Start would defer to state and local childcare standards, which some researchers have found to be less stringent than the program’s longtime requirements.
HHS also plans to reduce the cap on administrative overhead from 15% to 5% of total program costs. According to an August press release, the agency estimates the changes could save $2.2 billion and support as many as 236,000 additional Head Start slots nationwide.
“This is really a multipronged attack at all of the things that make Head Start what it is,” Merrill Gay, executive director of Connecticut Early Childhood Alliance, said of the proposed changes.
In an emailed statement, an HHS spokesperson said the changes would bolster Head Start by “expanding access for eligible children, reducing unnecessary federal bureaucracy and empowering local providers.”
The spokesperson stressed that the agency will still require Head Start programs to provide support for mental and physical health, family and disability services and school readiness preparation, as is mandated by federal law. 
“What changes is that programs will have more latitude in how they meet these requirements, based on the needs of their specific community, rather than a one-size-fits-all federal directive,” the spokesperson added.
But Gay and Eva Bermúdez Zimmerman, executive director of Child Care for CT, argued that eliminating Head Start’s longtime requirements would reduce the quality of care participants receive.
“If anybody believes that this is about reducing burdensome bureaucratic regulations, that’s like saying, ‘we’re going to make the food system safer by firing inspectors,’” Gay said.
The proposed changes to Head Start come a year after Connecticut launched a state-funded childcare program, Early Start CT. Starting in July 2027, the program aims to provide free childcare to eligible families earning up to $100,000 each year and cap the childcare contribution at 7% of household income for eligible families earning more than $100,000.
“We’re in the beginning of blossoming changes to child care,” Bermúdez Zimmerman said. “If in fact the federal government starts chipping away at the things that we thought were fundamental, that we were depending on to build on, it’s not a great reality.”
Head Start’s proposed rule is accepting feedback from the public until Oct. 6. 
According to Bermúdez Zimmerman, Child Care for CT has sent out email and social media blasts and held a community meeting on Monday urging people to submit public comments condemning the changes. The organization has created a toolkit that breaks down the proposed changes to Head Start and explains how to draft a public comment.
Child Care for CT also sent an email blast on Monday to each member of Connecticut’s state legislature. The organization’s goal is to get at least 50% of state legislators to submit public comments criticizing the changes, Bermúdez Zimmerman said.
Senate President Pro Tem Martin Looney and Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff released a joint statement Thursday morning lambasting the proposed changes and urging state Republicans to join their demand for the rule’s withdrawal. 
“The Trump regime wants to strip away more than 90% of the standards that make Head Start work, from limits on class size to the requirement that young children be supervised at all times,” the Democratic senators said in the statement. “This is inhumane, and it’s how you kill a program without having the courage to vote on it.”
But Senate Minority Leader Stephen Harding, R-Brookfield, voiced support for the proposed changes in an emailed statement. 
“To get kids ready for school, it makes sense to simplify complex, outdated federal rules and give states more flexibility in decision-making,” he said. “Let states like Connecticut debate and craft their own common sense rules and reforms to better serve children.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: National Dems expand US House battlefield, targeting Knott in NC-13
description: Cook Political Report rates the race as “solid Republican.”
text:
U.S. Rep. Brad Knott (Photo: House.gov)National Democrats say they’re expanding their attack map, with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee adding North Carolina’s 13th Congressional District to its “Districts in Play” program on Friday. 
In NC-13, Democrat Paul Barringer is challenging freshman U.S. Rep. Brad Knott, who defeated Democrat Frank Pierce by 17 points in 2024. Incumbent Democrat Wiley Nickel chose not to seek reelection after state Republicans redrew the district to heavily favor the GOP. 
Cook Political Report rates the race as “solid Republican.”
According to the DCCC, the “Districts in Play” program focuses on competitive seats held by vulnerable Republicans across the country as Democrats seek to regain a majority in the House. 
National Democrats are concentrating on rising costs under GOP leadership. They’re highlighting Knott’s voting record, including his support for President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” Act, last year’s tax cuts and spending cuts package.
“Knott’s disastrous record, highlighted by his votes to kick thousands of North Carolinians off their health insurance, give tax breaks to billionaires, and support Trump’s cost-hiking agenda, has made life unaffordable for working families,” DCCC chair Suzan DelBene said in a statement. “The voters in his district know he’s been a failure and are ready to send him packing in November.”
“We are obviously happy and excited to have been added to the list,” Barringer campaign manager CJ Robinson told NC Newsline. “It shows what we’ve known for a while – that there is real movement in this district, and that there is a real possibility of flipping the seat.”
NC-11 candidates offer competing ‘mountain values’ in unique ads

The DCCC added seven other districts to the program on Friday, each of which the Cook Political Report has rated as “likely” or “solid” Republican. That means the DCCC currently considers 66 House districts “in play,” double the number to receive the designation in 2024. 
Earlier targets announced this election cycle include U.S. Rep. Greg Murphy in NC-03 and National Republican Congressional Committee Chair Richard Hudson in NC-09. 
Unlike the DCCC’s “Red to Blue” program, “Districts in Play” doesn’t provide financial support for candidates, but Barrington will receive a designated page on the DCCC website linking to a donation site. 
Democrat Jamie Ager is in the DCCC’s “Red to Blue” program. He’s facing GOP state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom in NC-11, which Cook Political Report rates as “toss up.”
At the moment, Republicans hold a 218-212 majority in the House, with four vacancies. One independent, U.S. Rep. Kevin Kiley of California, caucuses with the GOP. 
Republicans say they’re not worried about the 13th. Trump won the district by double digits in the past two presidential elections. 
“Democrats are once again foolishly wasting time and money trying to compete in solidly Republican districts where they have zero chance of winning,” NRCC spokesperson Reilly Richardson told NC Newsline. “While DC Democrats chase butterflies and rainbows in fantasyland, Republicans are focused on winning the fight on the ground and over the airwaves in the real battleground districts nationwide.”
But Knott could be hurt by the tough political climate for Republicans. Trump’s approval rating in the Tar Heel State has hovered around the mid-thirties, and GOP candidate Michael Whatley continues to trail Democrat Roy Cooper by a substantial margin in recent polls for North Carolina’s open U.S. Senate seat. 
The Knott campaign did not respond to requests for comment.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming lawmakers could pursue some of the nation’s strictest limits on Flock-like cameras
description:
Draft legislation would severely restrict the technology's use in the Equality State.
The post Wyoming lawmakers could pursue some of the nation’s strictest limits on Flock-like cameras appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
LARAMIE—Amid rising concerns about Flock-style cameras in Wyoming, a state legislative panel this week briefly discussed a draft bill that would create some of the strictest automatic license plate reader regulations in the country.
The Select Committee on Blockchain, Financial Technology and Digital Innovation Technology took no action when the draft bill came up for discussion Tuesday afternoon. The bill would severely limit the use of ALPR cameras while creating an enforcement mechanism for cases of abuse. The measure, which is preliminary and has notes for further research, will likely be updated and changed before the next legislative session begins on Jan. 12.
“This bill is drafted to be consistent with the strongest legislation in the country,” Select Committee Co-Chair Senator Chris Rothfuss, D-Laramie, said during the public meeting. The measure incorporates the best practices from around the country, intended to create strong information protections. Lawmakers sought to give law enforcement access during emergency situations while preventing “casual access,” Rothfuss said.
“The take I kind of get is that the public really doesn’t like these,” Rothfuss said.
“This is not a critique on our law enforcement, and it’s not an accusation on the practices of our law enforcement but a response to public outcry,” Select Committee Co-Chair Rep. Daniel Singh, R-Cheyenne, said before public comment. 
Automatic license plate readers use artificial intelligence to monitor and photograph passing vehicles. That information is usually uploaded to a central system that participating law enforcement agencies can search — though some communities opt out of participating in national databases.

A screenshot shared by the Cheyenne Police Department shows an example of an image taken by a Flock camera of a passing department vehicle, highlighting the vehicle’s license plate. (Cheyenne Police Department)

The technology, in some cases, has moved faster than legislation, Singh, who pursued similar legislation during this year’s session, said in a separate interview.
“Our (Cheyenne) police department and city officials embraced the technology without really consulting the public or getting their input,” Singh said. “Because of that, now we’re facing the repercussions of that, and so we wanted to have the legislature address it, because there are some serious implications around privacy … your Fourth Amendment rights don’t change just because technology changes.” 
Allison Moore, deputy director of the Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation’s Criminal Justice Information Services told lawmakers about the state’s process when it comes to entering information into the National Crime Information Center database. When an officer takes a report — a stolen car, for example — that information is entered into NCIC. A hot list, or the list an ALPR checks as cars pass by, is compiled by the private vendor, whether it be Motorola, Axon, Flock or others using information entered into NCIC.
The information from that federal database is called a “hot file,” which in turn, comprises the hot list. The information that is entered into NCIC is tightly regulated; a missing child report must be entered into NCIC within two hours, Moore said. DCI regulates information but does not operate any of its own Flock-style cameras, she told lawmakers. 
The discussion largely focused on the language of the bill, clarifying certain points to not be overly prohibitive. Wyoming Highway Patrol Lt. Kyle McKay asked for the language to be clarified, as the state uses license plate readers on commercial vehicles during the routine course of inspection. He worried the language was broad enough to ban the state’s license plate readers, which have been in use for some time, as opposed to Flock-style cameras.
Notably, the draft bill would establish a three-minute retention period for data. When an ALPR camera records a license plate, the system would hold on to it for three minutes while the system checks it against the hotlist. After that, it would be permanently deleted. 
Part of the reason for the short retention period is while it’s common in ALPR contracts for law enforcement agencies to own the data, the vendor holds it and compiles the list. Agency policies on data retention currently vary For example, Jackson has a 90-day retention period, while Glenrock’s is 30 days.
“Privacy laws are inconvenient. Surveillance is handy. Law enforcement (is) always easier if we know where everyone was for the last year at all times, and it’s true, but it still creeps people out for good reason.”Sen. Chris Rothfuss, D-Laramie
Wyoming Association of Sheriffs and Police Chiefs Executive Director Allen Thompson suggested the three-minute limit could hinder law enforcement investigations. Thompson said the association supports regulation of these systems, and that “nobody hates a bad cop more than a good cop.”
But Rothfuss said the public wants systems in place to protect their privacy.
“Privacy laws are inconvenient,” Rothfuss said. “Surveillance is handy. Law enforcement (is) always easier if we know where everyone was for the last year at all times, and it’s true, but it still creeps people out for good reason.”
The draft bill effectively bans ALPRs except in certain narrow instances. The “real-time” hot list matches with the three-minute deletion window, as well as eliminating the ability to search a stored database of ALPR captures. Federal or out-of-state sharing would be banned unless it’s superseded by federal law or a Wyoming court order, and would require the government to obtain a warrant for plate data held by private entities. Flock, Motorola or Axon would be prohibited from owning data collected in Wyoming. The draft bill would also include language to give the Wyoming attorney general the ability to investigate and audit these systems for abuse.
Cato Institute’s Matthew Cavedon, the final speaker, applauded the committee for regulating the retention period. He also spoke about other states’ regulations of similar systems.
Vermont will be the first state to outright ban ALPR systems come July 1, Florida has banned the systems on state highways, while Texas has halted all funding and installation of the systems across the state.
While the bill would be one of the most strict in the U.S., critics have argued that it won’t be enough.
During the U.S. Senate Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism regarding ALPR usage last week, ACLU Senior Policy Counsel Chad Marlow called for an outright ban of the technology, which he characterized as an “Orwellian nightmare.”
“The time has come for Congress to ban any law enforcement entity who receives federal funding from using ALPRs,” Marlow said in his statement to the subcommittee. “And this prohibition should be without exceptions.”
The post Wyoming lawmakers could pursue some of the nation’s strictest limits on Flock-like cameras appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Ever wonder what happens to roadkill? We asked the Oklahoma Department of Transportation
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — From dead deer to dogs, it’s not uncommon to drive by the remains of animals hit by vehicles driving on Oklahoma roadways and interstates. Last year, the Oklahoma Department of Transportation, whose crews are responsible for keeping state highways and interstates clear of debris, spent $5 million alone cleaning up litter, which […]
text:
A mule deer is pictured. The number of deer hit by vehicles increases in the fall. (Photo by Ed Godfrey/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — From dead deer to dogs, it’s not uncommon to drive by the remains of animals hit by vehicles driving on Oklahoma roadways and interstates.
Last year, the Oklahoma Department of Transportation, whose crews are responsible for keeping state highways and interstates clear of debris, spent $5 million alone cleaning up litter, which includes roadkill. The agency employs about 865 heavy equipment operators to remove animal carcasses, said Emily Long, an ODOT spokesperson.  
Logan County ODOT Superintendent Bradley Eads said crews prioritize removing roadkill because it’s dangerous for drivers, is a distraction and an eyesore.
Most animals are killed by motorists driving on the highways, and reports are phoned in by residents or Oklahoma Highway Patrol troopers, Eads said. 
State troopers will remove the animal debris off the road if they can, but when they can’t, state transportation workers try to respond within 30 minutes, he said.
There is a need for fast removal so that additional animals don’t get hit while scavenging the carcasses, Eads said.
Workers generally work in teams of two, using their hands to drag the roadkill off the road and out of sight. They wear personal protective equipment like sanitary gloves and safety vests, Eads said.
When maintaining the grass near the highways, motorists might notice there is a 15-foot strip of mowed grass that is kept clear at all times for vehicles that need to pull off the highway, but workers also leave a five-foot strip of unmowed grass in the middle, Eads said. That’s where crews move roadkill to decompose, hidden from the passing cars. 
However, Eads said sometimes removal crews are not always necessary because  scavengers have gotten to the roadkill before they do. 
“You would be surprised by how fast they’re gone, they’re usually gone by overnight,” he said.
He said when a lane needs to be closed in Logan County to remove a large animal, the Highway Patrol or the Logan County Sheriff’s Office will help direct traffic. If law enforcement is unable to assist, ODOT does its own traffic control.
ODOT removes roadkill off the highways for the safety of travelers, said Tim Hardcastle, the transportation maintenance manager for District Three, which includes Oklahoma and Canadian counties. 
Hardcastle said that highways near populated areas have less roadkill than rural areas due to animals’ habitats being farther away from the roads.
It is more dangerous to remove animal carcasses in high traffic areas, which also have more driving lanes.
Removal crews have to plan in advance for the more dangerous areas, like an inside shoulder where there is less space for ODOT workers to park and get out of their vehicles, he said. 
In high-traffic areas, such as Interstate 44 near Oklahoma City, the state Department of Transportation may tap its contractors to help, said Travis Yarbrough, a maintenance coordinator for ODOT who removes roadkill from urban areas of the highways.
Most of the time, “they are pretty much flung off the lanes,” Yarbrough said of the impact. 
He said increases in the number of animals struck aligns with the mating seasons. For example, more deer are hit in November during the autumn mating season.
Kelly Adams, a spokesperson and education supervisor for the Oklahoma Department of Wildlife Conservation, says there is no need to contact a game warden when a motorist hits and kills a deer.
But if someone wants to take the carcass home they need to get permission from the county’s game warden, Adams said.
When dogs are hit, the rural and urban areas handle them differently.
In rural areas, workers have limited options to contact the owners. They can check the collar and go to nearby houses to ask if they own the animal or know the person who does, Eads said.
In urban areas, the workers have more tools at their disposal; they can ask animal control to check if the dog has a microchip that can inform them who the owner is.
Editor’s note: This story was produced through a reporting partnership between Oklahoma Voice and the University of Central Oklahoma’s journalism program.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Amid bleak financial forecast, Brown Health announces buyouts, executive layoffs
description: The state’s largest hospital operator is offering buyouts to 200 non-clinical supervisors and laying off 10 executives amid financial pressures. Brown University Health announced a series of cost-cutting measures on Thursday, the first day of its new fiscal year. Like healthcare providers nationwide, the hospital conglomerate is struggling against rising cos[...]
text:
Rhode Island Hospital, the largest hospital in the state, is also a founding and principal teaching hospital of Brown University Health and The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)The state’s largest hospital operator is offering buyouts to 200 non-clinical supervisors and laying off 10 executives amid financial pressures.
Brown University Health announced a series of cost-cutting measures on Thursday, the first day of its new fiscal year. Like healthcare providers nationwide, the hospital conglomerate is struggling against rising costs, a function of market pressures and federal budget cuts under H.R. 1.
“Healthcare organizations across the country continue to face significant financial pressures, and Brown Health is no exception,” John Fernandez, president and CEO of Brown University Health, said in a statement. “Rising pharmaceutical, labor and supply costs, combined with increasing levels of uncompensated care, insurer denials and bad debt, are creating unprecedented challenges. The actions we’re taking will help strengthen our financial foundation while protecting access to care and supporting future growth.” 
Brown Health has been sounding the alarm on its lopsided ledger for more than a year, suggesting in July 2025 that it might close the Newport Hospital birthing center, among other program and service cuts. It later committed to keeping the 10-unit labor and delivery center open amid pressure from local and state officials and advocates, and a $1.6 million earmark in the state’s fiscal 2027 budget.
But an increase in uncompensated care, the result of new federal policies restricting Medicaid eligibility and ending discounts for people who purchase their own insurance through state health exchanges, have started to take hold. 
Brown Health reported $90.5 million in costs associated with charity care, debt and insurance denials in the three-month period ending June 30, equal to more than 8% of the company’s net revenue. The company remained in the black, with a $23.4 million operating profit for that quarter — the most recent financial data available
But projections for fiscal 2027 look bleak. Brown Health said it expects to spend $346 million on charity care, insurance denials and debt in the new fiscal year — $71 million more than it spent in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30 — due to federal policy changes.
The healthcare operator projects a $64 million deficit for this fiscal year.
That’s after a series of “efficiency measures,” including an executive restructuring completed in September that included consolidating or eliminating 10 jobs, as first reported by WPRI-TV 12. 
Voluntary buyouts were offered for up to 200 supervisors, managers and directors, who were eligible if they are 60 or older and have been with the company for five years as of Sept. 30. And, starting Jan. 1, Brown Health’s employee health plan won’t cover GLP-1 drugs prescribed solely for weight loss, though insurance coverage will continue for employees who use the medication to treat diabetes.
Information on how many employees use GLP-1s for weight loss was not immediately available.
The Newport Hospital birthing center was not named as a program at risk of closing, nor were any other services at The Miriam, Rhode Island Hospital, and Bradley. 
Jessica Wharton, a Brown Health spokesperson, confirmed in an email Friday that the birthing center will remain open, with fundraising efforts underway to close the $4.6 million gap needed to sustain the labor and delivery program. There are no plans to close or reduce other clinical programs right now, Wharton said.
Capital projects at The Miriam and Rhode Island hospitals, already underway, are expected to continue in fiscal 2027, with $210 million budgeted for facility upgrades, Brown Health said. There will also be a merit increase for employees in January, and ongoing investments in technology and equipment upgrades.
“Building a financially sustainable organization is essential to our ability to serve patients, support our workforce and invest in the future,” Fernandez said. “These decisions position Brown Health to continue delivering high-quality care and meet the evolving needs of the communities we serve.” 
While Brown Health’s bottom line has dipped into the red on and off since the pandemic, its Rhode Island hospitals remain profitable, with a $97.4 million combined revenue in the first nine months of fiscal 2026. By contrast, its Massachusetts hospitals, purchased from bankrupt former owner Steward Health Care in 2024, have underperformed. Staffing shortages and low patient volume led to operating losses at St. Anne’s Hospital in Fall River, Morton Hospital in Taunton, and associated ambulatory centers. 
Results of the full fiscal 2026 financial performance, including breakdowns by hospitals are expected to be published by the end of the month. 
Doctors picket outside Rhode Island Hospital
On Friday, unionized resident physicians staged a picket and rally outside Rhode Island Hospital . The 700-member labor group, the first unionized doctors in Rhode Island, have been locked in contract negotiations with Brown Health for almost a year.
Melissa Uribe, a spokesperson for the Committee of Interns and Service Employees International Union, said salary and benefits are the major points of contention. However, doctors also want Brown Health to establish policies limiting access for federal immigration agents at the Providence hospital, and ensuring employees who need to miss work for mandatory immigration visa appointments don’t lose their jobs.
Dr. Samantha Palacios, a senior resident physician in the hospital emergency room, acknowledged the financial challenges her employer is facing, but insisted residents and interns should not sacrifice their demands for wage increases.
“It doesn’t change what our bottom line is,” Palacios, 30, said in a phone interview after the picket. “We are aware there are issues across all of the United States when it comes to funding things. We shouldn’t be what gets cut.”
A Nevada native with more than $400,000 in student loan debt, Palacios said she has not had a raise, even for cost-of-living, in her two years working for Brown Health.
“Our ability to live a life where we can survive can’t be what’s on the chopping block at the end of the day,’ she said.
Kelly Brennan, a Brown Health spokesperson, did not comment on the picket, but said there has been “substantial progress” in the negotiations with union doctors, including 90 tentative agreements.
“We remain focused on reaching a fair, sustainable agreement that recognizes the contributions of our interns and residents while ensuring we can uphold our commitments to high-quality patient care, our workforce, and the communities we serve,” Brennan said in a statement.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico group seeks to ban all corporate, ‘dark’ money spending on politics
description: A new coalition concerned about money’s growing influence on New Mexico politics is urging state lawmakers to consider legislation this January that would ban corporations from political spending.
text:
A new group, Money Out of Politics New Mexico, formed Oct. 1, 2026, to push the New Mexico Legislature to take up a measure that would prohibit corporations from spending money on political campaigns. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)A new coalition concerned about money’s growing influence on New Mexico politics is urging state lawmakers to consider legislation this January that would ban corporations from political spending. 
The newly formed group, Money Out of Politics New Mexico, announced Thursday that it was launching a campaign modeled after similar efforts in Montana and Hawaii. Chair Natalie Wright Curley told Source NM that eliminating corporate and “dark” money from politics is a key step in returning democracy to the hands of regular people instead of the wealthy. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The “Corporate Money Out of Politics Act” would revoke corporations’ power to donate to political campaigns or ballot measures. 
Wright, a patent attorney, argues that states have constitutional authority under the 10th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution — which grants all powers to states that are not explicitly granted to the federal government — gives the Legislature authority to regulate state-issued corporate charters. That includes revoking corporate ability to spend money directly on campaigns or political action committees. 
The legislation aims to bypass the 2010 Citizens United ruling from the U.S. Supreme Court, which held that corporations have a First Amendment right to spend unlimited funds on campaigns. 
In May, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green signed Act 11, which established new restrictions on political spending activities by corporations and other “artificial persons” and limited the powers granted to those entities.
Groups including the Hawaii Chamber of Commerce have already challenged the law in court on First Amendment grounds, citing the Citizens United ruling.
Montana voters this November will also have a chance to pass a similar law through a ballot initiative known as the Montana Plan. 
According to Wright’s group, corporations and businesses have spent at least $3.7 million on various political campaigns so far in 2026. The group, citing news reports and Secretary of State’s Office filings, has totaled at least $2.6 million in “dark or otherwise opaque” spending this year, as well.
So-called “dark” money refers to donations from corporations or others funneled through Super PACs, a practice that leaves the public unable to determine donors’ identities. 
New ‘dark money’ group backs array of New Mexico House Democratic candidates

Wright said her group has already received tentative interest from lawmakers interested in carrying the bill, though the coalition is still securing a sponsor for the 60-day session beginning Jan. 19. 
The bill is necessary to begin to undo the damage of unfettered corporate spending in politics over the last 16 years, she said. 
“After Citizens United came out in 2010, I think it totally changed how our democracy operated,” she said. “It just really concerns me, how that’s continued to grow and be a problem, and how it affects the voices of everyday Americans.”
The group’s proposal follows a suite of legislative ethics reform proposals unveiled earlier this week by the think tank Think New Mexico, including several aimed at closing loopholes around “dark” money in state politics.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi households could pay more for energy because of federal policy changes
description: FILE - A natural gas meter operates Jan. 22, 2025, in Portland, Ore. (AP Photo/Jenny Kane, File)
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Households in the contiguous United States will pay thousands of dollars more for energy through 2040 because of federal policy changes since President Donald Trump returned to office such as canceling new clean energy projects, according to modeling released Friday by a nonpartisan think tank.
The Energy Innovation analysis found that households will pay an average of $6,500 more for energy, cumulatively through 2040. In five states, households will pay roughly $9,000 more: Oregon, Mississippi, South Dakota, Virginia and Wyoming.
The California-based think tank said there will be more demand for natural gas for electricity because the administration is canceling new wind, solar and hydrogen projects and there will be more gasoline demand for transportation because Trump and Congress are revoking policies that incentivized efficient and lower-emissions vehicles. Higher demand increases prices.
Energy prices are elevated in many countries. The International Energy Agency said after Russia invaded Ukraine, record prices were observed between 2022 and 2024 in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Japan and Korea. In many countries, the rise has outpaced income growth and inflation since 2019, including the European Union and the United States.
In some areas of the U.S., demand from data centers is being blamed. The Iran war has sent oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, too. The Energy Information Administration expects residential U.S. customers to pay about 18.6 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2027, compared to 17.3 cents in 2025 and 18.2 cents in 2026.
FILE – Cars drive through an intersection along the Las Vegas Strip, May 1, 2026, in Las Vegas. (AP Photo/John Locher, File)
The independent research firm Rhodium Group has also examined the issue, saying in April the U.S. has entered a new period of rising electricity prices. It cited increasing price volatility in natural gas, which is increasingly used to generate power; needed grid improvements; inflation; storm recovery and wildfire mitigation; and shifting policies.
Absent significant policy action, electricity prices likely will continue their significant rise over the next five years, the firm said.
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said Wednesday that lowering electricity prices remains a top priority and Trump is unleashing reliable energy like coal and natural gas to reverse the damage Democrats did to the grid by increasing clean energy. A 2025 Department of Energy report, mandated by Trump, warned of increasing blackouts if the U.S. continued closing coal and natural gas plants.
“Joe Biden created a grid crisis; President Trump is fixing it,” Rogers wrote in an email. “If the Democrats had their way, these costly and unreliable renewable energy projects would still be failing our grid and our communities.”
The Republican president prioritizes fossil fuels to produce electricity, unlike Biden, who saw clean energy as a climate solution. The conservative Institute for Energy Research said in December that blue states have high rates because they have embraced aggressive renewable mandates, 100% carbon-free targets, premature coal and nuclear retirements and restrictions on natural gas infrastructure. It said high electricity prices are not an inevitability; they are a choice.
Analysis examined impact on states solely from federal policy changes
It focused on the sweeping package of tax breaks that slashed funding for clean energy tax credits, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump signed; environmental rollbacks, including clean air and power plant rules and the revocation of a scientific finding that underpinned the U.S. fight against climate change; the loosening of fuel economy standards and blocking of California’s novel rule banning the sale of new gas-powered cars by 2035; and federal actions to stop wind, solar and hydrogen projects.
FILE – Cars drive through an intersection along the Las Vegas Strip, May 1, 2026, in Las Vegas. (AP Photo/John Locher, File)
These changes will result in annual household energy costs rising in every state in the contiguous U.S., plus job losses in 47 of 48 states and losses to the gross domestic product in 46 states, Energy Innovation said. It’s projecting 37,000 additional premature deaths from air pollution, $72 billion in additional healthcare costs and more than 9 billion tons of additional carbon pollution because of the environmental rollbacks. The analysis did not include Alaska or Hawaii because key federal data is not available for those two states, said Robbie Orvis, senior director for modeling and analysis.
“Across pretty much every state, things are worse. The outlook now is worse for states and the affordability crisis will be worse because of the combined set of policies,” Orvis said.
Climate Justice Alliance legislative director Mar Zepeda said her Washington, D.C., electric bill increased $200 in the past month. Zepeda blames electricity demands from data centers, and said federal “affordability” policies only exacerbate this.
“They may call it affordability, but affordable for whom and at what cost? Not for regular people,” Zepeda said in an email.
White House says the think tank is partisan
Rogers said it is “irresponsible” to classify Energy Innovation as nonpartisan because its employees have donated to Democrats and worked with Democrats on climate policy.
Spokesman Silvio Marcacci said Energy Innovation works with policymakers who want to cut emissions and lower bills, regardless of party. He said multiple Republican-led states have used their tool designed to model policies affecting energy use and emissions. Much of their data comes from government sources, including the EIA.
Rogers also said states led by Democrats that have embraced aggressive renewable mandates see higher energy costs, notably California and New York. She said this proves Republican policies are working.
However, in the Energy Innovation analysis, three of the five states facing the highest costs have Republican governors. Its research has found that states with high levels of wind and solar generation, including Republican-led Iowa and Oklahoma, have experienced the lowest rate increases.
The average price residential customers pay for electricity increased during Biden’s term and has continued to rise under Trump, according to EIA data.
Oregon households’ annual energy spending slated to increase the most
The modeling projects federal policy changes will increase annual energy spending in Oregon by $840 per household in 2035 and $1,200 per household in 2040, with a cumulative $9,300 increase from 2026 to 2040 — the highest of any state.
The Oregon Citizens’ Utility Board advocates for residential utility customers. Executive Director Bob Jenks called those numbers “frightening” because Oregon already has an energy affordability problem. He cited steep rate increases as utilities make upgrades and data centers use more power.
As costs rise, Jenks expects utilities to disconnect more customers who can’t afford their bills.
Jenks said wind and solar are essential for affordable electricity, and he wants the federal government to partner with states to develop the energy they need.
“We’re trying to optimize among the resource options we have, and they’re trying to take things away and raise the costs,” he said.

text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, front, is briefed on heavy rain and severe flooding in northern Lancaster County that occurred the night before on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Office of Gov. Jim Pillen)LINCOLN — Southeast Nebraska is under a state of emergency following heavy rain and severe flooding as state officials assess damage to potentially apply for federal support.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen declared the emergency Thursday afternoon while surveying affected areas in northern Lancaster County, as first reported by 10/11 News, which was reporting on scene before the governor arrived. The record-setting rainfall Wednesday resulted in flooded roadways and multiple rescues of stranded motorists.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signs a disaster declaration following heavy rain and severe flooding in northern Lancaster County that occurred the night before on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Office of Gov. Jim Pillen)
Lancaster County Engineer Pam Dingman told KETV Newswatch 7 that the storm could have lasting effects on county infrastructure, such as bridges and the county pipe culvert system.
“Please continue to exercise extreme caution around flooded areas and damaged infrastructure, and join me in expressing gratitude for the first responders and road crews who have worked around the clock responding to this flooding and keeping Nebraskans safe,” Pillen said in a Thursday social media post.
A spokesperson for the governor said Friday that damage assessments are still occurring, so the state will identify specifically affected counties later.
The declaration frees up state resources for recovery and requires state and federal agencies to support the state’s adjutant general, who leads the Nebraska Emergency Management Agency.
NEMA and the Nebraska National Guard, plus representatives for Lancaster County and the Lower Platte South Natural Resource District, joined Pillen in surveying the damage.
NEMA is working with the Federal Emergency Management Agency, Small Business Administration and Natural Resources Conservation Service, Pillen’s office said Friday, to sling resources as damage assessments are completed. The governor’s office said that work will help determine if and what level of assistance will be available for recovery.
A disaster declaration for southeast Nebraska following heavy rain and severe flooding Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Office of Gov. Jim Pillen)
